s: “They hated me for no reason.”—John 15:25

Most people agree that the words our Savior quotes here come from Psalm 35:19. There David is speaking about himself first, but he is also speaking ahead of time about the Savior. He says, “Don’t let my enemies celebrate over me. Don’t let those who hate me for no reason wink at each other in scorn.”

Our Savior says those words apply to him. So he is really telling us that many of the Psalms are Messianic—they are about the Messiah. That means Dr. Hawker was not wrong when he said he believed the Psalms were about the Savior, even if he may have pushed that truth too far.
So when we read the Psalms, it is a good plan to keep seeing them as being not so much about David, but about the one David pictured ahead of time: Jesus Christ, David’s Lord.
No one was ever more lovely than the Savior. It would seem almost impossible not to love him.
At first glance, it would certainly seem much harder to hate him than to love him.
And yet, as lovable as he was—in fact, “completely lovely”—no one ever met hatred so early. No one ever suffered such constant persecution as he did.

As soon as he is born into the world, King Herod’s sword is ready to kill him. The innocent babies of Bethlehem were horribly murdered. That gave a sad early taste of what Christ would suffer, and of the hatred people would pour out on the head of the one who was marked out to suffer.
From his first moment until the cross—except for a short quiet time while he was a child—it seemed as if the whole world had teamed up against him. Everyone seemed to be trying to destroy him.

That hatred showed itself in different ways. Sometimes it was open action. Once they took him to the edge of a hill and wanted to throw him off. Another time they picked up stones to stone him, because he said that Abraham had longed to see his day, and did see it, and was glad.

At other times the hatred came out in lies, like this: “He is a drunk who loves his wine, a friend of tax collectors and sinners.” Or it came out in looks of contempt, as when they eyed him with suspicion because he ate with tax collectors and sinners and sat down to eat without washing his hands.
At other times the hatred stayed completely in their thoughts. They said to themselves, “This man is insulting God,” because he said, “Your sins are forgiven.”

But almost all the time there was hatred toward Christ. Once they took hold of him and wanted to make him king. A shallow wave of popular cheering would have carried him onto a shaky throne. But even then a hidden hatred was there. It was kept down only by the loaves and fishes. All it needed was for the priests to offer the same amount of loaves and fishes, and it would turn into the cry, “Crucify him, crucify him!” instead of the shout, “Hosanna! Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord.”
People from every level of society hated him.
Most people meet with some opposition. But often it comes from just one group, and there are other groups who respect them.
A crowd-pleasing leader whom the poor admire has to expect the rich to look down on him. And the one who works for the upper class will, of course, be scorned by ordinary people.

But here was a man who walked among the people and loved them. He spoke to rich and poor as if they were on the same level in his blessed eyes—and in fact they are. Yet every group joined together in hating him. The priests shouted him down because he ruined their teachings. The nobles wanted to kill him because he talked about being a king. And then there were the poor. They admired how well he spoke, and often they would have bowed down and worshiped him because of the amazing things he did. Yet even they were led by men who should have guided them better, and for reasons only they know, they plotted to kill him. They finished their guilt by nailing him to the cross. Then they shook their heads at him and told him that if he could build a temple in three days, he should save himself and come down from the cross.
Christ was the one people hated, lied about and mocked. He was “despised and rejected by people, a man of sorrows who knew grief well.”

This morning we will try to do three things. First, we will show that the Savior was right to say he was hated for no reason. Second, we will think about the sin of people—that they hated him for no reason. Third, we will give Christ’s own people a lesson or two that they can learn from the fact that their Savior was hated for no reason.
I. So first, dear friends, let us SHOW THAT WHAT THE SAVIOR SAID IS TRUE: “They hated me for no reason.”
Here is our point. If we leave aside the fact that people are sinful and Christ is pure, there is certainly no reason at all to be found for why the world should have hated him.
First, let us look at Christ as a person.
When he lived in this world as a man, was there anything about him that would naturally make anyone hate him?
Notice that almost everything that makes people hate each other was missing in him.
To begin with, Christ had no high rank that would make people jealous.

Everyone knows this: however good a man is, if riches or a title raise him even a little above other people, then people may respect him one by one, but the crowd often speaks against him. They do it not so much because of who he is, but because of his rank and his title.

It seems natural for people in a crowd to look down on nobles. Each person on his own thinks it is a wonderful thing to know a lord. But put people together, and they will look down on lords and bishops and speak very lightly of rulers and people in power.

But Christ had none of the outward signs of rank. He had no fancy carriage, no long official sleeves, nothing that lifted him above others. When he went out, no heralds walked with him, and there was no grand show to honor him.
In fact, you would think the way Christ looked would naturally have made people feel sorry for him.
Instead of being raised above people, in a way he seemed to be below them. Foxes had holes and birds had nests, but the Son of Man had no place to lay his head.

Many a man who is against the upper classes has shouted angrily at the archbishop as he went past Lambeth Palace. But would he curse him or look down on him if he were told that the archbishop had no place to lay his head, and simply worked hard for the sake of the truth, with no reward?

So the jealousy that rank and position naturally stir up could not have worked against Christ. There was nothing about his clothes to draw attention. They were the clothes of a country worker from Galilee—“made in one piece, woven from top to bottom.”
And there was nothing about his social rank either.
He may have come from an ancient royal family, but that royal line seemed to have died out. He was known only as the carpenter’s son.
So in that way, they hated him “for no reason.”
Many people seem to feel jealous of those who rule or govern over them.
Just the fact that a man has authority over me stirs up bad feelings in me. I begin to look at him with suspicion simply because he has that authority.

Some people naturally go along and obey simply because the rule has been made. Rulers and authorities are set in place, and these people submit to them for the Lord’s sake. But most people, especially in these days when so many want to get rid of kings, seem to have a natural urge to fight against authority, simply because it is authority.

I believe that in some countries, like France, even if the rulers and governments were changed every month, there would be just as many revolutions under one government as under another. In fact, people there hate all government. They want to live without laws, so that everyone can do whatever seems right to him.
But this did not apply to Christ. He was not a king. He did not take control over the crowds.
It is true that he was Lord over storms and seas. It is true that he could give orders to demons, and if he had wanted to, people would have had to obey him. But he did not take power over them.
He gathered no armies. He announced no laws. He did not make himself an important man in the country. As far as any authority he used over them was concerned, the people did just what they liked.

In fact, instead of putting hard laws on them, he seemed to loosen their strict system. When the woman caught in adultery was brought to him—a woman who would otherwise have been put to death—he said, “I don’t condemn you either.”
To some extent he also eased the strict rules about the Sabbath, which in some ways were too heavy a burden. He said, “The Sabbath was made for people.”
So surely they hated him “for no reason.”
Some people make others dislike them because they are proud.

I know some men I would have liked very much if the stiffness had been taken out of them. I would really feel for them and admire them if they were even a little willing to come down to other people’s level. But they seem to walk around the world acting so proud!
Maybe they are not really proud—very likely they are not. But as an old preacher said, “When we see a fox’s tail sticking out of a hole, we naturally expect that the fox is in there.”
And somehow the human mind cannot stand pride. We always push back against it.
But there was nothing like that in our Savior.
How humble he was!
Why, he was willing to lower himself to do anything.

He washed his disciples’ feet. When he walked among people, he never showed off, as if to say to them, “Look at my talent! Look at my power, my rank, my importance! Get out of my way—I am greater than you.”
No, he sits down right there with them.

There is Matthew the tax collector sitting beside him. Jesus does not think it will hurt him to be near the tax collector, even though he is the worst of sinners. There is a prostitute, and he speaks to her. There is another woman who has seven demons, and he drives the demons out of her. There is someone else with leprosy, and he even touches that person. All of this shows how humble he was, and that there was no pride in him at all.
Oh, if only you could have seen the Savior! He was the perfect example of humility!
He didn’t have any of your fancy manners and polite rules. He had the true politeness that is friendly to everyone, because it is kind and loving to everyone.
There was no pride in the Savior, so there was nothing about him that would make people angry for that reason.
So they hated him “for no reason.”

There are other people you just can’t help disliking, because they are so snappy, so prickly and so angry. They look as if they were born on some terribly dark, stormy day, and as if a lot of vinegar was mixed in when their bodies were made.

You can’t sit with them for long without feeling that you have to keep your tongue on a tight leash. You can’t talk freely, or there will be a quarrel, because they will treat you as guilty over a single word.
You might say, “That man is no doubt a good man. But honestly, I can’t stand that temper of his.”
And when a man with a nasty, sour personality is well known to the public, people feel like disliking him.
But there was nothing like this in our Savior.
“When people insulted him, he did not insult them back.” If people spat in his face, he said nothing to them. When they hit him, he did not curse them. He sat still and put up with their scorn.
He walked through the world while people kept pouring scorn and shame on him. But “he did not answer a word.” He was never angry.

If you read the Savior’s life, you won’t find him speaking one angry word—except the words of holy anger that he poured like boiling oil on the heads of the proud Pharisees. Then his anger really did boil, but it was holy anger.
With such a loving, kind and gentle spirit, you would think he could have gone through the world as easily as anyone could.
But in spite of all that, they hated him.
We can truly say, “They hated him for no reason.”
There is another kind of people you can hardly help disliking: selfish people.
We know some people who are very good-tempered and very honest and fair. But they are so selfish!
When you are with them, you feel that they are only your friends for what they can get from you. When you have been useful to them, they will just put you aside and look for someone else.
Even when they try to do good, their good deed has a hidden purpose. But somehow they always get found out. No one in the world is disliked by the public more than a person who lives a selfish life.
One of the most miserable people in the universe is the selfish miser. He gets kicked around the world like a football.
But there was nothing selfish in Christ. Whatever he did, he did for others.

He had an amazing power to do miracles, but he would not even turn a stone into bread for himself. He saved his miracle-working power for others. There did not seem to be one bit of selfishness in his whole nature.
In fact, the story of his life could be written very briefly: “He saved others, but he did not save himself.”

He walked around and touched the poorest people, the lowest people, and the sickest people. He did not care what people might say about him. He did not seem to care at all about fame, or importance, or comfort, or honor.
He did not care in the least about his own comfort, either in body or in mind.
Christ’s life was one of giving himself up for others. But he did it so easily that it did not even seem like a sacrifice.

Oh, dear friends, in that way they certainly hated Christ for no reason. There was nothing in Christ to make them hate him. In fact, it was the other way around: there was everything in him to make the whole world love and respect someone so completely unselfish.

There is another kind of people I don’t like: people who are fakes. In fact, I think I could even live with a selfish man if I knew he was selfish. But the hypocrite—don’t let him come anywhere near me!
If a public figure is a hypocrite even once, the world will hardly ever trust him again. They will hate him.
But Christ could not be blamed for this at all. If they hated him, it was not for that, because there was never a more genuine man than Christ.

You know, he was called the child Jesus. A child says openly what is on his mind. He holds nothing back and plays no tricks. It was just like that with Jesus. There was nothing fake about him and no deceit.
He never changed. He was “without any change, not even a shadow of turning.”
Whatever the world may say about Christ, people never said they believed he was a hypocrite. Among all the lies they told about him, they never questioned that he was sincere.

If they could have shown that he had really been fooling them, they might have had some reason to hate him. But he lived in the bright sunlight of sincerity. He walked on the very mountaintop, where people watched him all the time.
He could not be a hypocrite, and people knew he could not. And yet people hated him.

Truly, my friends, look at the character of Christ. Look at how lovely it is, how kind, how sincere, how devoted, how eager he was to do people good. Then you must say, “They really did hate him for no reason.” There was nothing in who Christ was that should make people hate him.
Next, was there anything in Christ’s mission that could make people hate him?
Suppose they had asked him, “Why have you come from heaven?” Would there have been anything in his answer to make them angry and full of hate?
I don’t think so. Why did he come?

First of all, he came to explain mysteries. He came to tell them the meaning of the lamb that was sacrificed, the meaning of the scapegoat, and what the ark, the bronze snake and the jar of manna were meant to show. He came to tear open the curtain of the Most Holy Place and to show people secrets they had never seen before.
Should they have hated someone who lifted the curtain of mystery, made dark things clear, and explained riddles?
Should they have hated the one who taught them what Abraham had longed to see—things that prophets and kings had longed to know but died without knowing?
Was there anything in that to make them hate him?
What else did he come for?
He came to earth to bring back people who had wandered away. Is there anything in that which should make people hate Christ?

He came to change the drunkard, to win back the prostitute, to gather in the tax collectors and sinners, and to bring runaway sons back to their father’s house. Surely everyone who wants to help others should agree with that goal! It is the very reason our governments are set up—to bring people into a better condition. So if Christ came for that purpose, was there anything in that to make people hate him?
What else did he come for?
He came to heal the diseases of the body. Is that a fair reason to hate someone?
Should I hate a doctor who goes around healing every kind of disease for free?
Are deaf ears opened? Are mute mouths made to speak? Are the dead raised? Are the blind made to see, and are widows blessed by getting their sons back?
Are these reasons for a man to be hated?
Surely he could well say, “For which of these good deeds are you stoning me?
If I have done good things, why do you speak against me?”
But none of these works were the reason people hated him. They hated him for no reason.
And did he come to earth to die, so that sinners would not have to die?
Was that a reason to hate him?
Should I hate the Savior because he came to put out the flames of hell for me?
Should I look down on the one who let his Father’s flaming sword be put out in his own life’s blood?
Should I be angry with the one who took my place—who takes my sin and my griefs on himself and carries my sorrows?
Should I hate and despise the man who loved me more than he loved himself—who loved me so much that he went down into the dark grave to save me?
Are these reasons to hate someone?
Surely his mission should have made us sing his praise forever and join the angels with their harps in their joyful songs.
“They hated me for no reason.”
But one more thing: was there anything in Christ’s teaching that should have made us hate him?
No, we answer. There was nothing in his teaching that should have made people hate him.
Take his teaching about how to live.
Didn’t he teach us to treat others the way we would want them to treat us?
Didn’t he also stand for everything that is lovely and honorable and well spoken of?
Wasn’t his teaching the very heart of goodness? Even if goodness itself had written it, it could not have written such a perfect set of lovely morals and excellent virtues.
Was it his teaching about right and wrong that people hated?
He taught that rich and poor must stand on the same level. He taught that his good news was not to be kept for one nation, but was to spread gloriously until it covered the world.
Maybe this was one of the main reasons they hated him. But surely there was no good reason in this for them to be angry.
There was nothing in Christ to make people hate him.
“They hated him for no reason.”
II. And now, second, I want to talk about MAN’S SIN—that people would hate the Savior for no reason.
Oh, dear friends, I will not tell you about people’s adulteries, sexual sins, murders, poisonings and sodomy.

I will not tell you about people’s wars, bloodshed, cruelty and rebellions. If I want to tell you about man’s sin, I must tell you that man is a God-killer. He put his God to death and killed his Savior. When I have told you that, I have given you the heart of all sin, the worst crime of all, the very top point of the terrifying pyramid of human guilt.

People went beyond anything they had ever done when they put their Savior to death. Sin was even worse than Herod when it killed the Lord of the universe, the one who loved the human race and came to earth to die.
Sin never looks so extremely sinful as when we see it aimed at Christ himself, whom it hated for no reason.
In every other case where people have hated goodness, there has always been something that made it a little less bad.

In this world we never see goodness that is completely pure. However good a man is, there is always something we can find to criticize. However excellent a person is, there is always some fault that can lessen our admiration or our love.
But there was nothing like that in the Savior.
There was nothing that could spoil the picture. Holiness stood out perfectly, just as it really is. There was holiness—only holiness.

Suppose a man hated Whitefield, one of the holiest men who ever lived. He would tell you he did not hate his goodness. He would say he hated his loud, wild preaching and the unusual stories he told. Or he would pick out something Whitefield had said and hold it up to make fun of it.
But in Christ’s case people could not do that. Even though they looked for false witnesses, their witnesses did not agree with each other.
There was nothing in him but holiness. Anyone with half an eye can see that what people hated was simply that Christ was perfect. They could not have hated him for anything else.
So you see how horrible and disgusting the evil of the human heart is: people hate goodness simply because it is good.

It is not true that we Christians are hated because of our weaknesses. People use our weaknesses as a hook to hang their laughter on. But if we were not Christians, they would not hate our weaknesses.

They make fun of the ways we don’t live up to what we say. But I don’t believe that is what they really care about. We could be as inconsistent as the rest of the world, if only we did not claim to be religious, or if they did not think we had any religion.

But the Savior had no inconsistencies and no weaknesses. So people lost all their excuses for hating him. And it became clear that people naturally hate goodness, because they are so evil that they can’t help hating it.
And now let me speak to every sinner here. Let me ask each one whether he ever had any reason to hate Christ.
But someone says, “I don’t hate him. If he came to my house, I would love him very much.”
But here is something very striking: Christ lives next door to you, in the person of poor Betty over there.
She goes to a certain chapel, and you say she is nothing but a poor Methodist who is always spouting religious talk.
Why don’t you like Betty?
She is part of Christ’s body, and he said, “Whatever you did to one of the least of these, you did to me.”
You say you don’t hate Christ.
Now, look across the chapel.
Don’t you know a man who is a member here, a very holy man, and somehow you can’t stand him because he once pointed out your faults?
Oh, sir, if you loved Christ, you would love the members of his body.
What! Are you telling me you love my head, but you don’t love my hands?
My dear friend, you can’t cut off my head and have me still be the same person.
If you love Christ, who is the head, you must love the members of his body.
But you say, “I do love his people.”
Very well. If you love your fellow believers, then you have passed from death to life.
But you say, “I’m not sure that I have been changed. Still, I don’t know of anything in my heart that is against Christ and his good news.”
You may not know about it. But the fact that you don’t know about it makes your situation even sadder.
Maybe if you knew it and cried over it, you would come to Christ. But since you don’t know it and don’t feel it, that proves you are against him.
Now come! Unless you love Christ, I have to assume you are against him. I know there are only two ways to think about him.
You must either hate him or love him.
Being neutral about Christ is simply impossible.
A man might as well say, “I don’t care one way or the other about honesty.”
Well, then he is dishonest, isn’t he?
You don’t care one way or the other about Christ?
Then you hate him.
And why do you hate him?
Many times the good news has tried to win you over. You have resisted many invitations. So come now: for which of Christ’s good deeds do you hate him?
Is there anyone here who persecutes Christ’s people?
Sinner! Why do you hate Christ?
Do you curse him?
Tell me what he has done to make you angry with him.
Point to one single thing he did wrong in the way he treated you. Has Christ ever hurt you?
“Oh,” someone says, “he has taken my wife and made her one of his children. She has been baptized and goes to chapel, and I can’t stand it.”
Oh, sinner, is that why you hate Christ?
Would you have hated Christ if he had pulled your wife out of a fire, if he had saved her from dying?
No, you would love him.
And he has saved your wife’s soul.
Oh, even if he never saves you, if you love your wife, you will have reason enough to love him when you think how good he has been to you.
I tell you, if you hate Christ, you don’t just hate him for no reason. You hate him when you have a clear reason to love him.
Come, poor sinner, what have you gained by hating Christ?
You have a guilty conscience that stings you.

Many sinners, by hating Christ, have ended up locked in jail, with a ragged coat, a sick body, and a nasty, filthy house with broken windows. They have a poor wife who has been beaten nearly to death, and children who run out of the way as soon as their father comes home.
What have you gained by hating Christ?
Oh, if you added up what you have gained, you would find that getting Christ would be a real gain, but hating him is a total loss for you.

Now, if you hate Christ and Christ’s religion, I tell you that you hate Christ for no reason. And let me give you one serious warning: if you keep hating Christ until you die, you will not hurt Christ by it, but you will hurt yourself terribly.
Oh, may God save you from being people who hate Christ!
There is nothing to gain from it, and everything to lose.
Sinner, what reason do you have to hate Christ?
Persecutor, what reason do you have to hate Christ?
You worldly, ungodly people, what reason do you have to hate Christ?
Why do you hate Christ’s good news?
His ministers—what harm have they done to you?
What harm can they do to you, when they want so badly to do you all the good in the world?
Why do you hate Christ?
Oh! It is only because you are so set on doing wrong—because snake poison is under your lips, and your throat is an open grave.
Otherwise, you would love Christ.
They hated him “for no reason.”
And now, Christians, I must preach straight at you for just a moment.
Surely you have great reason to love Christ now, because you once hated him for no reason.
Have you ever treated a friend badly without realizing it?
Most of us have had the bad luck of doing that at some time.
We suspected that a friend had done us wrong. We argued with him for weeks, and he hadn’t done it at all.
All he had done was warn us.
Oh! No tears are like the ones we cry when we have hurt a friend.
And shouldn’t we cry when we have hurt the Savior?
Didn’t he come to my door one cold, wet night, and I shut my door on him?
Oh, I have done something I can’t undo. I have ignored my Lord. I have insulted my friend. I have brought shame on the one I admire.
Shouldn’t I weep for him?
Oh, shouldn’t I spend my whole life for him? My sins, my own betrayal, spilled his blood.
I will build monuments—oh, monuments!—wherever I live and wherever I go.
I will pile up monuments of praise so that his name will spread. Wherever I go, I will tell what he did, with many tears, because I treated him badly for so long and misunderstood him so terribly.
We hated him for no reason, so let us love him.

blocks.x: III. TWO LESSONS FOR GOD’S PEOPLE.

s: First, if your Master was hated for no reason, don’t expect to have an easy time in this world.
If your Master went through all this scorn and all this pain, do you think you will always ride through this world in a fancy carriage?
If you do, you are badly mistaken.
Your Master was persecuted, so you must expect the same.
Some of you feel sorry for us when we are persecuted and looked down on.
Oh, save your pity! Keep it for the people the world speaks well of. Keep it for the people that the warning of trouble is aimed at.
“How terrible it will be for you when all people speak well of you.”
Save your pity for the world’s favorites. Save your pity for the great people of this world, whom everyone cheers.

We don’t ask for your pity. No, friends, we are glad in all these things. We “boast in our troubles too, knowing that the things that happen to us help the good news move forward.” And we think of it as nothing but joy when all sorts of hard tests come our way, because we are glad that the name of Christ becomes known and his kingdom grows.
The other lesson is this: if the world does hate you, make sure it hates you for no reason.
If the world is going to be against you, there is no point in making it be against you.
This world is bitter enough without me adding vinegar to it.
Some people seem to think the world will persecute them, so they get ready to fight, as if they were asking to be persecuted.
Now, I don’t see any good in doing that.
Don’t try to make other people dislike you.
Honestly, the opposition some people face is not because they do what is right. It is because of their own sin, or their own nasty temper.
Many a Christian lives in someone’s household—perhaps a Christian servant girl. She says she is persecuted for doing what is right.
But she has a bad attitude. Sometimes she speaks sharply, and then her mistress scolds her.
That is not being persecuted for doing what is right.
Then there is another person, maybe a businessman in the city. People don’t think very highly of him.
He says he is persecuted for doing what is right. But really it is because he didn’t keep a deal he made some time ago.
Another man says he is persecuted for doing what is right. But he goes around bossing everyone, and every now and then people turn around and tell him off.
Christians, make sure that if you are persecuted, it is for doing what is right. If you bring persecution on yourself, you have to carry it yourself.
Christ has nothing to do with the persecutions you bring on yourself by your own sins. They are discipline for you.
They hated Christ for no reason, so don’t be afraid of being hated.
They hated Christ for no reason, so don’t go looking to be hated. Don’t give the world any reason for it.
And now, may you who hate Christ come to love him! Oh, I wish he would bring himself to you right now!
Oh, I wish he would show himself to you!
And then surely you could not help loving him right away.
Whoever believes in the Lord Jesus will be sure to love him, and whoever loves him will be saved.
Oh, I pray that God would give you faith and give you love, for the sake of Christ Jesus! Amen.

“That is why God also lifted him up very high and gave him a name that is greater than every other name. He did this so that at the name of Jesus every knee will bow—everything in heaven, on earth, and under the earth. And every tongue will openly say that Jesus Christ is Lord, bringing glory to God the Father.”—Philippians 2:9-11
This morning I almost wish I had not dared to stand in this pulpit. I feel completely unable to preach to you in a way that will do you good.

I had thought that the last two weeks of peace and rest had taken away the effects of that terrible disaster. But now I have come back to the same place. And especially now that I am standing here to speak to you, I feel some of the same painful emotions that almost crushed me before.
So please forgive me this morning if I say nothing, or almost nothing, about that serious event.
I could not preach to you on any subject that is even a little connected to it.
If I let myself remember that terrifying scene, where I had the solemn duty of standing, I would have to stop speaking.
I have no doubt that God will rule over it and bring good out of it.

Some people have said that men did this out of pure hatred. That may not be so. Perhaps it was just plain wickedness—people wanting to disturb a church meeting. But they certainly never meant to commit such a terrible crime as killing those poor people.
May God forgive the people who started that horrible act!
I forgive them from the bottom of my heart.
But it will not stop us. We are not scared off by it at all.
I will preach there again. Yes, and God will save people there, and Satan’s kingdom will shake more than ever.
“God is with us. So who can stand against us?”
The text I have chosen has comforted me. In a big way, it has given me the strength to come here today. Just thinking about it brought great comfort to my discouraged heart.

Here it is: “That is why God also lifted him up very high and gave him a name that is greater than every other name. He did this so that at the name of Jesus every knee will bow—everything in heaven, on earth, and under the earth. And every tongue will openly say that Jesus Christ is Lord, bringing glory to God the Father.”—Philippians 2:9-11.

I will not try to preach a real sermon on this text. I will only share a few thoughts that have come to my mind. I could not preach today. I have not been able to study at all. But I thought that even a few words might be welcome to you this morning. And I trust your loving hearts to forgive how little it is.
Oh, Spirit of God, show your strength in your servant’s weakness. Help him to honor his Lord, even when his soul feels crushed inside him.
When your mind is strongly fixed on one thing, it always comes back to it. Troubles may throw it this way and that. But it returns to the place it has chosen as its home.
You have seen this in the story of David.
His soldiers had won the battle, and they came back excited by their victory.

David’s mind had surely been very troubled while he waited. He was afraid of what would happen if they won, and just as afraid of what would happen if they lost. But have you noticed how quickly his thoughts went straight back to the one he loved most?
“Is the young man Absalom safe?” he asked. It was as if nothing else that had happened mattered, as long as his dear son was safe!
Dear friends, it is the same with the Christian.

Disasters may come. Nations may be wrecked, empires may crash, revolutions may shake the world, or war may strike. But in the middle of it all, the big question the Christian asks himself, and asks others too, is this: Is Christ’s kingdom safe?
When he suffers in his own life, his biggest worry is this: Will God be glorified? Will God’s honor grow because of it?

If so, he says, “I may be only like a wick that is barely smoking. But if the sun is not dimmed, I will be glad. I may be a bruised reed. But if the pillars of the temple are not broken, what does it matter that my reed is bruised?”

Everything around him may be breaking into pieces. Yet it is enough comfort for him to think that Christ’s throne stands firm and steady. The earth may have shaken under his own feet, but Christ stands on a rock that can never be moved.
I think some of these feelings have gone through our minds too.

Our thoughts have been in turmoil, rushing back and forth with worry. But our souls have come back to the one we love most. And after all, it has been a great comfort to say, “It does not matter what happens to us. God has lifted him up very high and given him a name greater than every other name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee will bow.”
This text has brought sweet comfort to every person who will inherit heaven.
Let me share its comforts with you, very briefly.
For the true Christian, there is a lot of comfort in the simple fact that Christ has been lifted up.
Second, there is great comfort in the reason why he was lifted up.
“That is why God also lifted him up very high.” That means: because he had first been humbled.
And third, there is truly heavenly comfort in thinking about who it was that lifted Christ up.
“That is why God also”—even though people look down on him and throw him down—“God also lifted him up very high.”
I. So first: THE SIMPLE FACT THAT CHRIST HAS BEEN LIFTED UP GIVES EVERY TRUE CHRISTIAN A GREAT DEAL OF COMFORT.

Many of you have no share in spiritual things. You do not love Christ, and you do not care about his glory. You will just laugh when I say this: the fact that Christ is glorified after all is like a refreshing drink for a tired Christian.
It gives you no comfort, because your heart is not in the right condition to find this text sweet.
There is no joy in it for you. It does not move your heart. It adds no sweetness to your life. And here is the reason: you are not joined to Christ’s cause, and you do not sincerely try to honor him.

But the true Christian’s heart jumps for joy when he remembers that Christ is lifted up—even when he is weighed down by all kinds of sorrows and temptations. That thought is enough to cheer his heart.
Notice this, dear friends: the Christian has certain qualities in his character that make Christ being lifted up a great joy to him.
First, he is related to Christ. He believes this, and it is not just his opinion—it is really true. So he cares about the success of his relative.

You have seen how happy a father is as his son climbs, step by step, to wealth or fame. You have seen a mother’s eyes sparkle with delight as her daughter grows up into a young woman and blossoms in all her beauty.
You may have asked why they cared so much. And you were told it was because the boy was his son, or the girl was her daughter.
They were happy to see their children do well because they were family.
If they had not been related, those children could have become kings, emperors, or queens, and the parents would hardly have felt any joy.
But because they were family, every step up mattered deeply and stirred their hearts.
It is the same with the Christian.
He feels that Jesus Christ, the glorified “ruler over the kings of the earth,” is his brother.

He worships him as God. But he also admires him as the man Christ, who shares our very bones and flesh. And in his quiet, peaceful times of closeness with Jesus, he loves to say to him, “O Lord, you are my brother.”
His song is, “The one I love belongs to me, and I belong to him.”
He loves to sing—

blocks.x: “Sharing one blood with sinners,”

s: That is what Christ Jesus is. For he is a human being, just like us. He is not any less human than we are, and not any more—except that he has no sin.
So when we feel that we are related to Christ, his being lifted up surely gives our spirits the greatest joy. We are delighted by it, because it is someone from our own family who has been honored.
He is the Elder Brother of God’s one great family in heaven and on earth. He is the Brother we are all related to.
But the Christian does not only feel related to Christ. He also feels that he and Christ share the same cause.
He feels that when Christ is lifted up, he himself is lifted up in a small way too. That is because he shares Christ’s desire to spread God’s great cause and honor in the world.

I am sure that every ordinary soldier who stood beside the Duke of Wellington felt honored when people cheered their commander for the victory. Each one said, “I helped him. I backed him up. My part was small. I only held my place in line. I only stood firm under the enemy’s fire. But now the victory is won.
I feel honored by it, because I helped, in a small way, to win it.”
In the same way, when the Christian sees his Lord lifted up, he says, “It is the Captain who is honored, and all his soldiers share in his honor.
Didn’t I stand by his side?

The work I did was small, and I had little strength to serve him. But still, I helped with the work.” Even the most ordinary soldier in God’s army feels that he himself is lifted up a little when he reads this: “That is why God also lifted him up very high and gave him a name greater than every other name”—a fame greater than any other name—“so that at the name of Jesus every knee will bow.”
And there is more. The Christian knows not only that he shares Christ’s goal. He knows there is a real union between Christ and all his people.
The Bible teaches this truth, but people seldom talk about it at length. Yet we can never think about it too much. It is the teaching that Christ and his members are all one.
Dear friends, don’t you know that every member of Christ’s church is a part of Christ himself?

We are “of his flesh and of his bones.” We are parts of his great spiritual body. So when we read that our Head has been crowned, rejoice, you who are his members, whether you are his feet or his hands! The crown is not on you, but it is on your Head. So you share the glory, because you are one with him.
Look at Christ up there, sitting at his Father’s right hand!
Believer! He is the promise that you will be glorified too. He is the guarantee that God accepts you. And he also stands for you as your representative.

Christ holds his seat in heaven by his own right, because he is God. But he also holds it on behalf of the whole church. He has gone ahead of them, and he sits in glory representing every single one of them.
So rejoice, believer, when you see your Master raised from the grave, and when you see him lifted up to heaven.

Picture him climbing the stairs of light and sitting on his high throne, so high that even angels can hardly see that far. Hear the cheers of a thousand seraphs. Listen to the loud, ringing choir of millions of redeemed people. When you see him crowned with light, remember this: you are lifted up in him too, because you are a part of him.
You are blessed if you know this—not only as a teaching, but also as a sweet experience.

We are joined to Christ, married to him, grown into him. We are parts of his very self. We beat with the heart of the body. When the Head is glorified, we share in the praise. We feel that his glory brings honor to us too.
Oh, dear friends, have you ever felt that oneness with Christ?
Have you ever wanted the very same things he wants?

If you have, you will find this full of comfort. But if not—if you do not know Christ—then his being lifted up will bring you sorrow instead of pleasure. You will have to realize that he is lifted up to crush you, to judge you and condemn you. He is lifted up to sweep the sins off this earth and pull the curse out by the roots—and you along with it—unless you repent and turn to God with all your heart.
There is one more feeling that I think is really needed if we are to enjoy this truth fully—the truth that Christ is lifted up.
It is the feeling of giving your whole self completely to the great work of trying to honor him.
Oh, I have worked hard for that! How I wish God would help me reach it!
I have now gathered all my prayers into one. And that one prayer is this: that I may die to self and live completely for him.

To me this seems to be the highest place a person can reach. It means having no wish, no thought, no desire except Christ. It means feeling that dying would be pure happiness, if it were for Christ. It means feeling that living in poverty, pain, scorn, contempt, and misery would be sweet, if it were for Christ. It means feeling that it does not matter what happens to you, as long as your Master is lifted up. It means feeling like a dry leaf blown about in a storm, and not caring at all where you are going, as long as you know the Master’s hand is guiding you the way he wants.

Or rather, it means being like a diamond that has to be cut. You do not care how sharply you are cut, as long as you are made fit to be a sparkling jewel in his crown. You hardly care what is done to you, as long as you can honor him.

If any of you have reached that sweet feeling of losing yourself completely, you will look up to Christ as if he were the sun. And you will say about yourself, “O Lord, I see your rays of light. I feel that I am not even a ray from you. I am only darkness, swallowed up in your light.
All I ask is that you would live in me. I want the life I live in this body not to be my own life, but your life in me. Then I can say with all my heart, as Paul did, ‘To me, life is Christ.’”
A person who has reached this never needs to worry about what the world thinks.
He can say, “Are you praising me?
Are you flattering me?
Take your flattery back. I did not ask you for it. I was trying to praise my Master. You have put the praise at my door. Go and put it at his door, not mine.
Are you mocking me?
Do you look down on me?
I am very, very happy to put up with it.
Just do not mock him and look down on him!”

And even if you do, know this: he is far beyond your mocking. So go ahead and strike the soldier because of his Captain. Yes, hit him, hit him! But you cannot touch the King. He is lifted up high. You may think you have won. You may have beaten one soldier of the army. But the main army is winning.

One soldier seems to be knocked down into the dust. But the Captain is coming with his winning troops. And he will trample you under his conquering feet, while you are still excited about your fake victory.
As long as even a tiny bit of selfishness is left in us, it will spoil our sweet joy in Christ. Until we get rid of it, we will never have joy all the time.
I really believe that the root of sorrow is self.
If we could just get rid of self, then—as far as our feelings go—sorrow would be sweet, sickness would feel like health, sadness would be joy, and poverty would feel like riches.
Those things might not change. But the way we feel about them would be very different.
If you want to find happiness, look for it at the roots of your selfishness. Dig up your selfishness, and you will be happy.

I have found this: whenever I gave in to even the smallest joy, I was set up to feel the enemy’s arrows very painfully. But when I said about people’s praise, “Yes, and what are you? Worthless things!”—then I could also say about their contempt, “Come on! Come on!

I will send you all to the same place I sent the praise. You can go off together and fight your battles with each other. But as for me, let your arrows bounce off my armor. They must not reach my skin, and they will not!”
But if you give in to the one, you will give in to the other.
You must seek and learn to live completely in Christ. Be sad when you see people speak evil of Christ and dishonor him. Be glad when you see him lifted up. Then you will always have a reason for joy.

So sit down now, you who are insulted, poor, looked down on, and tempted. Sit down, lift up your eyes, and see him on his throne. And say to yourself, “I may be small, but I know I am joined to him. He is my love, my life, my joy. I do not care what happens, as long as it is written, ‘The Lord reigns.’”
II. Now, briefly, the second point.
Here too is the very spring and source of joy: THE REASON WHY CHRIST WAS LIFTED UP.
“That is why God also lifted him up very high.”

Why? Because “though he was in the form of God, he did not think that being equal with God was like stealing. But he made himself someone of no importance. He took on the form of a servant and became like a human being. And when he was found looking like a man, he humbled himself and obeyed, all the way to death—even death on a cross.
That is why God also lifted him up very high.”
Of course, this is about the human nature of our Lord Jesus Christ.
As God, Christ did not need to be lifted up. He was already higher than the highest. He is “God over all, blessed forever.”

But for a while the signs of his glory were hidden. He wrapped his divine nature in a human body that could die. Then his body, together with his divine nature, went up to heaven. The God-man, Christ Jesus, who had bent down low to shame, sorrow, and humiliation, was lifted up high, “far above all rulers and powers.” He was raised so that he could reign as the royal Prince over all worlds—yes, over heaven itself.
Let us think for a moment about how low Christ went down. Then, dear friends, it will make you glad to know that for that very reason his human nature was lifted up high.
Do you see that man—

blocks.x:
“The humble Man in front of his enemies,
The tired Man, so full of sorrows?”

s: Do you see him as he speaks?
Notice the amazing words that pour from his lips. And see how the crowds follow him?
But do you hear, far away, the rumbling thunder of lies and scorn?
Listen to what his accusers say.
They say he is “a man who eats too much and drinks too much wine, a friend of tax collectors and sinners.” They say “he has a demon, and he is crazy.”
They use every insulting word there is to attack him.
He is lied about, insulted, and persecuted!
Wait! Do you think this knocks him down? Do you think this makes him less?
No! For this very reason, “God lifted him up very high.”
Look at the shame and the spit on the cheek of that man of sorrows over there!
See how cruel hands pull out his hair. Notice how they torture him and mock him.
Do you think all this brings dishonor to Christ?
It looks that way. But listen to this: “He became obedient,” and so “God lifted him up very high.”

Oh, there is an amazing connection between that shame and spitting and the seraphs bowing their knees. There is a strange and mysterious link that joins the lies and slander to the singing of worshiping angels.
In a way, the one was the seed of the other.
It is strange, but that black, bitter seed grew into a sweet and glorious flower that blooms forever.
He suffered, and then he reigned. He bent low to win. He won because he bent low. And he was lifted up because he won.
Think about him some more.
Can you picture him in your mind, nailed to that cross!
Oh, eyes! You are full of pity, and thick with tears!
Oh, I can see the streams pouring down his cheeks!
Do you see his hands bleeding, and his feet too, pouring out blood?
Look at him! The bulls of Bashan surround him, and the dogs are chasing him to his death!
Listen to him! “Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani?”
The earth jumps in terror.
One who is God is groaning on a cross!
What? Doesn’t this dishonor Christ?
No! It honors him!
Each thorn becomes a sparkling jewel in his crown of glory. The nails are shaped into his royal scepter. And his wounds dress him in the purple robe of an emperor.
Treading the winepress has stained his clothes. But these are not stains of shame and dishonor.
The stains are like beautiful embroidery on his royal robes forever.
Treading that winepress has made his clothes purple with the rule of a whole world. And he is Master of the universe forever.
O Christian, sit down and think about this: your Master did not climb into heaven from the earth’s mountains, but from its valleys.
He did not step into everlasting happiness from high points of happiness on earth. He rose to glory from the depths of suffering.
Oh, what a huge step that was! In one mighty step, from the grave to the throne of the Most High, the man Christ, who is God, rose up in glory.
And think about this! In some way, mysterious but true, he was lifted up because he suffered.
“When he was found looking like a man, he humbled himself and obeyed, all the way to death—even death on a cross.
That is why God also lifted him up very high and gave him a name greater than every other name.”
Believer, there is comfort here for you, if you will take it.
If Christ was lifted up by going low, the same will happen to you.
Do not measure your steps toward victory by the steps that go up. Measure them by the ones that seem to go down.
The road to heaven goes downhill. If you want to be honored forever, you must think less of yourself. And often other people will think less of you too.

Oh, do not think that fool over there will safely reach Paradise! He is climbing toward heaven on his own shallow ideas about himself and on the flattery of his friends. No, the thing he is standing on will burst. He will fall and be smashed to pieces.
But whoever goes down into the mines of suffering will find endless riches there. And whoever dives into the depths of grief will find the pearl of everlasting life in its caves.

Remember, Christian, that you are lifted up when you are put to shame. When your enemies tell lies about you, read them as if good people were applauding you. When wicked people mock and sneer at you, count it as equal to praise and honor from godly people. Their blame is criticism, and their criticism is praise.

And if your body is ever attacked because of your faith, remember that it is no shame to you—just the opposite. And if you are given the privilege (and you might be) of wearing the blood-red crown of a martyr, do not think it is a disgrace to die.
Remember, the most honored people in the church are “the noble army of martyrs.”

Remember too that the more they suffered, the greater their “eternal weight of glory.” So if you are standing where the battle is thickest and hardest, remember that you will stand in the middle of glory.
If you have the hardest things to carry, you will have the sweetest things to enjoy.
So keep going—through floods, through fire, through death, even through hell, if it is in your way.
Do not be afraid. The one who glorified Christ because he bent low will glorify you too. After he has let you suffer for a while, he will give you “a crown of life that never fades.”
III. And now, finally, dear friends, here is one more comfort for you.
We should notice WHO it was that lifted Christ up.
“GOD also lifted him up very high.”
The emperor of all the Russians crowns himself. He is a ruler with total power, and he puts the crown on his own head. But Christ has no such foolish pride.
Christ did not crown himself.
“GOD also lifted him up very high.”

God put the crown on Christ’s head. And I find a very sweet thought in this. The same hand that put the crown on Christ’s head will one day put a crown on ours. The same Mighty One who crowned Christ “King of kings, and Lord of lords” will crown us too, when he makes us “kings and priests to him forever.”
Paul said, “I know there is a crown of glory stored up for me that will never fade. God, the righteous judge, will give it to me on that day.”

Now stop and think about this for a moment. Christ did not crown himself; his Father crowned him. He did not lift himself up to the throne of majesty; his Father lifted him there and set him on his throne.
Think of it like this: people never lifted Christ up.
Now put this next to it: “God also lifted him up very high.”
People hissed at him, mocked him, and jeered at him.
Words were not hard enough, so they wanted to use stones.
“They picked up stones again to stone him.”
And when stones failed, nails had to be used, and he had to be crucified.
Then came the taunting, the jeering, and the mocking, while he hung dying slowly on the cross.
People did not lift him up.
Put that dark picture there.
Now put this glorious, bright scene right next to it. Each one will make the other stand out.
People dishonored him; “God also lifted him up.”
Believer, if everyone speaks badly of you, lift up your head and say, “People did not lift up my Master. I am thankful that they do not lift me up either.
The servant should not be above his master, nor the servant above his lord, nor the messenger greater than the one who sent him.”

blocks.x:
“If for his dear name my face
Must suffer shame and blame,
I’ll gladly greet the blame and shame,
For he’ll remember me.”

s: God will remember me. And in the end he will lift me up high, even though people knock me down.
Now put it next to another fact: Christ did not lift himself up.
Poor Christian! You feel that you cannot lift yourself up.
Sometimes you cannot lift your own sad, discouraged spirits.
Some people tell you, “Oh, you shouldn’t feel like this.”
They tell you, “Oh, you shouldn’t say such things or think such thoughts.”
Ah! “Only the heart knows how bitter it is, and a stranger does not get involved in it.” Yes, and I will make it even better: “and neither does a friend.”
It is not easy to tell how another person should feel or how they should act.
Our minds are all made differently. Each one is made in its own mold, and then the mold is broken. There will never be another one just like it.
We are all different, every one of us. But I am sure there is one thing we all share in times of deep sorrow: we feel helpless.
We feel that we cannot lift ourselves up.
Now remember, our Master felt just like that.
Psalm 22, if I understand it correctly, is a beautiful speech that Christ spoke to himself on the cross. In it he says, “I am a worm, not even a man.”
It is as if he felt so broken and so crushed that, instead of feeling more than a man—which he was—he felt for a while less than a man.

And yet, at the moment when he could not lift a finger to crown himself, when he could barely think a thought of victory, when his eyes could not even catch a faraway glimpse of triumph—right then his God was crowning him.
Christian, are you that broken?
Do not think you have been thrown away forever. For “God also lifted him up very high”—the one who did not lift himself up. And this is a picture and a promise of what God will do for you.
And now, dear friends, I cannot say much more about this text. I only ask you to spend a few minutes now thinking deeply about it.
Oh, lift up your eyes! Ask heaven’s blue curtain to open. Ask God for power—I mean spiritual power from above—to see behind the curtain.
I am not asking you to look at the streets of gold, or the walls of jasper, or the city with gates of pearl.
I am not asking you to look at the crowds dressed in white, who sing loud hallelujahs forever. But look over there, my friends, turn your eyes there,
Do you see him?

blocks.x:
“The head that once wore a crown of thorns
Now wears a crown of glory;
A royal crown now decorates
That mighty Winner’s head.

No more the bloody crown,
No more the cross and nails:
For hell itself shakes when he frowns,
And all of heaven worships him.”

s: Look at him! Can you picture him in your mind?
Look at his amazing glory!
The greatness of kings is swallowed up. The splendor of empires melts away like white morning mist before the sun. The shine of great armies gathered together fades into nothing.
He himself is brighter than the sun, and more awesome than armies marching with their flags.
See him! See him!
Oh, hide your faces, you kings! Put away your showy parades, you rulers of this poor, small earth!
His kingdom has no borders. His huge empire stretches out without any limit.
Everything above him belongs to him. Many steps below him are the angels, and they are his. They throw their crowns down at his feet.
Beside them stand his chosen and rescued people, and their crowns belong to him too.

And down here on earth stand his holy people. They are his, and they worship him. And under the earth, among those in hell, where devils growl in their hatred, even there they tremble and bow. Lost spirits are there, weeping and grinding their teeth and forever mourning that they exist. Even there, they admit that he is God—even though that confession adds to the fire that torments them.
In heaven, on earth, and in hell, every knee bends before him, and every tongue confesses that he is God.
If it is not happening now, it will happen in the future. Every creature God has made will admit that his Son is “God over all, blessed forever.
Amen.” Oh, my soul looks forward to that blessed day, when this whole earth will gladly bow its knee to its God!
I really believe a happy time is coming, when not one knee will stay unbent before my Lord and Master.

I am looking for that time, that glory of the last days. Kings will bring him gifts. Queens will care for the church like nursing mothers. The gold of Sheba, the ships of Tarshish, and the camels of Arabia will all belong to him. Nations and tribes of every language will

blocks.x:
“Linger on his name with the sweetest songs,
And little children’s voices will announce
Their first blessings on his name.”

s: Sometimes I hope I will live to see that wonderful time. It will be a golden age for this world, which is now so crushed with grief and sorrow by the cruelty of its own people.

I hope to see the day when people will say, “Shout, for the great Shepherd reigns, and his kingdom without suffering has now come!” Then the earth will be one huge orchestra of praise, and everyone will sing the glorious hallelujah song of the King of kings.
But even now, while we wait for that time, my soul is glad about this fact: in a real way every knee already bows—not willingly, but truly.
When the mocker shouts his insults up at heaven, does he think he is insulting God?
He thinks so. But his insult dies long before it gets even halfway to the stars.
When in his hatred he makes a sword to fight against Christ, does he think his weapon will succeed?

If he does, I can easily imagine how God laughs at him. For God sees the wildest rebel and the most hopeless scoffer still carrying out God’s great plans. They are still doing what God decided from all eternity. Even in the middle of their wild rebellion, they are running in the very track that was mysteriously marked out for them before time began—the track they would surely follow.

Some people say, “The wild horses of the earth have broken their bridles. The driver has lost the reins.” But they have not. Or if they have, the horses are running the same course they would have run if the Almighty were still holding the reins.

The world has not fallen into chaos. Chance is not God. God is still in charge. Let people do whatever they want, and hate the truth we treasure. In the end they will still do what God wants. Even their worst rebellion will turn out to be a kind of obedience, though they do not know it.
But you will say, “Then why do you still find fault? Who has ever resisted a will like that?”
“Wait—O man, who are you to argue back at God?
Should something that was shaped ask the one who shaped it, ‘Why did you give me this shape?’
Isn’t the potter in charge of the clay? From the same lump, can’t he make one jar for honor and another for dishonor?

What if God wanted to show his anger and make his power known? What if he patiently put up with the jars that deserved his anger and were ready to be destroyed? And what if his purpose was to make known his rich glory on the jars of mercy, which he had made ready long before for glory?”
Who can blame him?
How terrible it will be for anyone who fights against his Maker!
He is God—know that, all you people who live in the land. And in the end, everything will serve his will.

I like what Luther says in his bold hymn. Those who hate the teaching of predestination may say whatever they like. But Luther knew it, and he boldly declared, “He rules everywhere, and all things serve his power.”
No matter what they do, God is still in control after all.
Go on, you who insult God! God knows how to turn all your insults into songs!
Go on, you who fight against God, if you want to. But know this: your sword will help to make God great and to carve out glory for Christ, even when you planned to slaughter his church.
It will happen that everything you do will fail. For God drives the fortune-tellers mad, and he says, “Where is the wisdom of the scholar?
Where is the wisdom of the wise?”
Surely, “God has lifted him up and given him a name greater than every other name.”

And now, finally, dear friends: if it is true—and it is—that Christ is lifted up so high that he will have a name above every name, and every knee will bow to him, then won’t we bow our knees before his Majesty this morning?
One day you will have to bow your knee, whether you want to or not.
O stubborn sinner, with muscles like iron, bow your knee now!
You will have to bow it, man, on that day when the lightning is let loose and the thunder rolls in wild anger. You will have to bow your knee then.
Oh, bow it now!
“Kiss the Son, so that he does not get angry and you die on the road, when his anger burns even a little.”
O Lord of hosts, make people bend their knees!
Make us all willing subjects of your grace. Otherwise, later we will become unwilling slaves of your terror, dragged down to hell in chains of punishment.
Oh, may the people on earth bend their knees willingly now! Otherwise, in hell these words will come true: “Things under the earth will bow the knee before him.”
God bless you, my friends. That is all I can say.
God bless you, for Jesus’ sake! Amen.
“There is a friend who stays closer to you than a brother.”—Proverbs 18:24.
Cicero said it well: “Friendship is the only thing in the world that all people agree is useful.”
To live a happy life in this world, friendship seems just as necessary as fire or water, or even the air we breathe.

A man can drag himself through a miserable life all alone, proud and dignified. But that is hardly life at all. It is just existing. It is like a tree of life stripped of its leaves of hope and its fruit of joy.
If you want to be happy here, you must have friends. And if you want to be happy in the life to come, you must, above all, find a friend in that world. That friend is God, the Father of his people.

But friendship, even though it is so pleasant and such a great blessing, has also caused people terrible misery. That happens when the friend is unworthy and unfaithful. The sweeter a good friend is, the more bitter a false friend is.
“A friend who betrays you hurts more than a snake’s bite.”
It is sweet to lean on someone. But oh, how bitter it is when that support snaps, and you fall hard just because you trusted!
A true friend simply must be faithful. We cannot be happy with people unless they stay loyal to us.
Solomon says that “there is a friend who stays closer than a brother.”
I do not think he ever found that friend in the showy, empty things of the world.
He had tried them all, and he found them empty. He went through all their pleasures, and he found them to be “empty, completely empty.”
Poor Savage knew this from his own sad experience when he said—

blocks.x:
“You will find that the world’s friendship is just a show!
Only a show on the outside! It is like a prostitute’s tears,
A politician’s promise, or a fake patriot’s passion.
It looks good, but it is all a lie.”

s: And most of the time, that is exactly what the world’s friendships are.
The world’s friendship always breaks easily.
If you trust it, you have trusted a robber. If you lean on it, you have leaned on a thorn. Yes, worse than that, you have leaned on a spear that will stab you to the heart with terrible pain.
And yet Solomon says he had found “a friend who stays closer than a brother.”

He did not find him in the places where he chased wild pleasures, or while roaming through all his endless riches. He found him in the tent of the Most High, the hidden home of God. That friend is Jesus, the Son of God, the Friend of sinners.
It is a big thing to say that “there is a friend who stays closer than a brother.” After all, the love between brothers has led to some very brave deeds.
We have read stories of what brothers have done for each other. We think those stories could hardly be beaten anywhere in the history of friendship.
Timoleon stood with his shield over the body of his brother, who had been killed. He protected him so the enemy could not treat his body with disrespect.
People counted it a brave act of brotherly love that he would face the spears of a whole army to defend his brother’s dead body.
And there have been many examples like this in wars, both long ago and in recent times, of how much brothers love each other.

There is a story about a regiment of Highland soldiers who got lost while marching through the Highlands. A terrible storm came over them, the kind that sometimes catches travelers by surprise. The snow blinded them, and they lost their way in the mountains.
They were almost frozen to death, and they could hardly keep marching.
One man after another fell into the snow and disappeared.

But there were two brothers there named Forsythe. One of them fell flat on the ground. He would have stayed there and died. But his brother, who could barely drag his own legs across that white desert, lifted him onto his back and carried him. As the others fell one by one, this brave, loyal brother kept carrying the one he loved. At last he himself fell down, worn out, and died.
But his body had kept his brother so warm that the brother was able to reach the end of the journey safely. And so he lived.
Here is an example of one brother giving his life for another.
I hope there are some brothers here who would be ready to do the same if they were ever in the same kind of trouble.
So it is a big thing to say that “there is a friend who stays closer than a brother.”

It puts that friend at the very top of the list of those who love us. Surely, next to a mother’s love, there is no deeper love in the world than a brother’s love for someone born of the same father and bounced on the same knee. And there should not be.
People who have “grown in beauty side by side, and filled one house with joy” ought to love one another.
And we believe there have been many wonderful examples and strong proofs of the love between brothers.
And yet Solomon says, “there is a friend who stays closer than a brother.”
Let me say again what we believe: this friend is the blessed Redeemer, Jesus Christ.

This morning, here is my plan. First, I will prove that he really does stay closer than a brother. Then, as briefly as I can, I will show you why he stays closer than a brother. And last, I will give you some lessons we can learn from this teaching, that Jesus Christ is a faithful Friend.
I. So first, dear friends, we say that CHRIST IS “A FRIEND WHO STAYS CLOSER THAN A BROTHER.”
To prove this with facts, we turn to those of you who have had him as your friend.
Won’t each of you say right away that this is simply the truth, not stretched one bit?

He loved you before any world existed. Long before the morning star sent its light across the darkness, before an angel had ever flapped its wings through the empty skies, before anything at all had come out of nothingness, God, our God, had set his heart on all his children.
Since then, has he ever wavered even once? Has he ever turned aside or changed?
No. Those of you who have tasted his love and know his grace will back me up. He has been a friend you can count on when nothing else is certain.

blocks.x:
“He has always stood right by your side.
His kind love—oh, how good it is!”

s: You fell into sin with Adam. Did he stop loving you?
No. He became the second Adam to rescue you.
Then you sinned in your own life, and you brought God’s judgment down on your head. You deserved his anger, his full fury. Did he give up on you then? No!

blocks.x:
“He saw you ruined when mankind fell,
Yet he loved you in spite of it all.”

s: He sent his preacher after you, and you looked down on him. He preached the good news in your ears, and you laughed at him. You broke God’s day of rest, and you treated his Word with contempt.
Did he give up on you then? No!

blocks.x:
“He was set on saving you, so he watched over your path,
While you, Satan’s blind slave, were playing games with death.”

s: And at last his grace stopped you in your tracks. He humbled you. He made you sorry for your sins. He brought you to his feet, and he forgave you all your sins.
Since then, has he ever left you?
You have often left him. But has he ever left you?
You have had many hard times and troubles. Has he ever walked out on you?
Has he ever turned his heart away from you and shut off his tender love?
No, children of God. You owe it to him to say “No,” and to tell others how faithful he is.
You have gone through terrible suffering and dangerous situations. Did your friend walk out on you then?
Other people have been unfaithful to you. Someone who ate at your table has turned against you. But has Christ ever abandoned you?
Has there ever been a moment when you could go to him and say, “Master, you have betrayed me”?
Even in the darkest hour of your sorrow, could you ever dare to say he was not faithful?
Could you dare to say about him, “Lord, you promised something and did not do it”?
Won’t you say right now, “Not one good thing the Lord God promised has failed. Every bit of it has come true”?
And are you afraid that he may still leave you one day?
Then go and ask the shining ones who stand before God’s throne—“You spirits who are now in glory!
Did Christ abandon you?
You have crossed the river Jordan. Did he leave you there?
You have gone down into the black flood of death. Did he abandon you there?
You have stood before God’s throne. Did he turn his back on you then?”

And they answered, “No. Through all the troubles of our lives, in all the bitterness of death, in all the pain of our last moments, and in all the terror of God’s judgment, he has been with us. He has been ‘a friend who stays closer than a brother.’”
Of all the millions of people God has rescued, he has not abandoned even one.
They have been poor, looked down on, and in trouble. But he has never turned away from their prayers, and he has never stopped doing them good.
He has always been with them.

blocks.x:
“For his mercy will last forever,
Always faithful, always sure.”

s: But I will not spend more time on this. I cannot prove it to people who do not know God. And for those who do know God, it is already proven, because they have lived it. So I hardly need to do more than state the fact: Christ is a faithful friend. He is a friend in every moment of need and every time of trouble.

blocks.x: II. And now I need to tell you THE REASONS WHY WE CAN COUNT ON CHRIST TO BE A FAITHFUL FRIEND.

s: Some things about who he is make it certain that he will stay close to his people.
1. Real friendship can only be made between people who are true and genuine.
Honor lives in the heart.
Bad people can never have a friendship that lasts.

Bad people may pretend to love each other. But their friendship is like a rope made of sand. It will break the moment it suits them. But if a man has a sincere heart, and he is honest and noble, then we can trust him.
Spenser says it in fine old English poetry—

blocks.x:
“No, that kind of friendship can never last long,
No matter how bright and fine it looks,
If it serves a bad cause or leads to an evil end,
For goodness is the band that ties hearts together most firmly.”

s: But who can find any stain on the character of Jesus? Who can spoil his good name?
Has his shield of honor ever had a single spot on it?
Has his flag ever been dragged through the dirt?
Isn’t he the true witness in heaven, the faithful and fair one?
Isn’t it said about him that he is God, who cannot lie?
Haven’t we found him to be like that right up to this moment? We know that he is the “Holy, holy, holy Lord.” So can’t we trust him to stay closer to us than a brother?
His goodness guarantees that he will stay faithful. He cannot let us down.
2. A sure sign that a friend is loyal is that he is honest with us about our faults.
You can count on the person who will tell you about your faults in a kind and thoughtful way.
Two-faced people who suck up to you, and sneaky flatterers, are the garbage and leftovers of friendship.
They are just parasites living on that noble tree.
But true friends trust you enough to tell you openly about your faults.

Give me a friend who will be honest about me to my face. I want someone who will not go telling one neighbor and then another. I want someone who will come straight to my house and say, “Sir, I see this particular thing in you. As your brother, I have to tell you about it.”

That man is a true friend. He has proved it. After all, no one ever praises us for pointing out people’s faults. We are more likely to make them dislike us. A person will sometimes thank you for it, but he usually does not like you any more than before.
We all love praise.

The other day I met a man who said flattery had no effect on him at all. I was walking with him at the time. I turned to him rather sharply and said, “Well, sir, at least you seem to be very good at flattering yourself. That is exactly what you are doing when you say flattery has no effect on you.”
“You cannot flatter me,” he said.
I answered, “I can if I want to try. And maybe I will before the day is over.”

I found I could not flatter him directly. So I started by saying what a fine child he had. He soaked it up like a delicious drink. And when I praised this thing and that thing that belonged to him, I could see he was very easy to flatter. It just could not be direct. It had to be in a roundabout way.

All of us can be flattered. We like its soothing comfort, as long as no one calls it flattery. We have a holy horror of flattery when it goes by that name. But call it anything else, and we drink it in, just as an ox drinks water.
Now, child of God, has Christ ever flattered you?
Hasn’t he told you about your faults very honestly?
Hasn’t he pricked your conscience, even about things you hoped to cover up—your little secret sins?
Hasn’t he stirred up your conscience until it thundered terrifying warnings in your ears because of the wrong things you did?
Well, then, you can trust him. He shows the kind of faithfulness that makes someone truly trustworthy.
So I have shown you that there are reasons in who he is that let us trust him.
3. Next, there are some things about his friendship that make us sure we will not be fooled when we put our trust in him.
True friendship should not grow up too fast.
As the colorful old writer Master Fuller says: “Let friendship climb slowly to its height. If it rushes up, it may soon run out of breath.”
That is exactly right.
I think it was Joanna Baillie who said—

blocks.x:
“Friendship is not a plant that grows fast.
Even when it is planted in the deep, firm soil of respect,
It needs the slow, patient care of kind time together
Before it grows to its full strength.”

s: Jonah, it is no use trusting the vine over your head. It will not help you much. It sprang up in one night, and it may wither in one night.

It is the strong, sturdy oak that has grown for ages that will stand through the storm. It will spread out its branches like wings to shade you from the sun. And later, when it is gray and old and its branches shake in the wind, it can even give you a shelter inside its trunk if you need it.
Friendship is real when it starts. But we have to have someone’s friendship for a long time before we can say he will stay closer than a brother.
So how long has Christ loved you?
You cannot even say.

Before time began, he loved you. When this world was a baby, wrapped in blankets of mist, he loved you. Before anyone started building the ancient pyramids, his heart was set on you. And ever since you were born, he has loved you deeply.
He looked at you in your cradle, and he loved you then. He promised himself to you when you were a tiny baby only a hand’s length long. And he has loved you ever since.
I see some of you with gray hair, and some of you completely bald with age. He has loved you all this time. Will he leave you now?
Oh, no! His friendship is so old that it has to last. It has grown strong through so many storms. It has put down deep roots through so many winds of trouble. It cannot help but last. It must stand.

It is like the granite peak of a mountain. It will not melt, because, unlike the snow, it has stood up to the wind and put up with the heat of the burning sun. It has always stood tall, taking every blow that nature throws at it, and yet it has not moved or been harmed.
It will last, because it has already lasted.
And even when the elements melt and flow away in a river of fire, Christ’s friendship will still be there. It is older than they are.

He must be “a friend who stays closer than a brother.” His friendship is ancient. It is as white with age as his own head, about which it is said, “His head and his hair are white as snow, as white as wool.”
