4. But notice something else. The kind of friendship that lasts does not start at parties, and it does not grow fat on fun and games.
Young lady, you talk about a dear friend you met last night at a dance.
Please, I beg you, do not misuse that word. If you only met him there, he is not a friend. Real friends are better than the kind that grow in the greenhouse of pleasure.
Friendship is a plant that lasts much longer than those.
So you have a friend, do you?
Yes, and he owns a pair of horses and has a fine household.

Ah! But the best way to test your friend is to know that he will still be your friend when you do not even have a poor little cottage. He will stay your friend when you have no home and no clothes and have to beg for food.
That is how you would really test a friend.
Give me a friend who was born in winter, whose cradle was rocked in the storm. That friend will last.
Our fair-weather friends will run away from us.
I would rather have a robin as a friend than a swallow. A swallow only stays with us in the summer, but a robin comes to us in the winter.
The friends who hold on tight are the ones who come closest to us when we are in the most trouble. But people who rush off when hard times come are not friends.
Believer, do you have any reason to fear that Christ will leave you now?
Hasn’t he been with you in the house where people were grieving?
You found your friend where people find pearls, “in deep caves, where darkness lives.” You found Jesus in your time of trouble.

It was when you were sick in bed that you first learned how precious his name is. It was in a time of terrible inner pain that you first reached out and grabbed the edge of his robe. And ever since then, your closest and sweetest times with him have been in the dark hours.

Well, then, think of such a friend. He was proven faithful in the house of sorrow. He gave his heart’s blood for you, and he poured out his soul in one great river of blood. A friend like that never can and never will abandon you. He stays closer than a brother.
5. Also, a friend you win by doing something foolish will never last.

Do something foolish, and you may make a man your friend. But that is just two people teaming up in wrongdoing. You will soon find out his friendship is worthless. You are better off without a friendship you get by doing wrong.

Oh, how many silly friendships spring up that are nothing but gushy feelings! They have no roots at all. They are like the plant our Savior talks about: “It shot up quickly because the soil was not deep.”

Jesus Christ’s friendship is not like that. There is nothing foolish in it at all. He loves us wisely. He does not wink at our foolish ways or quietly go along with them. Instead, he fills us with his wisdom.
His love is wise. He chose us according to his wise plan. He did not choose blindly or carelessly, but with complete good sense and care.
Under this same point, I can also say that a friendship built on not really knowing someone is not worth much.
I do not want anyone to call himself my friend if he does not know me.
Let him love me as much as he knows me.
If he loves me for the little he knows, then when he learns more he may drop me.
“That man,” someone says, “seems to be very nice.”
“I am sure I could love him,” says another, as he studies his face.

Yes, but do not write down “friend” yet. Wait a little while until you know more about him. Just watch him, look him over, try him, test him. Only then should you put him on your precious list of friends.
Be friendly to everyone, but do not make anyone your friend until they know you and you know them.
Many friendships that started in the dark, when people did not really know each other, have suddenly died once the light came on and they got to know each other better.
You thought people were different from how they really were. And when you found out what they were really like, you stopped caring about them.
I remember someone once said to me, “I really like you, sir,” and he told me a certain reason why.
I answered, “My dear fellow, your reason is completely wrong. The very thing you love me for is not true of me, and I hope it never will be.”
So I told him, “I really cannot accept your friendship if it is based on misunderstanding something I may have said.”
But our Lord Jesus can never abandon those he has once loved. He can never discover anything in us worse than what he already knew. He knew everything about us ahead of time.

He saw our leprosy, and he still loved us. He knew how deceitful we were and how little we believed, and still he hugged us close to his heart. He knew what poor fools we were, and still he said he would never leave us or abandon us.
He knew we would rebel against him and ignore his advice many times. He knew that even when we loved him, our love would be cold and weak. But he loved us for his own sake.
So surely he will stay closer than a brother.
6. Here is another point. For friendship and love to be real, they must be shown in actions, not just in words.
Friendship that is nothing but polite compliments is the style of our time. That is because this is an age of lies.
The world is one big house of fakes.
Wherever you go in London, fakeness stares you in the face. You can find very few things that are real.
I do not just mean tricks in business, or food that has been secretly mixed with cheaper stuff, and things like that.
Lying is not only found in shops.
It is everywhere in society. Even the church is not free of it.
The preacher puts on a fake voice.
You hardly ever hear a man talk in the pulpit the way he would talk in his living room.

Why, I sometimes hear fellow preachers at tea or dinner speaking in a very relaxed, normal English voice. But when they get into their pulpits, they put on a holier-than-thou tone and fill their mouths with puffed-up words. Or else they whine in the most pitiful way.
They bring the pulpit down by pretending to honor it. They speak in a voice God never meant any human being to have.
This is the great house of fakes. And little things like this show which way the wind is blowing.
You leave your calling card at a friend’s house. That counts as an act of friendship—the card!
I wonder, if he were short of money, would you leave him your bank book!
You write “My dear sir” and “Yours very truly.” It is fake. You do not mean it.
“Dear!” That is a sacred word. It should only be used for people you really love. But now we put up with lies as if they were true, and we call them good manners.
They may be good manners. But in many cases, they are lies.
Now, Christ’s love is not found in words, but in actions.
He does not say, “My dear people.” Instead, he opened up his heart, and we could see what was in it.
He does not just come and say, “Dearly beloved.” He hangs on the cross, and there we read “Dearly beloved” written in red letters.
He does not come to us first with kisses from his lips. He gives us blessings with both hands. He gives himself for us, and then he gives himself to us.
Do not trust a friend who only pays compliments. Rely on the person who gives you real gifts worth having, and who does things for you that show his heart is true.
A friend like that—and Jesus is that kind of friend—“stays closer than a brother.”
7. One more point, and I hope I will not tire you out.
A friend you buy will never last long.
Give a man something nineteen times, then say no the twentieth time, and he will hate you. His love only came from your gifts.

If I could buy someone’s love with gold, I would sell it for trash. If I could buy a friendship with pearls, I would trade it away for pebbles. It would be worthless, so the sooner it was gone, the better.
But oh, believer, Christ’s love was never bought.
You did not bring him any gift.
When Jacob’s sons went to Egypt, he said, “Take the man a gift: a little oil, a little healing balm, some nuts and almonds.” But you took Christ no gifts at all.
When you came to him, you said,

blocks.x:
“I bring nothing in my hands;
I simply hold on to your cross.”

s: You did not even promise to love him. Your heart was so unfaithful that you did not dare to say it.
You asked him to make you love him. That was the most you could do.
He loved you for nothing at all. He loved you simply because he chose to.
Well, a love that lived on nothing but its own supplies will not starve just because you give so little back. A love that grew in a rocky heart like yours will not die for lack of soil.
That love sprang up in a dry desert, in your soul that had no water. It will never, never die for lack of water. It must live. It cannot die.
Jesus must be “a friend who stays closer than a brother.”
8. Should I stop and give you more reasons?
I will just mention one more. It is this: nothing could ever possibly happen that would make Christ love us less.
You ask, how can that be?
One man loves his friend. But suddenly he becomes rich, and now he says, “I am more important than I used to be. I will forget my old friends.”
But Christ cannot become any richer. He is as rich as anyone can be. His riches have no limit.

He loves you now. So it is impossible that he will leave you because his own glory has grown. Everlasting glory already crowns his head. He can never become more glorious or great than he is. So he will keep on loving you.

Other times, one friend becomes poorer, and then the other friend leaves him. But you can never become poorer than you are right now. Right now you are “a poor sinner and nothing at all.” You have nothing of your own. Everything you have is borrowed. He gave you all of it.
So he cannot love you less because you have become poorer. When you have nothing, you are as poor as anyone can be. You can never sink any lower.
That is why Christ must love you, even with all your nakedness and all your poverty.
“But I may turn out to be sinful,” you say.
Yes, but you cannot be any more sinful than he already knew you would be. And he loved you anyway, knowing ahead of time about every one of your sins.

So when it happens, it will not surprise him at all. He knew it all ahead of time, and he cannot turn away from his love. Nothing could ever possibly happen that would pull the Savior away from his love for his people, or pull his people away from their love for their Savior.
He is “a friend who stays closer than a brother.”
III. Now, then, HERE IS A CONCLUSION WE CAN DRAW FROM THIS.

Lavater says, “Your friends and your enemies will be alike. If your friends are cold, your enemies will be cold. If your friends are halfhearted, your enemies will be halfhearted. If your enemies are fierce, your friends will be warm.”
Since I know this is true, I have often felt pleased with myself when my enemies have said fierce things against me.
I have thought, “Well, my friends love me strongly and firmly. Let my enemies be as angry as they like. It only shows that my friends are just as firm in their love.”
So here is the conclusion we draw. If Christ stays close, and he is our friend, then our enemies will also stay close. They will never leave us alone until we die.

Christian, because Christ stays close, the devil will stay close too. He will keep coming at you and hanging around you. That dog of hell will never stop howling until you reach the other side of the Jordan. There is no place in this world that is out of reach of that great enemy’s bow. Until you have crossed the river, his arrows can reach you, and they will.

If Christ gave himself for you, the devil will do everything he can to destroy you. If Christ has been patient with you, Satan will keep at it, hoping Christ might forget you. He will chase after you, and keep chasing, until he sees you safely landed in heaven.
But do not be discouraged. The louder Satan roars, the more proof you will have of Christ’s love.
Old Rutherford said, “Give me, give me a roaring devil rather than a sleeping one. Sleeping devils make me doze off, but roaring ones push me to run to my Master.”
So be glad if the world yells at you, and if your enemies attack you fiercely.
Christ is just as full of love for you as they are full of hate. So,

blocks.x:
“Stand firm and be strong;
Let grace be your shield, and let Christ be your song.”

s: And now I have a question to ask. I am asking it of every man and every woman here, and of every child too: Is Jesus Christ your friend?
Do you have a friend at court—at the court of heaven?
Is the judge of the living and the dead your friend?
Can you say that you love him? And has he ever shown you his love?
Dear listener, do not answer that question for the person next to you. Answer it for yourself.
Noble or farmworker, rich or poor, educated or unable to read, this question is for each one of you. So ask it: Is Christ my friend?
Have you ever thought about that question?
Have you ever asked it?
Oh, to be able to say “Christ is my friend” is one of the sweetest things in the world!
One day a man who had lived a very sinful life happened to walk into a church.
Before the sermon, they sang this hymn—

blocks.x: “Jesus, Lover of my soul.”

s: The next day a man he knew met him and asked how he liked the sermon.
He said, “I don’t know. But there were two or three words that gripped me so hard I didn’t know what to do with myself.
The minister read out that hymn, ‘Jesus, Lover of my soul.’
Ah!” he said—and he was not a religious man at all—“if I could say that, I would give up everything I own!
But do you think,” he asked, “that Jesus will ever be the lover of a man like me?
‘Jesus, Lover of my soul!’
Oh, if only I could say it!”
And then he buried his face in his hands and cried.
I have every reason to fear that he went back to his sin and stayed the same as before.
But you see, his conscience was awake enough to show him how precious it is to have Christ as the one who loves you and as your friend.
Ah, rich man, you have many friends.

There are some people here who have worked hard for the good of their country. They deserve to be honored by their country. But because of one mistake—or something that maybe was a mistake—they have been ignored by too many people who once seemed to be their most loyal supporters.
Oh, you great and rich people, do not put your trust in the loyalty of your friends.
David once said in a hurry, “Everyone is a liar.” One day you may have to say it after calmly thinking it over.
And oh, you kind and loving people, who are not rich in money but are rich in love—and that is the best wealth in the world—add this golden coin to your silver ones, and it will make them all holy.
Let Christ pour his love into your hearts. Then your mother’s love, your daughter’s love, your husband’s love, and your wife’s love will become sweeter than ever.
The love of Christ does not push out your love for your family. Instead, it makes all our loves holy and much sweeter.

Remember, dear listener, the love of men and women is very sweet. But all of it must pass away. So what will you do when death comes, if your only riches are riches that fade away, and your only love is a love that dies?
Oh, to have the love of Christ!

You can take that love with you across the river of death. You can wear it like a bracelet in heaven and set it like a seal on your hand. His love is “as strong as death and more powerful than the grave.”
I think it was good old Bishop Beveridge who, when he was dying, did not recognize his closest friends.
Someone asked him, “Bishop Beveridge, do you know me?”
He said, “Who are you?” When they told him the name, he said, “No.” “But don’t you know your wife, Bishop?”
“What is her name?” he asked.
She said, “I am your wife.”
“I didn’t know I had one,” he said.
Poor old man! His mind had completely failed him.
At last someone bent down and whispered, “Do you know the Lord Jesus Christ?”
“Yes,” he said, struggling to speak. “I have known him for forty years, and I can never forget him.”
It is amazing how memory holds on to Jesus when it cannot hold on to anyone else. And it is just as amazing that,

blocks.x: “When everything God made has run dry, Christ’s fullness stays the same.”

s: My dear listeners, please think about this.
Oh, I wish you would make Christ your friend! He will never be your friend while you think you are good enough on your own. He will never be your friend while you keep living in sin.
But do you believe you are guilty?
Do you want to stop sinning?
Do you want to be saved?
Do you want to be made new?
Then let me tell you: my Master loves you!
You poor, weak, helpless worms, my Master’s heart is full of love for you. Right now his eyes are looking down on you with pity.
“O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, Jerusalem!”
He is telling me now to say that he died for all of you who admit you are sinners and truly feel it.
He tells me to say to you, “Put your trust in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved.”
He tells me to announce a salvation that is full and free. It is full, so it needs nothing from you to help it. It is free, so it needs nothing from you to pay for it.

blocks.x:
“Come, all who are thirsty, you are welcome;
Praise God for his free gifts:
Real faith and real turning from sin,
Every grace that brings us close—
Without money,
Come to Jesus Christ and buy.”

s: There is nothing I feel I fail at more than speaking to sinners.
Oh, I wish I could cry my heart out and preach my heart out, to you and at you!

blocks.x:
“Dear Savior, draw hearts that hold back,
Let sinners run to you
And take the joy your love gives;
And drink, and never die.”

s: I say goodbye with this one thought: we will never all meet together here again.

It is a very serious thought. But judging by the way life goes and how many people die, even if all of you wanted to come back here next Sunday morning, it is very unlikely that all of you would still be alive. One person out of this congregation will surely have died by then.
Goodbye to you who are going to die. I do not know where you are. Maybe it is that strong man over there, or that young woman over there with the feverish red cheeks of tuberculosis.
I do not know who is going to die. But right now I very seriously say goodbye to that person.
Goodbye, poor soul. And is it goodbye forever?
Will we meet in the life to come, in the home of the blessed? Or am I saying goodbye to you now forever?
I do seriously say goodbye to you forever, if you live and die without Christ.
But I cannot stand that gloomy thought. So I say to you, poor sinner, stop and think. Think about the way you are living. And now “turn back, turn back! Why will you die?”
“Why will you die?”
“Why will you die?”
“Why will you die?”
Ah, you cannot answer that question.
May God help you answer it in a better way, by saying, “Here I am, Lord!

blocks.x:
Just as I am, with no excuse to give,
Except that your blood was shed for me,
O Son of God, I come to you.

s: I trust my soul to your kind hands.”
May the Lord bless you all for Christ’s sake! Amen.
“We love him, because he loved us first.” — 1 John 4:19
For the last two Sundays I have been preaching the good news to people who have not yet turned to God.

I have strongly urged even the very worst sinners to look to Jesus Christ. I told them that they do not need good works or a good attitude to get ready to come to Christ. They can come just as they are, to the foot of the cross. There they can receive the blood that forgives and everything the Lord Jesus Christ has earned for them, which is all they need.
Since then, a thought has come to me. Some people who do not understand the gospel might ask, “Will this help people live good lives?”
If the gospel announces forgiveness even to the very worst sinners, won’t that give people permission to sin?
In what way can the gospel be called a message that leads to holiness?
What effect will preaching like this have?
Will it make people better?
Will they pay more attention to the rules about how people treat one another?
Will they obey the commands about how people relate to God more closely?

So I thought we would go one step further this morning. I want to show you something about the gospel of God. At the start, it speaks to people who have nothing good in them at all. Yet it is meant to lead those very people to the highest kind of goodness. Yes, in the end it leads them to perfect holiness.
Our text tells us what happens when the gospel is welcomed into someone’s heart. It pushes and drives that heart to love God.
“We love him, because he loved us first.”

When the gospel comes to us, it does not find us loving God. It does not expect anything from us. Instead, the Holy Spirit brings it home to us, and it simply tells us that God loves us, no matter how deep we are in sin. Then this message of love has a result: “we love him because he loved us first.”
Can you imagine a being who is placed halfway between this world and heaven?
Can you picture him with such great powers that he could easily see what was happening in heaven and what was happening on earth?

I can imagine that, before humanity fell into sin, such a being would have been amazed by something. He would have noticed the wonderful harmony between God’s great world, called heaven, and the little world, the earth.

Whenever the bells of heaven rang, the great note of those huge bells was love. And when the little bells of earth were rung, and this small world sounded its music, the note was exactly the same: love.
The shining spirits gathered around God’s great throne in heaven to praise the Lord. At that same moment you could see the world dressed like a priest, offering its gift of the purest praise.

The cherubim and seraphim kept crying out, “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of armies.” And a note was heard coming up from paradise. It was perhaps weaker, but it was just as sweet: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of armies.”
There was no clash and no sour note. The thunder of heaven’s music matched the whispers of earth’s music exactly.
There was “glory to God in the highest,” and there was glory on earth too. The heart of man was like the heart of God. God loved man, and man loved God.
But now imagine that same great Spirit still standing between heaven and earth. How sad he must be when he hears the clashing noise and feels it scrape against his ear!
The Lord says, “I have made peace with you. I have taken away your sin.” But what does this earth answer?
The world answers, “Man is God’s enemy. God may be willing to make peace, but man is not.
Most people are still God’s enemies because of the evil things they do.”

When the angels praise God, they may listen to the sounds coming from earth. If they do, they hear the trumpet of cruel war. They hear the shouts of drunken parties and the songs of people who live for lust. What a clash that is in the great harmony of the universe!

Here is the truth. The world was once one great string on the harp of the universe. When the Almighty swept his kind fingers across that harp, nothing could be heard but praise. Now that string has snapped. Where grace has put it back, it is still not fully in tune. The note that comes from it has very little sweetness and a great deal of clashing.
But, shining Spirit, stay where you are, and live on.
The day is racing toward us on glowing wheels, and its axle is hot from the speed.
The day is coming when this world will be a paradise again.

Jesus Christ came the first time to bleed and suffer, so that he could wash the world clean of its sin. He is coming a second time to reign and win, so that he can dress the earth in glory. And the day will come when you, Spirit, will hear that everlasting harmony again.
Once again the bells of earth will be tuned to the music of heaven. Once again the eternal choir will find that no singer is missing and the music is complete.
But how will this happen?
How will the world be brought back?
How will it be restored?

Here is our answer. At the beginning there was harmony between earth and heaven because there was love between the two. And here is our great reason for hoping that perfect harmony between heaven and earth will one day be set up again. God has already shown his love to us. And in return, hearts that his grace has touched already love him now. When there are many more of those hearts, and love is set up again, the harmony will be complete.
Now that I have introduced my text, I must dive right into it.
We will look at where love comes from, what feeds it, and how it walks. And I will urge all the believers here to love God, because he loved them first.
I. First, WHERE TRUE LOVE FOR GOD COMES FROM.
A planet has no light except the light that comes from the sun. The moon has no light except borrowed light. In the same way, there is no true love in the heart except the love that comes from God.
Love is the light, the life, and the way of the whole universe.
And God is life, and light, and the way. Best of all, God is love.
All our love for God must flow out of this overflowing fountain, God’s endless love.
This will always be a great and certain truth: we love him for one reason only, because he loved us first.
Some people think that you could come to love God just by thinking about the things he has made.
We do not believe that.
We have heard a lot about philosophers who admire nature. And we agree that you can easily admire God when you study the things he has made.

We have heard a lot about explorers who are filled with wonder. We agree that a mind must be very low indeed if it does not wonder when it looks at God’s works. Sometimes we have also heard of a love for God that grew out of beautiful scenery. But we have never believed that such a love exists.

We do believe this: when love has already been born in someone’s heart, all the wonders of God’s care and creation can stir that love up again, because it is already there. But we do not believe, and we cannot believe, that just looking at God’s works could ever lift anyone up to real love. We have never seen it happen even once.
In fact, this big question has already been tested, and the answer was no.
Listen to what the poet says:

blocks.x:
“The spicy breezes may blow softly over the island of Java;
every view there is lovely, and only man is wicked.”

s: In the places where God shows off his works most brightly and gives his gifts most freely, people have been the most wicked and God has been the most forgotten.
Other people have taught that human nature can reach love for God on its own. Maybe they did not say it in so many words, but their teaching leads there.
Our simple answer is that we have never seen it happen.
We have carefully asked God’s people about this, and we believe others have asked them in every age. But we have only ever gotten one answer to this question: “Why have you loved God?”
The only answer has been, “Because he loved me first.”
I have heard people preach about free will. But I have never yet heard of a Christian who gave the credit to free will when he talked about his own life.

I have heard people say that humans can turn to God by their own free choice, and believe, and repent, and love. But I have heard those very same people describe their own experience differently. They say they did not turn to God that way. Instead, Jesus came looking for them when they were strangers, wandering away from God’s sheep pen.
The whole idea may sound convincing when it is preached. But when you actually feel it in your own life, it turns out to be a ghost.

A man might think it is fine to tell someone else that his own free will can save him. But when he has an honest talk with his own conscience, he has to say something else, no matter how wild his teaching is. He has to say, “Oh, yes, I do love Jesus, because he loved me first.”

I have been amazed at a Wesleyan brother. Sometimes he has attacked this teaching from the pulpit. Then he has announced this very hymn, and all the church members have sung it with all their hearts. Yet while they sang, they were ringing the funeral bell for their own special beliefs. For if that hymn is true, then Arminianism must be false.

Suppose it is a sure fact that we love God only because his love has been poured into our hearts. Then it simply cannot be true that anyone ever did or ever will love God before God has first shown his love to that person.
But let’s stop arguing. Don’t we all agree that our love for God is the sweet child of God’s love for us?
Oh, dear friends, anyone can have cold admiration. But the warmth of love can only be lit by the fire of God’s Spirit.
Let each Christian speak for himself. We will all hold on to this great and central truth: we love God because of the sweet influence of his grace.
Sometimes I am amazed that people like us were ever brought to love God at all.
Is our love so precious that God would try to win it, dressed in the red robes of a dying Redeemer?
If we had loved God, that would have been no more than he deserved.
But we rebelled, and he still went after our love. That was truly surprising.

It was a wonder when he took off all his glory, came down, and wrapped himself in a body of clay. But I think there is an even greater wonder. After he had died for us, we still did not love him. We rebelled against him. We rejected the message of the gospel. We resisted his Spirit. But he said, “I will have their hearts.” And he followed us day after day, hour after hour.
Sometimes he brought us down low, and he said, “Surely they will love me if I lift them up again!”
At other times he filled us with grain and wine, and he said, “Surely they will love me now.” But we still turned away. We still rebelled.
At last he said, “I will not keep struggling. I am the Almighty. I will not let a human heart be stronger than I am.

I turn a person’s will the way streams of water are turned.” And look! He used his power, and in a moment the current changed. We loved him, because now we could see God’s love in sending his Son to be our Redeemer.

But, dear friends, let’s go back to the truth we started with. We must admit that we would never have had any love for God if God had not planted it in us. His love for us was the sweet seed it grew from.
If anyone here loves Christ and disagrees with this teaching, let him disagree for now. But let him know that he will not disagree later. For in heaven they all sing praise to God’s free grace.
They all sing, “Salvation belongs to our God and to the Lamb.”
II. So love’s parent is the love of God poured into our hearts.
But once God has brought love to life in our hearts, God must also FEED it.
Love is like a plant from a faraway country. It does not grow naturally in human soil.

Love for God is a rich and rare thing. If it were left out in the icy winds of our selfishness, it would freeze and die. If the only food it got came from the rock of our own hard hearts, it would starve.
Love comes from heaven, so it must eat bread from heaven.
It cannot survive in this desert unless it is cared for from above and fed with manna from heaven.
So what does love feed on?
Well, it feeds on love.
The very thing that gave it life becomes its food.
“We love him because he loved us first.”
What keeps our love for God moving, and what keeps it going, is his love for us.
And I should point out that this great storehouse of love has different kinds of food.
When we are first made new, the only food we can live on is milk. That is because we are just babies and are not yet strong enough to eat deeper truths.
So the first thing our love feeds on while it is still a baby is knowing how much kindness it has received.
Ask a young Christian why he loves Christ. He will tell you, “I love Christ because he bought me with his blood!”
“Why do you love God the Father?”
“I love God the Father because he gave his Son for me.”
“And why do you love God the Spirit?”
“I love him because he has made my heart new.”
In other words, we love God for what he has given us.
Our first love lives on simple food: remembering with thanks the kindness we have received.
And notice this: no matter how much we grow in grace, this will always be a big part of what feeds our love.
But as the Christian grows older and has more grace, he loves Christ for another reason.
He loves Christ because he feels that Christ deserves to be loved.
I hope I can say that I now have a love for God in my heart that has nothing to do with my own salvation.
I feel that even now I have to love him, because his character is more lovely than words can say.

His love for other people seems like such a great thought to me. So, apart from what I get out of it, I hope I can say that I love Christ. I have seen something of Christ in the roles he fills, and something of the thrilling beauty of who he is as both God and man.

I feel as if I could come to his feet and say, “Sweet Lord, at first I loved you because of your gifts to me. But now it is the look in your eyes. You have thrilled my spirit with the glory of who you are. Now I love you, not just because I have eaten your bread and you have met my needs. I love you for who you are.” But notice: at the same time, we must always mix this with the old reason.

We must still feel that we start from that first stepping-stone, loving Christ because of his mercies. We have climbed higher. We have come to love him with a love that has a better reason. Even so, we still bring the old reason along with us.
We love him because he has been kind to us.

In fact, I really think a person can be so full of the love of Christ, and so strengthened by God’s grace, that he rises to an amazing level of love for Christ. If you could hear him speak, you would sit there in wonder, as if an angel were talking to you.
Have you ever read the heavenly letter of Rutherford?
I really think that if any bit of the old inspiration that guided Solomon’s pen is still left among people, it rested on Rutherford.
If you read the poems of sweet George Herbert, oh, how sweetly he sings about his Master!
If any of heaven’s harps was accidentally left behind on earth, George Herbert found one. He played its living strings with such heavenly skill that he made every string point to his Master.

These men did not love Christ only because of what he had done for them. You will find in their poems and letters that they loved him because he had spent close time with them. He had shown them his hands and his side. They had walked with him in the villages. They had rested with him on the beds of spices. They had entered the secret circle of friendship with him. And they felt that they loved Christ because he was glorious all over. He was so heavenly beautiful that if all nations could see him, surely they would be moved to love him too.
This, then, is what love feeds on. But when love grows rich (and sometimes it does), even the most loving heart grows cold toward Christ.
Did you know that the only food that suits sick love is the food it ate at the beginning?

I have heard doctors say that when a person is sick, the best place for him is the place where he was born. In the same way, if love gets sick and cold, the best place for it to go is the place where it was born: the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
Where was love born?
Was she born among romantic scenery? Was she raised on beautiful thoughts, sitting on the lap of beauty?

Oh, no. Was she born on the steep slopes of Mount Sinai, when God came from Sinai and the Holy One came from Mount Paran? When he melted the mountains with the touch of his foot and made the rocks run down like wax before his terrifying presence?
Oh, no. Was love born on Mount Tabor, when the Savior was transfigured and his clothes became whiter than wool, whiter than anyone could ever wash them?
Oh, no. Darkness rushed over the eyes of those who looked at him then. They fell asleep, because the glory was too much for them.
Let me tell you where love was born.

Love was born in the garden of Gethsemane, where Jesus sweated great drops of blood. It was raised in Pilate’s hall, where Jesus bared his back to the whip that cut into it like a plow. There he let his body be spit on and beaten.
Love was raised at the cross, among the groans of a dying God, under the drops of his blood. That is where love was raised.
Children of God, you can back me up.
Where did your love come from, if not from the foot of the cross?
Have you ever seen that sweet flower growing anywhere except at the foot of Calvary?

No. It was when you saw “love divine, all loves excelling,” going beyond even itself. You saw love tied up by its own choice, dying by its own blow. You saw it lay down its life, even though it had the power to keep it and to take it up again. That is where your love was born. So if your love is sick and you want it to get better, take it to those sweet places. Make it sit in the shade of the olive trees. Make it stand on the stone pavement and stare while the blood is still pouring down.
Take it to the cross, and tell it to look and see the bleeding Lamb all over again. Surely this will make your love grow from a dwarf into a giant. This will fan it from a spark into a flame.
And then, once your love has been built back up like this, let me urge you to give your love plenty of exercise, because that will make it grow.
You ask, “Where should I exercise my love by thinking, so that it will grow?”
Oh, sacred Dove of love, spread your wings and be an eagle now!
Come! Open your eyes wide and look straight into the face of the Sun. Fly upward, upward, upward, far above the highest heights of this created world. Keep going up until you are lost in eternity.
Remember that God loved you before the world was even made.
Doesn’t this make your love stronger?
Oh, how fresh and bracing the air of eternity is!
When I fly up into it for a moment and think about the great teaching of election—about

blocks.x:
“That vast love that no one can measure,
which from long ago
held all the chosen children close,
like sheep inside the fold.”

s: It brings tears to our eyes to think that we have a share in that decision made in the council of the Almighty Three. At that time, the name of every person who would be bought with blood was written in God’s eternal book.
Come, soul, I tell you now to stretch your wings a little. See if this does not make you love God.
He thought about you before you even existed.

He did this before there was a sun or a moon. The sun, the moon, and the stars were still asleep in God’s mind, like unborn forests inside an acorn cup. The old sea had not yet been born. This baby world was not yet wrapped in its blanket of mist. Long before all that, God had written your name on the heart and on the hands of Christ, where it can never be erased and will stay forever.
And doesn’t this make you love God?
Isn’t this sweet exercise for your love?
This is where my text comes in. It is like the final charge in this sweet battle of love, a charge that sweeps everything out of its way.
“We love God, because he loved us first.” He loved us before time began, when he lived alone in eternity.
And when you have flown back into the eternity before time, I have another flight for you.

Fly back over your whole life. Think of how the Lord your God has led you through the desert. Think of how he has fed you and clothed you every day. He has put up with your bad manners. He has put up with all your complaining and all your longing for the meat pots of Egypt. He has opened the rock to provide for you and fed you with manna that came down from heaven.
Think of how his grace has been enough for you in all your troubles. Think of how his blood has forgiven you in all your sins. Think of how his rod and his staff have comforted you.

And when you have flown over this sweet field of love, you can fly on even further. Remember that the oath, the covenant, and the blood hold more than just the past. It is true that “he loved us first.” But that does not mean he will ever stop loving. He is the Alpha, and he will be the Omega. He is the first, and he will be the last. So think about this: when you walk through the valley of the shadow of death, you do not need to fear any evil, because he is with you.

When you stand in the cold waters of the Jordan, you do not need to be afraid, because death cannot separate you from his love. And when you enter the mysteries of eternity, you do not need to tremble. For “I am sure that no rulers, no powers, nothing now, nothing to come, nothing high, nothing deep, and nothing else that was ever made will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.”
And now, soul, isn’t your love refreshed?
Doesn’t this make you love him?
When you fly over those endless open skies of love, doesn’t it set your heart on fire? Doesn’t it make you delight in the Lord your God?
This is the food of love.
“We love him, because he loved us first.” And we love him because that first love holds a pledge and a promise that he will love us all the way to the end.
III. Now we come to the third point: the WALK OF LOVE.
“We love him.” Children of God, if Christ were here on earth, what would you do for him?
Suppose there was news tomorrow that the Son of Man had come down from heaven, as he did the first time. What would you do for him?
Suppose there was a witness you could not doubt, who said that the feet that walked the holy fields of Palestine were now walking the roads of Great Britain. What would you do for him?
Oh, I can imagine the excitement of happy hearts. So many generous hands would be held out. There would be a sea of tearful eyes looking at him.
“Do for him!” someone says. “Do for him!
If he were hungry, I would give him food, even if it were my last crust of bread.
If he were thirsty, I would give him a drink, even if my own lips were burning as if on fire.
If he had no clothes, I would take off my own and shiver in the cold to dress him.
Do for him! I would hardly know what to do.
I would rush to him and throw myself at his dear feet. I would beg him to step on me and crush me into the dust, if that would honor him, if it would lift him even one inch higher.
If he wanted a soldier, I would join his army. If he needed someone to die, I would let my body be burned, as long as he stood by to watch the sacrifice and cheer me on in the flames.”
You daughters of Jerusalem, wouldn’t you go out to meet him? Wouldn’t you celebrate with tambourines and dancing?
Then you might dance like Miriam beside the waters of Egypt, red with blood.
And we men would dance like David before the ark, jumping for joy, if Christ had come.
Ah, we think we love him so much that we would do all that. But after all, there is a serious question about whether this is really true.
Don’t you know that Christ’s wife and family are here?
And if you love him, wouldn’t it naturally follow that you would love his bride and his children?
“Ah!” someone says, “Christ has no bride on earth.”
Doesn’t he? Hasn’t he promised himself in marriage to his church?
Isn’t his church, the mother of all believers, his own chosen wife?
And didn’t he give his blood as his wedding gift for her?

And hasn’t he said that he will never divorce her, because he hates divorce? Hasn’t he said that he will complete the marriage on the last great day, when he comes to reign with his people on the earth?
And doesn’t he have children here?
“The daughters of Jerusalem and the sons of Zion—who has brought these children into being for me?”
Aren’t they the children of the everlasting Father, the Prince of Peace, the child who was born, the son who was given?
Of course they are. And if we love Christ, as we think we do and as we claim we do, we will love his church and his people.
And do you love his church?
Maybe you love the part of it you belong to.
You love the hand.
Maybe it is a hand decorated with many sparkling rings of grand ceremonies, and you love that.
Or maybe you belong to some poor, struggling denomination. Maybe it is the foot, and you love the foot. But you speak with scorn about the hand, because it has more honors.
And meanwhile, maybe you who belong to the hand are looking down on those who belong to the foot.
Brothers and sisters, all of us tend to love only one part of Christ’s body and not the whole body. But if we love him, we should love all his people.
When we kneel to pray, I am afraid that when we pray for the church, we don’t mean everything we say.
We are really praying for our own church, our own part of it.

Now think of someone who loves Christ. Say he is a Baptist. He loves the teaching about baptism, because he knows it comes from Scripture. But at the same time, whenever he sees God’s grace in anyone’s heart, he loves that person, because he is part of the living church. He does not hold back his heart, his hand, or his home from him just because they happen to disagree on one point.
I pray that the church today will have a more loving spirit toward herself.
We should be glad whenever any denomination moves forward.
Is the Church of England waking up from its sleep?
Is she rising like a phoenix from her ashes?
May God be with her, and may God bless her!
Is another denomination taking the lead, and trying through its ministers to bring wanderers into God’s house?
May God be with it!
Is the Primitive Methodist working hard in the hedges and ditches, laboring for his Master?
God help him! Is the Calvinist trying to hold up Christ crucified in all his glory?
May God be with him!

And is there another man with much less knowledge who preaches a lot of error, but still holds on to the truth that “you are saved by grace through faith”? Then God bless him, and may he have success forever.
If you loved Christ more, you would love all of Christ’s church and all of Christ’s people.

Don’t you know that Christ still has a mouth on earth, and has left a hand and a foot on earth too? If you want to prove your love for him, don’t think you cannot feed him. Don’t imagine that you cannot fill his hand or wash his feet.
You can do all of this today.
He has left behind his poor and suffering people. Their mouths are hungry because they need bread. Their tongues are dry because they need water.
You meet them. They come to you. They have nothing, and they are suffering.
Do you turn them away?
Do you know who it was you turned away at your door?
“Every time you failed to do it for one of the least important of these my brothers, you failed to do it for me.”
When you turned down a poor person’s request when you could have helped, you turned down Christ.
In reality, Christ was the man you stingily refused to give the money he needed. So your Savior was turned away at the door of someone he himself had died for.
Do you want to feed Christ?

Then open your eyes, and you will see him everywhere. In our back streets, in our lanes, in our alleys, in all our churches, in every branch of Christ’s people, you will find the poor and the suffering.
If you want to feed Christ, feed them.
But you say you are willing to wash Christ’s feet. Well, you can do that.
Doesn’t he have children who have fallen?
Aren’t there brothers who have sinned and have gotten dirty by it?
You say that if Christ’s feet were dirty, you would wash them. Then if a Christian has wandered off the path, try to bring him back, and lead him once again in the right way.
And do you want to fill Christ’s hands with your generous giving?
His church is the storehouse for his gifts to the needy. The hand of his church is stretched out for help, because she always needs it.
She has a work to do that must be finished.
She is short of what she needs because you are holding back your help. Pour your gifts into her treasury, because everything you give to her is given to the Lord Jesus Christ.
Finally, to stir up your love, let me remind you that Christ Jesus faced two tests of his love. He stood firm through them, but they are often too much for us.
When Christ was high and glorious, I am amazed that he loved us.
I have known many men who loved a friend while they were both equally poor. But then the man rose up in the world, and he was too proud to know the friend whose table he had eaten at.
Rising to a high position tests the love we have for those who are below us in rank.

Now, Christ Jesus is the Lord of heaven and the King of angels. Yet he stooped to notice us even before he came to earth, and he always called us brothers. And since he has gone up to heaven, put his crown back on, and sat down again at God’s right hand, he has never forgotten us.
His high position has never made him look down on a single disciple.
When he rode into Jerusalem in triumph, we do not read that he was too proud to admit that the humble fishermen were his followers.
And “now, though he reigns exalted high, his love is still as great.” He still calls us brothers and friends. He still admits that we share the same blood.
And yet, strangely, we have known many Christians who lost much of their love for Christ when they rose in the world.
There was a woman who used to do a lot for Christ when she was poor. Then someone left her a large sum of money. “Ah!” she said, “I cannot do as much as I used to.”
“But why is that?” someone asked.
She answered, “When I had a purse with only a shilling in it, I had a heart worth a guinea. Now that I have a purse worth a guinea, I have a heart worth only a shilling.”
For some people, getting rich is a sad temptation.

When they had little, they were happy to go to the chapel and mix with the plain, ordinary congregation. Now they have become rich. There is an expensive Turkish carpet in the living room. Their home is now too fancy for them to invite the poor members of the church, as they once did. And Christ Jesus is not fashionable enough for them to bring up anything about faith when they meet their new friends.

On top of this, they say they now have to make this visit and that visit. They must spend so much time on their clothes and on keeping up their position and reputation that they cannot find time to pray as they used to.
They skip God’s house to go to parties, and Christ has less of their heart than he ever had.
“Is this how you treat your friend?”
Have you risen so high that you are ashamed of Christ? Have you become so rich that you look down on Christ in his poverty?
How sad, poor wealth! How sad, worthless wealth! Wicked wealth!
It would be good for you if all of it were swept away, if falling into poverty would bring back the burning warmth of your love.
Here is one more thing to think about. When Christ began to suffer for us, what a test of love that was!
I am sure there are many men who truly believe and who love their Savior. Yet they would shake with fear if their love were put to the test of suffering.

My brother, imagine that today you are taken into a dark prison cell of the Inquisition. Imagine that all the horrors of the Dark Ages have come back. You are led down a long, dark staircase and rushed along, and you have no idea where you are going. At last you reach a place deep down under the ground. All around you, hanging on the walls, you see pincers and torture tools of every kind and shape.
Two inquisitors are there, and they ask you, “Are you ready to give up your false beliefs and come back into the arms of the church?”
My brothers and sisters, I think you would have enough inner strength and grace to say, “I am not ready to deny my Savior.”

But then the pincers would start to tear your flesh. The hot coals would start to burn you. The rack would start to pull your bones out of their joints. Every torture tool would be doing its cruel, hellish work. Unless God’s supernatural hand were powerfully upon you, I am sure that in your weakness you would deny your Master. In that hour of danger you would abandon the Lord who bought you.

It is true that Christ’s love in our hearts is strong enough to carry us through, as long as his grace holds it up. But I am afraid that if many of us here today had no more love than we have now, we would come out of that Inquisition as miserable people who had given up the faith.
But now, think about Christ.
The tortures he faced were truly far more terrible.
No cruel torture machine of the Roman Catholics could ever match that awful agony that forced blood out like sweat from every pore of his skin.
Christ was whipped and he was crucified. But there were other sufferings that we could not see, and those were the very heart of his agony.

Now suppose Christ had said in that hour of terrible testing, “I want nothing to do with my disciples. I will not die.” Then he could have come down from the cross. And who could have blamed him for doing wrong?
He owed us nothing. We could do nothing for him.
The only ones he would be turning away were poor worms.
But our Master never once thought of turning his back on us, not even when the bloody sweat covered him like a cloak soaked in blood. NEVER.
Once he said, “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.”
But there were always those words: “If it is possible.”
If there was a way to save us without it, then let the cup be taken away. But if not, may your will be done.

In Pilate’s hall you never hear him say one word that would make you think he was sorry he had agreed to such a costly sacrifice for us. His hands are pierced. He burns with fever. His tongue is as dry as a piece of broken pottery. His whole body is sinking down into the dust of death. Yet you never hear a groan or a scream that sounds as if he wants to turn back.
It is the cry of someone who is determined to keep going, even though he knows he must die along the way.
It was a love that even death could not stop. It won the victory over all the horrors of the grave.
So what do we have to say about this?
We live in gentler times. Are we going to give up our Master when we are tested and tempted because of him?
Young man at work in the workshop! People make fun of you because you follow the Savior. Will you turn away from Christ just because someone mocks you?

Young woman! People laugh at you because you openly say you believe in Christ. Will a laugh break the bond of love that ties your heart to him? All the roaring of hell could not pull his love away from you!

And some of you are suffering because you stand firm for something your faith teaches. Are people shutting you out? Won’t you put up with having your home stripped bare, and even with eating the bread of the poor, rather than bring shame on such a Lord?

With the help of God’s Spirit, won’t you leave this place making a vow and declaring it? Declare that in life, whether you end up poor or rich, and in death, whether it brings pain or anything else, you belong to the Lord and always must. For these words are written on your heart: “We love him because he first loved us.”
“Blessed are the peacemakers, because they will be called the children of God.” — Matthew 5:9.
This is the seventh of Jesus’ “blessed” sayings, the Beatitudes.
The number seven has always had something mysterious about it.

For the Hebrews, seven was the number of perfection. So it seems as if the Savior put the peacemaker in seventh place, as if the peacemaker came very close to being the perfect person in Christ Jesus.
If you want perfect happiness, as far as anyone can have it on earth, you must work hard to reach this seventh blessing. You must become a peacemaker.
Where this verse is placed also means something, if you look at the verses around it.
The verse just before it speaks of the blessing on “the pure in heart, because they will see God.”
It is good for us to understand this.
We are to be “pure first, and then peaceful.”
Being peaceful must never mean making a deal with sin or teaming up with what is evil.
We must set our faces as hard as stone against everything that goes against God and his holiness.
Once that is settled in our souls, we can move on to being peaceful toward people.
The verse that comes after my text also seems to have been put there on purpose.

No matter how peaceful we are in this world, people will still get us wrong and tell false stories about us. And that is no surprise. Even the Prince of Peace, just by being so peaceful, brought fire on the earth.
He loved people and did nothing wrong. Yet he was “looked down on and rejected by people, a man full of sorrows who knew all about grief.”

So that peaceful people would not be surprised when they meet enemies, the next verse adds, “Blessed are those who are treated cruelly for doing what is right, because the kingdom of heaven belongs to them.”
So peacemakers are not only called blessed. They are surrounded by blessings on every side.
Lord, give us grace to climb up to this seventh blessing!

Make our minds pure, so that we may be “pure first, and then peaceful.” And make our souls strong, so that when people persecute us for your sake, our peacefulness will not leave us shocked and hopeless.
Now let us try to get into the meaning of our text.
This is how we want to handle it this morning, as God helps us.
First, let us describe the peacemaker. Second, let us announce how blessed he is. Third, let us put him to work. And fourth, let the preacher become a peacemaker himself.
I. First, LET US DESCRIBE THE PEACEMAKER.
The peacemaker stands out because of his character. But on the outside, his place and situation in life are just like everyone else’s.
He has all the same relationships in life that other people have.
So the peacemaker is a citizen. He is a Christian, but he remembers that being a Christian does not mean giving up his citizenship. Instead, he must use it and make the most of it for Christ’s glory.
So, as a citizen, the peacemaker loves peace.

If he lives in this country, he knows he lives among people who are very touchy about their honor. They get angry quickly and easily. They love a fight so much that just hearing the word “war” gets their blood boiling. They feel like charging in at once with all their strength.
The peacemaker remembers the war with Russia. He remembers what fools we were to get involved there. It brought us huge losses in trade and money, and no benefit at all that anyone can see.

He knows that this nation has often slid into war for political reasons. And he knows that the weight and cost of war usually falls on the poor working man, on people who have to earn their living by hard, sweaty work.
Like other men, he feels his blood get hot. He was born an Englishman, so he often feels the blood of the old sea kings in his veins. But he holds it back and says to himself,
“I must not fight. The servant of God must be gentle to everyone, able to teach, and patient.”

So he pushes against the current. When he hears the noise of war everywhere, and sees many people eager for it, he does his best to cool things down. He says, “Be patient. Leave it alone. Even if this thing is bad, war is worse than any other evil.
There has never yet been a bad peace, and never a good war,” he says. “Whatever we may lose by being too calm, we will certainly lose a hundred times more by being too fierce.”

And in the present case, he thinks how terrible it would be for two Christian nations to go to war. These two nations come from the same blood. These two countries are really closer to each other than any other two countries on earth. They compete with each other in having free institutions. They work together to spread the gospel of Christ. And these two nations have more of God’s chosen people and more true followers of Christ than any other nations under heaven.
Yes, he thinks to himself, it would be terrible if the bones of our sons and daughters were used again to fertilize our fields, as has happened before.

He remembers that farmers from Yorkshire brought home soil from Waterloo to fertilize their own fields. That soil held the blood and bones of their own sons and daughters. He does not think it right that the prairies of America should be made rich with the blood and bones of his children. On the other hand, he thinks he would never hit another man. He would rather be hit himself. To him, blood would be an awful sight.
So he says, “What I would not do myself, I would not want others to do for me. If I would not be a killer, I would not want others to kill for me either.”

In his mind, he walks across a battlefield. He hears the screams of the dying and the groans of the wounded. He knows that even the winners of battles have said that all the excitement of victory could not take away the horror of the terrible scene after the fight. And so he says, “No! Peace, peace!”

He may have some influence in the country. He may be a member of Parliament, or write for a newspaper, or speak at public meetings. If so, he says, “Let us think carefully before we rush into this fight.

We must protect our country’s honor. We must keep our right to take in people who run away from those who oppress them. We must insist that England will always be a safe home for every rebel who flees from his king. It must be a place from which the oppressed will never be dragged away by force. But still,” he says, “can’t all this happen without any blood being shed?”

He asks the government’s lawyers to look into it carefully. Perhaps they can find that a mistake was made, one that can be forgiven and let go without shedding blood and without pulling the sword out of its sheath.

He says that war is a monster. Even at its best, it is a devil. Of all the terrible punishments, it is the worst. He sees soldiers as the red sticks of a bloody rod of punishment. He begs God not to strike a guilty nation in this way, but to put the sword away for a while. He asks this so that we are not thrown into trouble, crushed with sorrow, and exposed to cruelty that could send thousands to the grave and many more into poverty.
That is how the peacemaker acts. And while he does this, he feels that his conscience approves of him. He is blessed, and one day people will admit that he was one of the children of God.

But the peacemaker is not only a citizen. He is also a person. He may sometimes stay out of national politics. But as a person, he believes that in his own personal life, his “politics” must always be peace.
In his own life, if someone insults his honor, he does not fight to defend it. He believes it would hurt his honor more to be angry with another person than to put up with an insult.

He hears others say, “Even a worm will turn on you if you step on it.” But he says, “I am not a worm. I am a Christian. So I do not turn on anyone, except to bless the hand that hits me and to pray for those who treat me cruelly.”

He has a temper, because a peacemaker can get angry. And pity the man who can’t! Such a man is like Jacob limping because of his injured hip. Anger is one of the soul’s holy feet when it walks in the right direction. But even though he can get angry, he learns to “be angry without sinning,” and he “does not let the sun go down while he is still angry.”

At home, the peacemaker tries to stay calm with his servants and his family. He puts up with many things rather than say one unkind word. If he has to correct someone, he always does it gently. He says, “Why are you doing this? Why are you doing this?” He speaks not with the harshness of a judge, but with the tenderness of a father.
Perhaps the peacemaker can learn a lesson from a story I found last week while reading the life of Mr. John Wesley.
Wesley was sailing to America with Mr. Oglethorpe, who was going to be the governor of Savannah. One day Wesley heard a loud noise in the governor’s cabin.
So Mr. Wesley went in, and the governor said, “I suppose you want to know what all this noise is about, sir. I have a good reason for it.

You know, sir,” he said, “that the only wine I drink is wine from Cyprus, and I need it. I brought it on board, and this rascal, my servant Grimaldi, has drunk all of it! I will have him beaten on the deck. And when the first warship comes by, I will have him forced into the navy to serve the King. He will have a hard time of it, because I will let him know that I never forgive.”
“Your Honor,” said Mr. Wesley, “then I hope you never sin.”

That correction was so well said, so sharp, and so needed, that the governor answered right away, “Oh, sir, I do sin. And I have sinned in what I just said. For your sake, he will be forgiven. I hope he will not do it again.”

So the peacemaker always thinks it is best not to be too hard a master to his servants. After all, he is a sinner himself, and he must answer to his own Master. If he provokes his servants, he may also be provoking his God.

The peacemaker also goes out among people. When he is with others, he sometimes meets with nasty remarks and even insults. But he learns to put up with them, because he remembers that Christ put up with so much hostility from sinners.

Cotton Mather, a holy man and a great Puritan preacher in America, received a number of letters from people who did not sign their names. The letters insulted him badly. He read them and kept them. Then he wrapped a piece of paper around them, and before he put them on a shelf, he wrote on the paper: “Slander — Father, forgive them!”
That is what the peacemaker does.

About all these things he says, “This is slander — Father, forgive them!” He does not rush to defend himself. He knows that the One he serves will make sure his good name is protected, as long as he himself is careful about how he lives among people.

He goes into business. Sometimes things happen that make the peacemaker very tempted to take someone to court. But he never does, unless he is absolutely forced to. He knows that going to court is like playing with sharp knives. Even people who know how to use them still cut their own fingers.

The peacemaker remembers that the law makes the most money for the people who run it. He also knows this: people will give sixpence to the church for the good of their souls, and a guinea to their doctor for the good of their bodies. But they will spend a hundred pounds, or five hundred, on extra fees for their lawyers in the Court of Chancery.
So he says, “No. It is better for me to be wronged by my opponent, and let him gain a little, than for both of us to lose everything.”
So he lets some of these things go. And he finds that, overall, he loses nothing by sometimes giving up his rights.
There are times when he has to defend himself. But even then, he is ready to meet the other side in every way he can. He is willing to give in at any time.

He has learned the old saying that “an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure.” So he takes care to make peace with his opponent quickly, while they are still on the way. He leaves a quarrel alone before it starts. Or if it has already started, he tries to end it as quickly as he can, knowing that God is watching.

The peacemaker is also a neighbor. He never tries to get involved in his neighbors’ quarrels, especially a quarrel between a neighbor and his wife. He knows very well that if those two disagree, they will quickly agree to turn against him if he gets in the middle. But if he is called in when two neighbors are quarreling, he never stirs up their anger. Instead he says to them, “You are not doing right, my brothers. Why are you fighting with each other?” He does not take the wrong side. He always tries to be fair. But he always mixes his fairness with mercy. And he says to the one who was wronged, “Can’t you be noble enough to forgive?”

Sometimes, when they are very angry, he steps between the two and takes the blows from both sides. He knows that this is what Jesus did. Jesus took the blows from his Father and from us too. By suffering in our place, he made peace between God and people.
That is how the peacemaker acts whenever he is asked to help. He does so especially if his position lets him do it with authority.
If he is a judge, he tries not to let a case go to trial if it can be settled some other way.

If he is a minister and his people disagree, he does not dig into the details. He knows very well that there is a lot of silly gossip. Instead he says “Peace” to the waves and “Hush” to the winds. And he tells people to live that way.
He thinks that they have so little time to live together that they really should live in harmony.
So he says, “How good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in unity!”
But once again, the peacemaker’s highest title is this: he is a Christian.
Because he is a Christian, he joins a Christian church. And there, as a peacemaker, he is like an angel of God.
Even in churches there are people who are weighed down by weaknesses. These weaknesses sometimes cause Christian men and women to disagree.

So the peacemaker says, “This is not right, my brother. Let us be at peace.” He remembers what Paul says: “I beg Euodias, and I beg Syntyche, to agree with each other in the Lord.” He thinks that if Paul begged these two to agree like this, unity must be a wonderful thing. So he works hard for it.

Sometimes the peacemaker sees that quarrels may break out between his own church group and others. Then he turns to the story of Abram. He reads how Abram’s herdsmen fought with Lot’s herdsmen. And he notices that the same verse says, “And the Canaanites and the Perizzites were living in the land.”
So he thinks it was shameful that followers of the true God would quarrel while the Perizzites were watching.

He says to Christians, “Don’t do this! We are giving the devil something to laugh at. We dishonor God. We harm our own cause. We ruin people’s souls.” And he says, “Put your swords back in their sheaths. Be at peace, and do not fight with one another.”

When people who are not peacemakers join a church, they will fight over the smallest pet idea and argue about the tiniest point. We have seen churches torn apart and Christian groups split over things so foolish that a wise man could not even see what the fuss was about. They were so silly that any sensible person would have ignored them.
The peacemaker says, “Go after peace with all people.”

Most of all, he prays that the Spirit of God, who is the Spirit of peace, will rest on the church at all times. He prays that the Spirit will bind believers together as one. Then, since they are one in Christ, the world will know that the Father has sent his Son into the world. After all, Christ’s coming was announced by the angels’ song: “Glory to God in the highest! Peace on earth, and good will to all people!”
Now, I hope that in describing the peacemaker I have described some of you. But I am afraid most of us would have to say, “Well, I fall short in many ways.”
But I would like to add this much.
If there are two Christian men here who are at odds with each other, I want to be a peacemaker. And I urge them to be peacemakers too.
Two men from Sparta had quarreled, and the Spartan king, Aris, told them both to meet him in a temple.

When they were both there, he listened to their quarrel. Then he said to the priest, “Lock the doors of the temple. These two will never leave until they have made up.” And there in the temple he said, “It is not right to quarrel.”
So they settled their quarrel right away and went home.
If this was done in a temple of idols, how much more should it be done in the house of God! And if the pagan Spartans did this, how much more should the Christian, who believes in Christ, do it!

This very day, put away all bitterness and all spite. Say to each other, “If you have offended me in any way, it is forgiven. And if I have offended you in any way, I admit I was wrong. Let’s heal the break between us. As children of God, let us be united with each other.”
Blessed are those who can do this, for “blessed are the peacemakers!”
II. Now that I have described the peacemaker, I will go on to DECLARE HOW BLESSED HE IS.
“Blessed are the peacemakers, because they will be called the children of God.”
The text gives him three kinds of praise.
First, he is blessed. That means God blesses him. And I know that anyone God blesses is truly blessed, and anyone God curses is truly cursed.
God blesses him from the highest heavens. God blesses him the way only God can. God blesses him with the rich blessings that are stored up in Christ.
And while God blesses him, that blessing also spreads all through his own soul.
His conscience tells him that, with God watching and with the help of the Holy Spirit, he has tried to honor Christ among people.
He is most blessed of all when he has been attacked with the most curses. Because then this promise comes to comfort him: “That is how they persecuted the prophets who lived before you.”
He is commanded to rejoice at all times. But he finds a special command to be very glad when he is treated badly.
So he takes it well if he is made to suffer for doing good. He is happy to carry part of the Savior’s cross this way.

He goes to bed, and no dreams of hatred trouble his sleep. He gets up and goes to work, and he is not afraid to face anyone. He can say, “There is nothing in my heart but friendship toward everyone.” Or if he is attacked with lies, and his enemies have made up a story against him, he can still say —

“The one who made the arrow and the one who threw it at me
Each has a place in my heart, like a brother.”

s: Because he loves everyone, he has peace in his own soul. He is blessed, like someone who inherits the blessing of the Most High God.
And quite often it even happens that wicked people speak well of him. They would like to hold back a kind word about him, but they cannot.
He defeats evil by doing good. That is like heaping burning coals on their heads. He melts their cold hatred, until even they say, “He is a good man.”

And when he dies, the people he helped make peace with each other stand by his grave and say, “It would be good if the world could see many more people like him. There would not be half the fighting, or half the sin, in the world if there were many like him.”
Second, notice that the text does not only say he is blessed. It adds that he is one of the children of God.
He is God’s child by adoption and by grace. But making peace is a sweet sign that the peaceful Spirit is at work inside him.
Also, as a child of God, he looks like his Father in heaven.
God is peaceful, patient, and tender. He is full of loving kindness, pity, and compassion.
This peacemaker is the same.
Because he is like God, he carries his Father’s likeness.
In this way he shows people that he is one of God’s children.
As one of God’s children, the peacemaker can come close to his Father.

He comes to him boldly and says, “Our Father who is in heaven.” But he would not dare to say that unless he could also pray with a clear conscience, “Forgive us what we owe, just as we forgive those who owe us.”
He feels connected like a brother to all people. So he feels that he can rejoice that God is his Father.
He comes with confidence and great joy to his Father in heaven. He is one of the children of the Most High, who is good even to ungrateful and evil people.
And there is still a third word of praise in the text.
“They will be called the children of God.”
They not only are God’s children, but they will be called God’s children.
That means even their enemies will call them that. Even the world will say, “Ah! That man is a child of God.”
Dear friends, perhaps nothing impresses ungodly people as much as a Christian who stays peaceful when he is insulted.
There was a soldier in India, a big man. Before he joined the army he had been a boxer, and later he did many brave things in battle.
When he became a Christian through a missionary’s preaching, all the soldiers he ate with made fun of him.
They thought it was impossible for a man like him to become a peaceful Christian.
So one day at dinner, one of them, just to be cruel, threw a whole bowl of boiling-hot soup in his face and down his chest.

The poor man tore his clothes open to wipe off the burning liquid. But even though he was badly shaken, he kept control of himself. He said, “I am a Christian. I must expect this,” and he smiled at them.
The man who did it said, “If I had known you would take it like that, I would never have done it. I am very sorry I did.”
His patience put their cruelty to shame, and they all said he was a real Christian.
In this way he was called a child of God.
What they saw in him was proof, and it struck them all the more because they knew they could never have done the same.
One day Mr. Kilpin of Exeter was walking down the street. A wicked man pushed him off the sidewalk into the gutter. As he fell, the man said, “Lie there, John Bunyan! That’s good enough for you.”

Mr. Kilpin got up and went on his way. Later, the man wanted to know how he had taken the insult. He was surprised that all Mr. Kilpin said was that the man had honored him more than he had shamed him. Mr. Kilpin thought that being called John Bunyan was worth being rolled in the gutter a thousand times.
Then the man who had done it said that Mr. Kilpin was a good man.
So those who are peacemakers are “called the children of God.”
They show it to the world so clearly that even the blind must see it and even the deaf must hear it: God is truly in them.
Oh, if only we had enough grace to win this wonderful praise!

My friend who is listening, God may have brought you far enough to hunger and thirst for what is right. If so, I beg you, never stop being hungry until he has brought you all the way to being a peacemaker, so that you may be called a child of God.
III. But now, third, I will try to PUT THE PEACEMAKER TO WORK.
I am sure you have a lot of work to do in your own homes and among the people you know.
Go and do it.

You remember that verse in Job: “Who can eat bland food without salt? Is there any taste in the white of an egg?” Job wants us to understand that tasteless things need something added to them, or they will not be pleasant to eat.
Now, to people, our religion tastes bland. We must add salt to it. And that salt must be our calm and peacemaking spirit.
Then people who would have avoided our religion by itself will see the salt added and say, “This is good.” They will find some flavor in this “white of an egg.”
If you want people to think well of your faith, start in your own homes. Do a clear and clean job of it. Get rid of the old yeast, so that you can offer God a sacrifice that is godly and heavenly.
If there are any quarrels or divisions among you, I beg you: forgive each other, just as God forgave you for Christ’s sake.

I ask you by the bloody sweat of the one who prayed for you, and by the agony of the one who died for you. As he was dying he said, “Father, forgive them, because they do not understand what they are doing.” So forgive your enemies. “Pray for those who treat you badly, and bless those who curse you.”
Let people always say about you as a Christian, “That man is gentle and humble in heart. He would rather be hurt himself than hurt someone else.”
But the main work I want to give you is this. Jesus Christ was the greatest peacemaker of all.
“He is our peace.”
He came to make peace between Jews and Gentiles, “for he has made the two into one, and has broken down the wall that divided us.”
He came to make peace between all the nations that fight each other. For now there is “no more Greek or barbarian, Scythian, slave or free, but Christ is everything, in everyone.”
He came to make peace between his Father’s justice and our sinful souls. And he has made peace for us through the blood of his cross.
Now, you who are children of peace, try to be tools in his hands to make peace between God and people.
Send up earnest prayers to heaven for your children’s souls.
Never stop praying for the souls of all your friends and relatives.
Pray that the people around you who are perishing will be saved.
That is how you will be peacemakers.
And when you have prayed, use every means you have.
