Preach, if God has given you the ability. Preach with the Holy Spirit sent down from heaven. Preach the word of life that brings people back to God.
If you cannot preach, teach.
Teach the Word. “Be eager to do it whether the time seems right or not.”
“Sow seed beside every stream.” For the gospel “speaks better things than the blood of Abel.” It calls out “Peace!” to all people.
Write to your friends about Christ. And if you cannot say much, say a little for him.
But oh, make it the goal of your life to win others for Christ!
Never be content to go to heaven alone.
Ask the Lord to make you a spiritual father to many children. Ask God to bless you so that you help bring in a big part of the Redeemer’s harvest.
I thank God that so many of you care deeply about people’s souls.

It makes my heart glad to hear about people coming to faith and to welcome the new believers. But I am happiest when many of you, who came to faith through my ministry with God’s help, are used to bring others to faith.

There are brothers and sisters here who keep bringing me people. They were the first to bring these people to this church. They watched over them and prayed for them. And at last they brought them to the minister, so that he could hear them tell about their faith.
Such peacemakers are blessed!
You have “saved a soul from death and hidden a great many sins.”
“Those who turn many people to what is right will shine like the stars for ever and ever.”
In fact, in heaven itself they “will be called the children of God.”
In that book where the names of all the Lord’s people are written, their family record will show this: through God the Holy Spirit, they brought souls into the bond of peace through Jesus Christ.

blocks.x: IV. Last of all, the minister must now PRACTICE HIS OWN TEXT AND TRY, THROUGH GOD THE HOLY SPIRIT, TO BE A PEACEMAKER THIS MORNING.

s: This morning I am speaking to many, many people who know nothing about peace. For “the wicked have no peace,” says my God.
“The wicked are like the stormy sea, which can never be still. Its waves throw up mud and dirt.”
I am not speaking to you because I want to give your souls a false peace.
How terrible it will be for the prophets who say, “Peace, peace,” when there is no peace!
Instead, so that we do a thorough job of this, let me first show you the truth: your soul has no peace and is at war.
O soul! This morning you are at war with your conscience.
You have tried to quiet it, but it keeps stinging you.

You have locked up your conscience, the Recorder of the town of Mansoul, in a dark place, and you have built a wall in front of his door. But still, when his fits come on him, your conscience will thunder at you and say, “This is not right! This is the path that leads to hell! This is the road to destruction!”
Oh! For some of you, conscience is like a ghost that haunts you day and night.
You know what is good, but you choose what is evil. When you try to pick the rose of sin, you prick your fingers on the thorns of conscience.

For you, the road down is not an easy one. It is blocked with hedges and ditches, and there are many bars and gates and chains along the way. But you climb over them all, determined to destroy your own souls.
Oh! There is war between you and your conscience.
Conscience says, “Turn around.” But you say, “I won’t.”

Conscience says, “Close your shop on Sunday.” Conscience says, “Change the way you do business. It is cheating.” Conscience says, “Don’t lie to each other, because the Judge is standing at the door.” Conscience says, “Get rid of that drinking cup. It turns a man into something worse than an animal.” Conscience says, “Tear yourself away from that immoral relationship. Be done with that evil. Lock your door against lust.” But you say, “I will drink the sweet stuff even if it damns me. I will keep going back to my drinking and my old hangouts, even if I die in my sins.”
There is war between you and your conscience.
And yet your conscience is God’s representative in your soul.
Let your conscience speak for a minute or two this morning.

Don’t be afraid of him. He is a good friend to you. He may speak roughly, but the day will come when you will realize that there is more music in the roaring of conscience than in all the sweet, tempting songs that lust uses to trick you into ruin.
Let your conscience speak.
But there is more. There is war between you and God’s law.
The Ten Commandments are against you this morning.
The first one steps forward and says, “Let him be cursed, because he denies me.
He has another god besides me. His god is his stomach. He bows down to his lust.”
All ten commandments are aimed at you today, like ten huge cannons. You have broken all of God’s laws, and every day you have ignored all his commands.
Soul! You will find it very hard to go to war with the law.
When the law came in peace, Mount Sinai was covered in smoke, and even Moses said, “I am shaking with fear.”

What will you do when the law comes in terror? What will you do when the archangel’s trumpet tears you out of your grave? When God’s eyes burn their way into your guilty soul? When the great books are opened, and all your sin and shame are made public?
Can you stand against an angry law on that day?
When the officers of the law come to hand you over to the torturers, and throw you away forever from peace and happiness, sinner, what will you do?
Can you live with fires that never go out?
Can you bear the burning that lasts forever?

O man! “Make peace with your enemy quickly, while you are still on the road with him. If you don’t, he may turn you over to the judge, and the judge may give you to the officer, and you will be put in prison.
I tell you the truth, you will never get out of there until you have paid every last penny.”
But sinner, do you know that this morning you are at war with God?
He made you and was your best friend, but you have forgotten him and ignored him.
He has fed you, and you have used your strength against him.
He has clothed you. The clothes on your back today are the uniform of his goodness. Yet instead of serving the one whose uniform you wear, you are the slave of his worst enemy.
The very breath in your nose is a loan from his kindness. And yet you may use that breath to curse him. Or at best you use it for dirty and careless talk that dishonors his laws.
The one who made you has become your enemy because of your sin. And today you still hate him and look down on his Word.
You say, “I don’t hate him.”
Then, soul, I command you: “Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ.”
“No,” you say, “I can’t. I won’t do that!”
Then you do hate him.
If you loved him, you would keep this great command of his.
“His command is not hard to keep.” It is sweet and easy.
You would believe in his Son if you loved the Father, for “everyone who loves the Father also loves the one who is born of him.”
Are you really at war with God like this? That is surely a terrible place to be!
Can you face the one who comes against you with ten thousand? Yes, can you stand against the Almighty? He makes heaven shake when he scolds, and he crushes the twisting serpent with a single word.
Do you hope to hide from him?
“Can anyone hide in secret places where I cannot see him? says the Lord.
Even if you dig down into Carmel, he will pull you out from there.
Even if you dive into the caves at the bottom of the sea, he will command the serpent there, and it will bite you.
If you make your bed in hell, he will find you.
If you climb up to heaven, he is there.”
All of creation is your prison, and he can find you whenever he wants.
Or do you think you can survive his anger?
Are your ribs made of iron? Are your bones made of bronze?

Even if they were, they would still melt like wax when the Lord God of armies comes. For he is mighty. Like a lion he will tear his prey to pieces, and like a fire he will burn up his enemy, “for our God is a fire that burns everything up.”
So this is where every man and woman here this morning stands, if you have not yet been converted.
You are at war with your own conscience. You are at war with God’s law. And you are at war with God himself.
So now, as God’s ambassadors, we come to talk with you about making peace.
Please listen carefully. “…place, make peace with God.” … moment.
Look and listen. … him speaking to some of you.
It is as if God were begging you through me. I beg you, in Christ’s … “In his place.”
Let the preacher disappear for a … It is Christ who is speaking to you now.
I think I hear … This is how he speaks: “Soul, I love you. I love you with all my heart. I do not want you to be my Father’s enemy.”
The tear in his eye proves that he means what he says. He cries out, “How often I wanted to gather you together, the way a hen gathers her chicks under her wing, but you would not let me.”
“Even so,” he says, “I come to talk with you about peace.
Come now, let us talk this through together. … of David.

I will make a covenant with you that lasts forever, the sure mercies … Sinner,” he says, “you are now invited to hear God’s message of peace for your soul. This is what it says: ‘You are guilty and condemned. Will you admit this?
Are you willing to throw down your weapons right now and say, Great God, I give up, I give up; I do not want to be your enemy any longer?’”

If you are, then peace is announced to you. … wicked give up his way of life, and the evil man his thoughts. Let him turn to the Lord, for he will have mercy on him. Let him turn to our God, for he will forgive him completely.’
Forgiveness is offered for free to every person who is truly sorry for their sin. But that forgiveness must come to you through faith.
“Let the … So Jesus stands here this morning. He points to the wounds on his chest, and he holds out his bleeding hands.
He says, “Sinner, trust me and live!”
God is no longer announcing his fiery law to you. Instead, he announces his sweet and simple good news: believe and live.
“Whoever trusts in the Son is not condemned. But whoever does not trust in him is condemned already, because he has not believed in the name of God’s only Son.”
“Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, the Son of Man must be lifted up too. Then everyone who believes in him will not be lost, but will have life that never ends.”
Dear soul, is God’s Spirit moving in you this morning?
Are you saying, “Lord, I want to be at peace with you”?

Are you willing to take Christ on his own terms? Really, they are no terms at all. His only condition is that you set no conditions of your own. Will you simply give yourself up to him, body, soul, and spirit, so that he can save you?
Now, if my Master were standing here where you could see him, I think he would plead with you so well that many of you would say, “Lord, I believe. I want to be at peace with you.”
But even Christ himself never turned a single soul to God without the Holy Spirit. Even he, as a preacher, did not win many people to himself, because their hearts were hard.
If the Holy Spirit is here, he can bless you just as much when I plead for Christ as if Christ were pleading with you himself.
Soul, will you take Christ or not?
Young men and young women, you may never hear this message preached to you again.
Will you die as God’s enemy?
Some of you sitting here have still not been converted. Your last hour may come before the sun rises on another Sunday.
You might not even live to see tomorrow.
Do you want to go into eternity as “enemies of God because of your wicked deeds”?
Soul, will you take Christ or not?
Say “No” if that is what you really mean.
Say, “No, Christ, I will never let you save me.”
Say it. Face the question honestly.
But please, do not say, “I will not answer at all.”
Come on, give some answer this morning. Yes, this very morning.
Thank God that you are still able to answer.
Thank God that you are not in hell.
Thank God that your sentence has not been announced. Thank God you have not been given what you deserve.
May God help you give the right answer!
Will you take Christ or not?
“I am not good enough.”
Being good enough is not the question. The question is: will you take him?
“My heart is black.” He will come into your black heart and make it clean.
“Oh, but my heart is so hard.”
He will come into your hard heart and make it soft.
Will you take him? You can have him if you want him.
When God makes a person willing, that clearly proves he plans to give that person Christ. If you are willing, he is willing too. If he has made you willing, Christ can be yours.
“Oh,” someone says, “I can’t believe that Christ could ever be mine.”
Dear soul, you can have him right now.
Mary, he is calling you!
John, he is calling you!

Sinner, whoever you are in this huge crowd, maybe there is a holy willingness in your soul this morning to come to Christ. Yes, maybe there is even just a small wish for him. If so, he is calling you! He is calling you!
Oh, don’t wait! Come and trust him.
Oh, if I could preach good news like this to the lost souls in hell, what a difference it would make to them!

Surely, surely, if they could hear the gospel preached to them one more time, I think tears would run down their poor cheeks. They would say, “Great God, if only we can escape your anger, we will grab hold of Christ.”
But here it is preached among you every day. It is preached so often that I am afraid you hear it as just an old, old story.
Maybe it is because I tell it so poorly. But God knows that if I knew how to tell it better, I would.
O my Master, send these people a better messenger, if that will win them over!
Send someone who pleads more earnestly and has a more tender heart, if that will bring them to you!
But oh, bring them! Bring them!
Our hearts ache to see them brought in.
Sinner, will you take Christ or not?
I know that for some of you, this morning is the day when God shows his power in your souls.
The Holy Spirit is at work, wrestling with some of you.
Lord, win them! Conquer them! Overcome them!
Are you saying, “Yes, what a happy day!
I want to be led along in my Lord’s victory parade, a prisoner of his great love”?
Dear soul, if you believe, it is done.
Trust Christ, and all your many sins are forgiven. Throw yourself down in front of his dear cross and say:

blocks.x:
“A guilty, weak, and helpless worm,
I fall into your arms;
Be my strength, be my goodness,
My Jesus and my all.”

s: And if he turns you away, tell us about it.
If he says no to you, let us know.
That has never happened yet.
He has always welcomed everyone who comes to him.
He always will. He is a Savior with open hands and an open heart.
O sinner, may God lead you to put your trust in him once and for all!
You spirits up in heaven, tune your harps again! A sinner has been born to God this morning.
Saul of Tarsus, you lead the song! And Mary, the sinner, you follow with your sweetest music!
Let music rise up before the throne today! For heirs of glory have been born, and runaway children have come home!
All the glory goes to God forever and ever! Amen.
“Then Jesus said, ‘Father, forgive them, because they don’t know what they are doing.’” — Luke 23:34.
At that moment, our Lord was feeling the first pains of being crucified. The executioners had just driven the nails through his hands and feet.

He must also have been very low and extremely weak. The night of agony in Gethsemane had worn him down. So had the whippings and the cruel mocking he had suffered all morning from Caiaphas, Pilate, Herod, and the soldiers of the Praetorian guard.
But neither the weakness he already had nor the pain he now felt could stop him from praying.
The Lamb of God said nothing to people, but he did not stop speaking to God.

Like a sheep that stays silent while it is being sheared, he said not one word to people to defend himself. But in his heart he kept crying out to his Father. No pain and no weakness could silence his holy prayers.
Dear friends, what an example our Lord gives us here!
Let us keep praying as long as our hearts are beating. Let no amount of suffering drive us away from God’s throne of grace. Instead, let it drive us even closer to it.

blocks.x:
“As long as Christians live, they should pray,
For only while they pray do they really live.”

s: If we stop praying, we give up the very comfort we need.
Great God, when our minds are troubled and our hearts are overwhelmed, help us to keep praying. May despair never drive us away from your throne of mercy.

Our blessed Redeemer kept on praying even when the cruel iron nails tore through his tender nerves. He kept praying as blow after blow of the hammer shook his whole body with pain. We can explain how he kept going: he was so used to praying that he could not stop. His prayers for others had built up such a powerful speed that he would not pause.

Think of those long nights on the cold mountainside. Think of the many days he spent alone. Think of the constant quick prayers he used to send up to heaven. All of these had built a habit in him so strong that even the worst torture could not hold it back.
But it was more than a habit.
Our Lord was baptized in the spirit of prayer. He lived in it, and it lived in him. It had become part of who he was.

He was like a precious spice. When you crush it, it does not stop giving off its perfume. In fact, it gives off even more as the grinding tool keeps pounding it. That is because its fragrance is not just on the outside. It is something deep inside, part of what it is. The pounding in the grinding bowl only draws it out and reveals the sweetness hidden in its heart.
So Jesus prays, just as a bundle of myrrh gives off its smell, or as birds sing because they can’t help it.
Prayer was wrapped around his soul like a piece of clothing. His heart went out dressed in it.
I say it again: let this be our example. Never, in any situation, no matter how hard the trial or how discouraging the problem, let us stop praying.
Notice also that in this prayer, our Lord still has strong faith that he is God’s Son.
Even the terrible trial he was now going through could not stop him from holding on to the fact that he was the Son.
His prayer begins with “Father.”
There was a reason he taught us to say “Our Father” when we pray. How well we pray will depend a lot on how sure we are of our relationship with God.

When we face great losses and hardships, we easily start to think that God is not treating us the way a father treats his child. We think he is treating us the way a harsh judge treats a condemned criminal. But Christ was pushed further than we will ever be pushed. And yet his cry shows no wavering at all in his trust that he is the Son.

In Gethsemane, when his bloody sweat was falling fast to the ground, his most bitter cry began with “My Father.” He asked that, if it were possible, the bitter cup might be taken away from him. He pleaded with the Lord as his Father, just as he had called him Father again and again on that dark and gloomy night.
And here again, in the first of the seven cries he spoke as he was dying, the word is “Father.”
Oh, may the Spirit who makes us cry “Abba, Father” never stop working in us!

May we never become spiritual slaves because of the whisper, “If you really are the Son of God…” And if the tempter attacks us that way, may we win, just as Jesus did in the wilderness when he was hungry.
May the Spirit who cries “Abba, Father” push back every fear that comes from unbelief.

We will be disciplined; we must be. After all, what son is there whose father never disciplines him? When it happens, may we lovingly submit to the Father of our spirits and live. But may we never be trapped by a slavish spirit that makes us doubt the love of our kind Father, or doubt that he has adopted us as his children.
But here is something even more remarkable. Our Lord’s prayer to his Father was not for himself.

It is true that he still prayed for himself on the cross. His sad cry, “My God, my God, why have you deserted me?” shows that his prayer was personal too. But the first of the seven great cries from the cross hardly mentions himself at all, not even indirectly.
It is: “Father, forgive them.”

The request is completely for other people. Yes, it hints at the cruel things they were doing to him, but only from a distance. And notice: he does not say, “I forgive them.” That goes without saying. He seems to forget that they were doing anything wrong to him. What is on his mind is the wrong they were doing to the Father. By what they did to the Son, they were insulting the Father. He does not think about himself at all.
The cry “Father, forgive them” is completely unselfish.
In this prayer, it is as if he himself were not even there. He forgets himself so completely that he loses sight of himself and his own suffering.
Brothers and sisters, if there was ever a time in the life of the Son of Man when he could have prayed only for himself, and no one would have complained, surely it was when he was starting to die.
Suppose any man here were tied to a stake or nailed to a cross. We would not be surprised if his first prayer, and his last, and all his prayers, were for help to get through such a terrible trial.
But look: the Lord Jesus began his prayer by pleading for others.
Can’t you see what a great heart this shows!
What a compassionate soul the Crucified One had!
How Godlike, how divine!
Was there ever anyone before him who, in the very pain of death, made his first prayer a prayer for others?
Brothers and sisters, let this unselfish spirit be in you too.
Don’t just look at your own things. Each of you should look at the things of others too.
Love your neighbors as yourselves. Christ has shown you the perfect model of unselfishness, so try to follow him and walk in his footsteps.
But there is one more jewel that tops off this crown of glorious love.

The Sun of Righteousness goes down over Calvary in amazing splendor. Among the bright colors that make his going so glorious, there is this one: the prayer was not only for others, but for his cruelest enemies.
Did I say “his enemies”? There is more to it than that.
It was not a prayer for enemies who had hurt him years before. It was for the people who were right there, right then, killing him.

The Savior did not pray calmly, long after he had forgotten the injury and could forgive it more easily. No, he prayed while the first red drops of blood were spurting onto the hands that drove the nails. While the hammer was still stained with his blood, his blessed mouth poured out this fresh, warm prayer: “Father, forgive them, because they don’t know what they are doing.”
I am not saying that the prayer was only for the men who were nailing him to the cross.

I believe it was a far-reaching prayer. It included the scribes and Pharisees, Pilate and Herod, Jews and Gentiles. Yes, in a certain sense it included the whole human race, since we all had a part in that murder. But the ones the prayer was poured on first, like precious perfume, were certainly the men who were right there committing the brutal act of fastening him to the cursed cross.
Seen in this light, how magnificent this prayer is!
It stands all alone on a mountain of glory.
No one had ever prayed like this before.
It is true that Abraham, Moses, and the prophets had prayed for wicked people. But they never prayed for wicked men who had pierced their hands and feet.

It is also true that since that day, Christians have prayed the same prayer. Stephen cried, “Don’t hold this sin against them.” And many martyrs, as they died at the stake, used their last words to pray with pity for the people who were killing them. But you know where they learned this. Now let me ask you: where did he learn it?
Wasn’t Jesus the original, the divine source?
He learned it nowhere. It sprang up from his own Godlike nature.

It came from a compassion that belonged to him alone. That is what made his prayer so new. The royal love inside him gave him the idea for such an unforgettable prayer. It can be a pattern for us, but before him there was no pattern for it.
Right now I feel I would rather kneel before my Lord’s cross than stand in this pulpit and talk to you.

I want to worship him. In my heart I worship him for that prayer. If I knew nothing else about him except this one prayer, I would still have to worship him. That one amazing plea for mercy convinces me, beyond all doubt, that the one who prayed it is God. It fills my heart with deep, respectful love.
So that is how I introduce to you our Lord’s first spoken prayer on the cross.
Now, if God’s Holy Spirit helps us, I will put it to use.

First, we will look at it as a picture of how our Savior prays for us. Second, we will see what the text teaches about the church’s work. Third, we will think about what it suggests to those who are not yet converted.

blocks.x: I. First, dear brothers and sisters, let us look at this wonderful text as A PICTURE OF HOW OUR LORD PRAYS FOR US.

s: He prayed for his enemies then, and he is praying for his enemies now. What he did on the cross was a promise of what he does now on the throne.
He is in a higher place and a nobler position, but he is doing the same work. He still stands before the eternal throne, pleading on behalf of guilty people and crying, “Father, oh, forgive them.”
All of his praying for us is, in some way, like his prayer on Calvary. The cries from Calvary can help us picture what all his praying in heaven is like.
Here is the first thing we can see about his praying for us: it is full of grace.
According to the text, the people our Lord prayed for did not deserve his prayer.
They had done nothing for him that he might reward with a blessing. In fact, they deserved nothing good at all. They had plotted together to kill him.
They had crucified him. They had done it for no reason at all and out of pure hatred. Even at that moment, they were taking his innocent life.
The people he spoke up for had no good deeds to their name. They did not deserve even one kind wish from the Savior’s heart.
They certainly never asked him to pray for them. It was the last thing on their minds to say, “Pray for us, dying King!
Speak to God for us, Son of God!”
I dare to believe that when they heard the prayer, they either ignored it and brushed it off with contempt, or maybe even grabbed it as something to joke about.
I admit it seems too harsh on human beings to think such a prayer could be laughed at. But other things done around the cross were just as brutal, so I can imagine this happening too.
Still, our Savior prayed for people who did not deserve the prayer. In fact, they deserved a curse. They did not ask for the prayer, and they even mocked it when they heard it.
In the same way, the great High Priest stands in heaven and pleads for guilty people. Yes, for guilty people, my listeners.
No one on earth deserves to have him pray for them.
He does not plead for anyone because he thinks they deserve it.
He stands there as the Righteous One, pleading for those who are not righteous.
It does not say, “If anyone is good,” but “If anyone sins, we have someone who speaks for us to the Father.”
Remember too that our great Advocate pleads for people who never asked him to.
Even while his chosen ones are still dead in their wrongdoing and sins, he prays for them with compassion. Even while they mock his good news, his loving heart is asking heaven to be kind to them.
So then, dear friends, if this is true, think how sure you are to succeed with God if you sincerely ask the Lord Jesus Christ to plead for you.
Have some of you been begging the Savior, with many tears and deep feeling, to speak up for you?
Will he turn you away?
Does it make sense that he could?
He pleads for people who reject his pleading. So he will surely plead for you, who value it more than gold.

Remember this, dear listener: maybe there is nothing good in you. Maybe there is every kind of evil and wickedness you can imagine. Even so, none of these things can stop Christ from speaking to God for you.
He will plead even for you.

Come and put your case in his hands. He will find reasons for mercy that you can’t find for yourself. And he will bring your case to God, just as he did for the men who killed him: “Father, forgive them.”
Here is a second thing about his praying for us: it is careful.
Notice the words of the prayer: “Father, forgive them, because they don’t know what they are doing.”

It is as if our Savior looked his enemies through and through, searching for something he could say in their favor. He found nothing, until his wise and loving eye landed on their ignorance: “they don’t know what they are doing.”
How carefully he studied the situation and the character of the people he was pleading for!
He does the same thing in heaven.
Christ is not a careless lawyer for his people.

He knows your exact situation right now. He knows exactly how your heart is doing with the temptation you are facing. More than that, he sees the temptation that is still coming. And when he prays for you, he keeps in mind what his all-seeing eye sees ahead.
“Satan has wanted to get hold of you, to shake you like wheat in a sieve. But I have prayed for you, so that your faith will not fail.”
Oh, how kindly our great High Priest stoops down to us!
He knows us better than we know ourselves.
He understands every secret sorrow and every groan.
You don’t need to worry about the wording of your prayer. He will fix the wording.
And if you can’t even figure out exactly what to ask for, he can. He knows the mind of God, and he knows your mind too.

He can find some reason for mercy in you that you can’t see in yourself. Sometimes your soul feels so dark and cloudy that you can’t find anything at all to say to heaven in your favor. But the Lord Jesus has the reasons already worked out and the requests already written. And he can present them before the mercy seat in a way God will accept.
So you see, his praying for us is full of grace. It is also very thoughtful.
Next, we must notice how earnest it is.
No one who reads these words, “Father, forgive them, because they don’t know what they are doing,” doubts that they were passionate enough to pierce heaven.
Brothers and sisters, you are sure, without even thinking about it, that Christ meant that prayer with all his heart.
But there is a reason we can give to prove it.
People who are truly in earnest are usually clever and quick to spot anything that might help their cause.
If you were pleading for your life, and someone asked you for a reason to spare you, I promise you would think of one, even when nobody else could.
Now, Jesus cared so deeply about saving his enemies that he hit on a reason for mercy that a less concerned person would never have thought of: “They don’t know what they are doing.”

Why, my friends, if you go by strict justice, that was a very thin reason for mercy. In fact, if people choose to stay ignorant, their ignorance does not make their sin any less. And many of the people around the cross had chosen not to know.
They could have known that he was the Lord of glory.
Hadn’t Moses made it clear enough?
Hadn’t Isaiah spoken very boldly?
Weren’t the signs and proofs so clear that doubting Jesus’ claim to be the Messiah was like doubting which light in the sky is the sun?

And yet the Savior was so amazingly earnest that it made him skillful. He took something that might not have been a good reason and turned it into one. He put it like this: “Father, forgive them, because they don’t know what they are doing.”
Oh, then how powerful his pleas in heaven must be, because he means them so deeply!
Don’t imagine that he is any slower to understand up there, or any less intense in how strongly he pleads.
No, brothers and sisters, the heart of Christ is still working hard with the eternal God.

He is not a sleepy intercessor. For Zion’s sake he does not keep silent, and for Jerusalem’s sake he does not stop. And he never will, until her righteousness goes out as bright as the light, and her salvation like a lamp that is burning.
Fourth, it is interesting to notice that this prayer helps us understand how his praying in heaven goes on and on. It continues, it keeps going, and it never ends.

As I said before, if there was ever a time when our Savior could have stopped praying for others, it was surely when they nailed him to the cross. They were actively and violently trying to kill him. He could have stopped asking God to help them then.
But sin cannot silence the Friend who prays for us.
Oh, what comfort there is in this!
Believer, you have sinned. You have grieved his Spirit. But you have not silenced that powerful voice that pleads for you.
My brother, perhaps you have not produced any fruit. Like the fruitless tree, you deserve to be cut down. But your lack of fruit has not driven the one who prays for you away from his place.
Right now he steps in, crying, “Spare it one more year.”

Sinner, you have made God angry by rejecting his mercy for a long time and going from bad to worse. But no amount of blasphemy, or wickedness, or unbelief will stop God’s Christ from pleading the case of even the very worst of sinners.
He is alive, and as long as he lives, he pleads. As long as there is a sinner on earth to be saved, there will be someone in heaven to plead for him.
These are only bits and pieces of thought. But I hope they help you see more clearly how your great High Priest prays for you.
Think about one more thing. This prayer of our Lord on earth is like his prayer in heaven because it is wise.
He asks for the best thing, the thing the people he is pleading for need most: “Father, forgive them.”
That was the main issue. What they needed most of all, right then and there, was God’s forgiveness.

He does not say, “Father, open their eyes, because they don’t know what they are doing.” Just opening their eyes would only have tormented their consciences and rushed them toward hell. Instead he cries, “Father, forgive.” And while he was speaking, the precious drops of blood falling from the nail wounds were pleading too. God heard, and surely he did forgive.
The first mercy guilty sinners need is to have their sin forgiven.
Christ wisely prays for the gift they need most.
It is the same in heaven. He pleads wisely and sensibly.
Leave it to him. He knows what to ask God for.

Go to the mercy seat and pour out your wishes as well as you can. But when you are done, always put it like this: “O my Lord Jesus, don’t grant any wish of mine unless you think it is right. And if I have failed to ask for what I really need, fix my prayer, because you are far, far wiser than I am.” Oh, how sweet it is to have a friend in the King’s court who perfects our requests before they reach the great King.

I believe that only perfect prayers are ever presented to God now. I mean that no prayer of his people ever reaches the great Father of us all in an imperfect state. Nothing is missing, and nothing needs to be crossed out. That is not because their prayers were perfect to begin with. It is because the Mediator makes them perfect with his endless wisdom. So they come before the mercy seat shaped to match the mind of God himself, and he is sure to grant prayers like that.
One more point. This unforgettable prayer of our crucified Lord was like all his praying in another way too: it wins what it asks for.
Many of the people he prayed for were forgiven.

Do you remember? When he sent his disciples out to preach, he told them to begin “at Jerusalem.” Then, on the day when Peter stood up with the eleven, he told the people plainly that with wicked hands they had crucified and killed the Savior. And three thousand of those very people, rightly accused of crucifying him, came to believe in him and were baptized in his name.
That was an answer to Jesus’ prayer.
The priests were behind our Lord’s murder. They were the most guilty. And yet the Bible says, “a large number of the priests also believed.”
That was another answer to the prayer.

All people, Gentiles as well as Jews, had a share in the death of Jesus through those who represented them. So the good news was soon preached to the Jews, and before long it was preached to the Gentiles too.

Isn’t this prayer, “Father, forgive them,” like a stone thrown into a lake? First it makes a small circle, then a wider ring, and soon a bigger one, until the whole lake is covered with rings of waves.

This prayer was thrown into the whole world like that. First it made a little ring of Jewish believers and priests. Then it made a wider circle of people under Roman rule. And today its circle is as wide as the whole globe. Tens of thousands are saved because of the power of this one prayer: “Father, forgive them.”
It is certainly the same with him in heaven. He never pleads for nothing.

Even with bleeding hands, he still won. Even with his feet nailed to the wood, he was still victorious. Forsaken by God and despised by the people, he still triumphed in his pleading. So how much more now! Now the royal crown is on his head, his hand holds the scepter over everything, his feet wear silver sandals, and he is crowned King of kings and Lord of lords!

His tears and cries in weakness were all-powerful. So the holy authority he claims now must be even mightier, if that is possible. As the risen Priest, he stands before the Father’s throne and speaks of the covenant the Father made with him.
Trembling believers, trust him with the things that worry you!
Come here, you who are guilty, and ask him to plead for you.
You who don’t know how to pray, come and ask him to pray for you.

Broken hearts, weary heads, and sad and lonely souls, come to him. He will put his own merits into the golden incense bowl, and then put your prayers in with them. So your prayers will rise like the smoke of incense, a sweet-smelling cloud before the Lord, the God of armies. He will enjoy the sweet smell and accept you and your prayers in his Beloved Son.
We have now given you more than enough open water for your thoughts to sail in at home this afternoon. So we will leave this first point.
The prayer of Christ on the cross has shown us what his prayers in heaven are always like.

blocks.x: II. Second, the text TEACHES US ABOUT THE CHURCH’S WORK.

s: As Christ was in this world, so his church is to be.
Christ came into this world not to have others serve him, but to serve others. He did not come to be honored, but to save others.

When the church understands her work, she will see that she is not here to collect wealth or honor for herself, or to chase worldly importance and position. She is here to live unselfishly, and if necessary to die unselfishly, to rescue the lost sheep and to save lost people.
Brothers and sisters, I told you that Christ’s prayer on the cross was completely unselfish.
He does not think of himself in it at all.
That should be the prayer of the church’s whole life. The church should actively step in on behalf of sinners.
She should never live for her ministers or for herself, but always for lost human beings.
Do you imagine that churches are formed just to support ministers?
Do you think the church exists in this country just so that salaries can be paid to bishops, deans, cathedral officials, curates, and who knows what else?
Brothers and sisters, if that were its only purpose, it would be better to get rid of the whole thing.

The purpose of the church is not to hand out welfare to the younger sons of noble families. When they are not smart enough to earn a living any other way, they get stuck into church jobs that their families control.
Churches are not made so that smooth talkers can stand up on Sundays and speak, and so earn their living from their fans.
No, the church has a completely different goal and purpose.
These places of worship are not built so that you can sit here comfortably and hear something that helps you pass your Sundays pleasantly.
Think of a church in London that does not exist to do good in the city’s slums, dens, and filthy hovels. That church has no reason to go on existing.

Think of a church that does not exist to win people away from paganism, to fight evil, to destroy error, and to stamp out lies. Think of a church that does not exist to take the side of the poor, to speak out against injustice, and to hold up what is right. That church has no right to exist.
O church, you do not exist for yourself, any more than Christ existed for himself.

His glory was that he laid his glory aside. And the church’s glory comes when she lays aside her respectability and her dignity. Her glory is to gather in the outcasts. Her highest honor is to search in the filthiest mud for the priceless jewels that Jesus shed his blood for.
To rescue souls from hell and lead them to God, to hope, and to heaven—this is her heavenly work.
Oh, if only the church would always feel this way!

Let her have her bishops and her preachers, and let them be supported. Let everything be done properly and in order, for Christ’s sake. But keep the goal in view. The goal is to turn back those who have wandered, to teach the ignorant, to help the poor, to stand up for what is right, to stop what is wrong, and at any cost to uphold the crown and kingdom of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Now, Christ’s prayer had a deeply spiritual goal.
Notice that he asks for nothing for these people except what has to do with their souls: “Father, forgive them.”

I believe the church will do well when she remembers this. Her fight is not against flesh and blood, or against rulers and powers, but against spiritual wickedness. What she has to give out is not the law and order that keeps officials in power or brings down tyrants. It is the spiritual rule by which hearts are won over to Christ and minds are brought under his truth.

Here is what I believe. The church should strive before God for the forgiveness of sinners. In the prayer of her whole life, she should try to teach sinners what sin is, and what the blood of Christ is. She should teach them what hell must follow if sin is not washed away, and what heaven is promised to all who are cleansed from sin. The more she does this, and the more she sticks to it, the better.
Brothers and sisters, press forward together as one, to get to the root of the matter: the forgiveness of sinners.

As for all the evils that trouble the human race, by all means do your part to fight them. Keep up the fight against drunkenness. Support education. Push forward reforms in government and in the church, as far as you have the time and energy to spare. But the first business of every Christian man and woman is with people’s hearts and consciences as they stand before the everlasting God.
Oh, don’t let anything turn you away from your God-given mission of mercy to souls that will live forever.
This is your one job.
Tell sinners that sin will condemn them forever, and that only Christ can take away sin. And make this the one passion of your soul: “Father, forgive them, forgive them!
Let them know how to be forgiven.
Let them really be forgiven. And let me never rest unless I am helping to bring sinners to forgiveness, even the guiltiest of them.”
Our Savior’s prayer teaches the church something more. Her spirit should be unselfish, and her goal should be spiritual, but the reach of her mission should have no limits.
Christ prayed for the wicked. In fact, I could say he prayed for the most wicked of the wicked, that foul-mouthed crowd gathered around his cross!
He prayed for the ignorant.
Doesn’t he say, “They don’t know what they are doing”?
He prayed for the people who were persecuting him. The very people who hated him most were closest to his heart.

Church of God, your mission is not to the respectable few who gather around your ministers and listen politely to what they say. Your mission is not to the upper class and the refined, the clever people who will criticize your words and judge every syllable you teach. Your mission is not to those who treat you kindly, generously, and lovingly. I mean, not to these alone, though of course to them along with everyone else. But your great task is to reach the prostitute, the thief, the swearer, and the drunkard—the most depraved and corrupt people of all.
If no one else cares about these people, the church always must. If anyone should come first in her prayers, it should be these people, who, sadly, usually come last in our thoughts.
We must also pay careful attention to the ignorant.

It is not enough for a preacher to preach so that people who were taught from childhood can understand him. He must think of people for whom the most common words about God’s truth are as meaningless as a foreign language. He must preach so that even the simplest mind can understand. And if the ignorant masses don’t come to hear him, he must use whatever means he can to persuade them. Yes, he must even compel them to hear the good news.
The gospel is also meant for those who persecute religion. It aims its arrows of love at the hearts of its enemies.
If there is anyone we should try to bring to Jesus first, it should be the very people who are farthest away and most opposed to the good news of Christ.
“Father, forgive them. Even if you forgive no one else, please forgive them.”

The church should also be as earnest as Christ was. If she is, she will be quick to notice any reason for hope in the people she works with. She will be quick to spot any argument she can use with God for their salvation.
She must also be hopeful. And surely no church has ever had a more hopeful field of work than the church of our own time.
If ignorance is a reason for God to show mercy, look at the heathen today. Millions of them have never heard the Messiah’s name.
Great God, forgive them. They truly don’t know what they are doing.

If ignorance gives some reason for hope, there is plenty of hope in this great city of London. Aren’t there hundreds of thousands of people all around us for whom the simplest truths of the gospel would be brand-new?

Brothers and sisters, it is sad to think that this country still lies under such a dark cloud of ignorance. But the sting of such a terrible fact is dulled by hope when we read the Savior’s prayer the right way. It helps us to hope as we cry, “Forgive them, because they don’t know what they are doing.”
It is the church’s job to go after the most fallen and the most ignorant people, and to keep going after them.
She should never stop doing good.

Even if the Lord is coming tomorrow, that is no reason for you Christians to settle down into people who just talk and read. It is no reason to meet only to comfort each other and forget the millions of souls who are dying.

Maybe it is true that this world will fall apart in two weeks and that Louis Napoleon is the beast in the book of Revelation. Or maybe it is not true. I don’t care one bit. It makes no difference to my duty, and it does not change my service.
Let my Lord come whenever he wants. As long as I am working for him, I am ready for him to appear.
The church’s business is still to watch out for the salvation of souls.

Suppose she just stood staring at the sky, as today’s prophecy teachers want her to. Suppose she gave up her mission to play with guesses about prophecy. Then she might well be afraid of her Lord’s coming. But if she goes about her work, and with nonstop effort searches out her Lord’s precious jewels, she will not be ashamed when her Bridegroom comes.
My time has been far too short for such a huge subject. But I wish I could speak words as loud as thunder, with meaning and passion as powerful as lightning.
I would love to stir up every Christian here and light a fire in each of you, so you see clearly what your work is as part of Christ’s church.

Brothers and sisters, you must not live for yourselves. You may make money, raise your children, build houses, and earn your daily bread. But if you are going to be like Christ, as you should be since you were bought with Jesus’ blood, there must be a bigger goal than all this.

Start living for others. Make it clear to everyone that you are not the whole point of your own life. Show them that you are spending yourself and being spent, so that through the good you do for people, God may be glorified, and Christ may see his own image in you and be satisfied.

blocks.x: III. I am running out of time, but the last point was going to be a word FOR THOSE WHO ARE NOT YET CONVERTED.

s: Listen carefully to these sentences.
I will keep them as short and to the point as I can.
Some of you here are not saved.
Now, some of you have been very ignorant. When you sinned, you didn’t know what you were doing.
You knew you were sinners; you knew that much. But you didn’t know how deep and far-reaching the guilt of sin is.
You haven’t been coming to church for long. You haven’t read your Bible. You don’t have Christian parents.
Now you are starting to worry about your souls.

Remember, your ignorance does not excuse you. If it did, Christ would not say, “Forgive them.” Even those who don’t know what they are doing need to be forgiven, so each of them is guilty. But still, your ignorance gives you a little glimmer of hope.
In the times when you did not know, God looked the other way. But now he commands all people everywhere to repent.
So let your life produce fruit that fits true repentance.
The God you have forgotten without realizing it is willing to pardon you and ready to forgive.
The gospel is simply this: trust Jesus Christ, who died for the guilty, and you will be saved.
Oh, may God help you to do this very morning! Then you will become new men and new women. A change will happen in you as big as being born again. You will be new creations in Christ Jesus.

But oh, my friends, there are some people here for whom even Christ himself could not pray this prayer, at least not in its fullest sense: “Father, forgive them, because they don’t know what they are doing.” You have known what you were doing. Every sermon you hear adds to your responsibility. This is even more true every time the gospel makes an impression on your mind and conscience. Each one takes away your excuse that you don’t know what you are doing.
Oh, my friends, you know that there is the world and there is Christ, and that you can’t have both.
You know that there is sin and there is God.
And you know that you can’t serve both.
You know that there are the pleasures of evil and the pleasures of heaven, and that you can’t have both.
Oh, God has given you light. In that light, may his Spirit also come and help you choose what true wisdom would lead you to choose.
Decide today for God, for Christ, and for heaven.
May the Lord lead you to decide, for the sake of his name. Amen.
“Forgive one another, just as God has forgiven you for Christ’s sake.”—Ephesians 4:32.

The pagan teachers of right and wrong could not point to their gods as an example when they wanted to teach people to be good. Their own storytellers described the gods as a mix of every evil you can imagine. I almost said: every evil you cannot even imagine.
Many of the old gods of Greece and Rome committed worse crimes than the worst human beings. They were supposed to be far more powerful than people, and they were just as much more wicked.
It is a sad day for a nation when its gods are worse than its people.
Our holy faith is wonderfully pure. You can see this in what it commands. But you can also see it in the character of the God it shows us.

Think of any good quality you could name. You will see it shining brightly in the Lord our God. Think of any way a Christian should live well. We can point to Christ Jesus, our Lord and Master, as the perfect example of it.
At the very top of the Christian faith, you find the very highest goodness. So the highest praise belongs to God our Father and to the Lord Jesus.
We want you to have the kindest, most forgiving spirit. And we can urge you toward it by pointing to God. For Christ’s sake, he has forgiven you.
What better reason could you need to forgive one another?
With such great examples in front of us, brothers and sisters, what kind of people should we be?

Sometimes we hear of people who were better than their religion. But that can never happen to us. We can never rise as high as our wonderful, God-given faith—not in our attitude and not in our actions.
We should keep rising above ourselves. We should even rise above the kindest Christians we know. And still, high above us, we will see our God and Savior.
We may grow stronger and stronger in good thoughts and in serving God. But Jesus is always higher still. As we climb the holy hill of grace, we must keep looking up to him.
Today we want to talk a little about our duty to love and forgive. Right away we notice that the apostle gives us God himself as our example.

We will spend most of our time on that bright example. But I hope we will not spend so much time that we forget the practical part. That part is badly needed these days by some unforgiving people who still call themselves Christians.

God’s forgiving love is such a wonderful subject that we may stay on it for a while—a long while, in fact. God has given us a bright example of forgiveness. As we look at it, I hope we will receive grace to forgive others, even “seventy times seven” times.
We will go through the verse word by word. That will give us the clearest outline.
I. The first words to think about are “FOR CHRIST’S SAKE.”
We say these words very often. But we have probably never thought about how powerful they are. Even today, we cannot explain everything they mean.
Let us think about them carefully. And let us pray that the good Holy Spirit will teach us.
“For Christ’s sake.” Every good thing God has given us has come to us “for Christ’s sake.” But this is especially true of the forgiveness of our sins. It has come “for Christ’s sake.”
That is exactly what the verse says.
What does it mean?
First, it surely means this: God forgives us because of the great sacrifice Christ offered to pay for sin.
The great God is a fair Lawgiver and King. Because Christ has made the payment for sin, God can freely let go of our wrongs.
If sin were only a personal insult to God, there is plenty of proof that he would gladly let it go without punishing it. But sin is much more than that.
People who think sin is only a personal insult to God are not thinking very deeply.

Sin is an attack on God’s moral rule over the world. It eats away at the foundations of society. If it were allowed to have its way, it would turn everything into chaos. It would even destroy the power that governs, and the Ruler himself.
God has a huge kingdom to rule. It is not only the people who live on the earth. Under his rule there are angels, rulers and powers, and who knows how many worlds of thinking beings.

Think of the countless worlds we see sparkling in the night sky. It would be a strange idea that God made them all without putting any living creatures there. It makes much more sense to think that our earth is just a tiny speck in God’s kingdom. It is only one small province in the endless empire of the King of kings.

Now, this world has rebelled against God boldly and openly. If God did not demand payment for that rebellion, he would be putting up with an attack on the rule of the great Judge of all. It would weaken his royal authority over his whole kingdom.

If human sin went unpunished, the news would soon spread through countless worlds. Millions upon millions of kinds of creatures would learn that they could sin and get away with it. If one race had done it, why not all the others?
It would be like announcing to everyone that they were free to rebel.
It would probably be the worst disaster that could ever happen—for the highest Judge to let any sin go unpunished.

Think of a country. If the lawmaker does not carry out the law against a murderer, people’s lives will be in danger. Nothing will be safe. So signing the death sentence becomes an act of mercy. It is the same with God and this world of sinners.
God’s holiness and justice make him judge sin strictly. But so does his love—if I may put it that way. This is why sin cannot and must not be wiped away until a payment for it has been made.

First there must be a sacrifice for sin. But notice this: the great Father supplies that sacrifice himself, to show his love. He gives his own Son to die. So the Father himself pays the ransom through his Son. And that Son is one with the Father. Their unity is a mystery, but it is extremely deep.

God’s justice demands the penalty, and God’s love pays it himself. The way of salvation through a sacrifice that pays for sin is an amazing mystery. But this much is clear: God has now forgiven us for Christ’s sake. God’s rule was dishonored, but full payment has been made for it, and justice is satisfied.
Think for a moment about how easily God can now wipe out sin, because Christ has died.
Wiping out sin seems hard until we look at the cross. Then it seems easy enough.

I have stared at sin until its horror almost blinded me. I said to myself, “This cursed stain can never be washed out. No soap in the world can change its color. An Ethiopian could sooner change the color of his skin, or a leopard its spots.
Oh sin, you deep and never-ending evil, what can take you away?”

But then I have seen the Son of God dying on the cross. I have read about the pain in his soul. I have heard the cries that showed how his spirit suffered when God his Father left him. And then it has seemed to me that wiping out sin is the easiest thing in the world.
When I have seen Jesus die, I could not understand how any sin could be hard to remove.

Let a person stand at Calvary and look at the one he has pierced. Let him believe and accept the payment Jesus made. Then it becomes the simplest thing in the world. His debt is cancelled, because it has been paid. He is set free, because the ransom has been found. He is no longer condemned, because the guilt that condemned him has been carried away by Jesus, his great Substitute and Lord.
So God has forgiven us for Christ’s sake because of what Jesus Christ suffered in our place.
Here is a second way to understand the verse. God has forgiven us because Christ acts as our representative—he stands in for us.
We should never forget that in the beginning we fell through a representative.
Adam stood in our place. He was our covenant head, acting on behalf of all of us.
At the very beginning we did not fall by our own actions. We fell through the one who represented us.
If Adam had kept the terms of God’s covenant, we would have stood firm through him. But because he fell, we fell with him.
Please do not complain about this arrangement. That is exactly where the hope of the human race was found.

The angels probably fell one by one, each for himself. That is why they fell with no way back—there was no restoring them. But we all fell in one man, Adam. So it was still possible for us to rise again in another Adam. That is why, at exactly the right time, God sent his Son Jesus Christ. He was born of a woman and placed under the law, to become the second Adam.
He took on the job of removing our burdens and meeting every condition for bringing us back.
According to God’s covenant, he had to come in our human nature. And at the right time he did become human.
He had to bear the penalty. He did that through his own suffering and death.
He had to obey the law. He did that completely.
So now Christ Jesus has borne the penalty and kept the law. He himself is declared right before God. And he stands before God as the representative of everyone who is in him.
For Christ’s sake, God has accepted us in him. He has forgiven us in him. And in him he looks at us with a love that has no limit and never changes.

This is how all our blessings come to us: in and through Christ Jesus. If we really are in him, the Lord does more than forgive our sin. He also gives us the endless riches of his grace in him. In fact, he treats us the way he would treat his Son. He deals with us the way he would deal with Jesus.
Oh, what a happy thought! When God, who is just, looks at us, he looks through the one who brings us back together with him. He sees us through the Mediator.
Sometimes we sing a hymn that says—

blocks.x:
“Look at him, and then see the sinner;
Look at me through Jesus’ wounds,”

s: and that is exactly what the Lord does.
He counts us as righteous because of our Savior’s sacrifice, and because Jesus represents us.
Now let us go a little further.
When we read “for Christ’s sake,” it surely also means this: because of the deep love the Father has for him.
My brothers and sisters, can you begin to imagine how much the Father loves his one and only Son?

We cannot poke into the amazing mystery of how the Son of God has been the Son forever. If we tried, the light would be so bright that it would blind us. But this we know: they are one God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. And the bond between them is deeper than we can imagine.
“The Father loves the Son.” That was always true, and it is true now. But no mind can grasp how deeply and how strongly he loves the Son.

Now, brothers and sisters, the Lord will do great things for the sake of a Son he loves the way he loves Jesus. He has always loved him, because they share one nature and being. But now there is another reason for his love. It comes from everything the Lord Jesus has done as the Father’s servant.

Remember that our Lord Jesus obeyed his Father’s will. He obeyed even to death—even to dying on the cross. That is why God has lifted him to the highest place and given him a name greater than every other name.
Here is one of the sweetest thoughts I know. Sometimes when I am alone, I suck the sweetness out of it. It is this: God the Father will do anything for Christ.
Here is another piece of honeycomb. When I can pray in Christ’s name, I am sure God will grant my request.
“For Christ’s sake” is a plea that always touches the heart of the great God.
Show that when you receive a certain blessing, it will bring glory to Christ. Then the Father cannot hold it back, because he loves to honor Jesus.
Of course, we are speaking in human terms. We must be careful with a subject like this. But we can only speak as humans, because that is all we are.
The Father loves to show his love to his Son.

Through all the ages, the Father and the Son have been close companions. They have always agreed in all their plans. They have never disagreed about anything, and they cannot disagree. Notice that when our Lord says, “Father, glorify your Son,” he is so closely joined with the Father that he adds, “so that your Son can glorify you.”
Their love for each other is greater than we can imagine. And so, brothers and sisters, God will do anything for Jesus.
God will forgive us for Christ’s sake. In fact, he has already done that for thousands of people around me.

And you, great sinner, stained black with sin: go to God right now. Say to him, “Lord, I cannot ask you to forgive me for my own sake. But please do it out of love for your dear Son.” If you do, he will forgive you. He will do anything for the sake of Jesus.
Maybe right now you feel your sin so much that you have given up on yourself. That is good. Giving up on yourself is just common sense, because there is nothing in you that you can depend on.

But grab hold of this hope. It is not a flimsy straw. It is a strong, solid life buoy. If you can ask for forgiveness for Jesus’ sake, remember this: God will do anything for Jesus. And for the sake of the Son he loves, he will do anything for you.
So let us read our verse once more. This time we read it in the light of a truth that comes from God’s love: God forgives sin in order to bring glory to Christ.
Christ took the shame so that he could bring honor to his Father. And now his Father loves to honor him by wiping out sin.
If you can show that a gift to you would bring glory to Christ, you can count on it: you will get it.
If there were anything in the world that would make Christ more glorious, the Father would not hold it back for a moment.
Maybe you can see that having your sin forgiven would make the Savior more famous. Then go and use that argument with God, and you will surely win.
Won’t it make Christ glad to save a sinner like you?
Then go to God with this argument on your lips: “Father, bring glory to your Son. Show that he is a glorious Savior by saving me.”

When I am stuck under a load that will not move, this is often a great lever for me. I say to the Lord, “Lord, you know the trouble I am in. You know how little I deserve. You know what a poor, ruined creature I am in front of you. But if your dear Son helps me and saves me, even the angels will stand in amazement at his mighty grace. So it will bring him glory. That is why I beg you to be kind to me.”
You can be sure you will win if you can argue that it will bring glory to Christ. And surely you would not want anything that would not bring him glory.

Your prayer will always win if your heart is in the right place. That means you are willing to have something or not to have it, depending on whether it will honor your Lord. If it will not bring glory to Christ, be more than happy to go without even the best thing on earth. But when God does give you a gift that brings honor to the dear and worthy name of Jesus, be twice as thankful.
“For Christ’s sake.” These are precious words. Think about them often. Store this sentence away in your memory: the Father will do anything for the sake of Jesus Christ his Son.
II. Now, second, let us look at what the verse says has been done for us and to us for Christ’s sake.
“God, for Christ’s sake, HAS FORGIVEN YOU.”
First, notice that he has certainly done this.
The apostle does not say, “I hope so.” He says, “God, for Christ’s sake, has forgiven you.”
My dear listener, are you one of the forgiven?
Have you believed in the Lord Jesus Christ?
Then, as surely as you have believed, God has forgiven you for Christ’s sake.
Have you put your trust in Jesus’ sacrifice for sin?
Then God has forgiven you for Christ’s sake.
I hope you did not start your Christian life thinking that someday, at some point in the future, you might be forgiven.
No. “God, for Christ’s sake, has forgiven you.”
Forgiveness is not a prize you have to run a race to win. It is a gift you receive at the very first step of the race.
If you have believed in Jesus, your sin is gone—all of it! Every sin has been erased from the records of the past. It will never be brought up against you again, ever.
The moment a sinner looks to Christ, the heavy load of his sin rolls off his shoulders. It will never come back.
Has Christ washed you? He has, if you have believed in him. Then you are completely clean. You stand before the Lord free from every trace of guilt.
Forgiveness is not something we only hope for. It is a fact.
Hope looks forward to many blessings still to come. But forgiveness is a gift we already have. Faith is holding it in her hand right now.
If Christ took your heavy load, it cannot still be on your back. If Christ paid your debts, they are no longer written against you in God’s books.
How could they be? It only makes sense. If Jesus, who took your place, has taken your sin and put it away, then your sin is no longer on you.
God has forgiven you for Christ’s sake.
Grab hold of that great truth. Hold on to it, even if all the devils in hell roar at you.
Grip it with a hand of steel. Hold on as if your life depended on it: “God has forgiven me for Christ’s sake.” May every one of us be able to say that.
We will not feel how sweet and powerful this verse is unless the Holy Spirit helps us make it personal.
Next, notice that God keeps on forgiving us.
He did not only forgive all our sins at the beginning. He keeps forgiving us every day. Forgiveness is an act that goes on and on.

I have sometimes heard people say that we were forgiven so fully when we first believed that we never need to ask for forgiveness again. Here is my answer. Yes, we were completely forgiven when we first believed. And that is exactly why we should keep asking God to continue that one great act of forgiveness, which reaches so far. We ask the Lord to keep showing us the same full, forgiving grace that set us perfectly free at the start. Then we can keep living before him, knowing clearly and without doubt that we are completely forgiven.
I know I was forgiven when I first believed in Christ. And I am just as sure of it today. That one pardon keeps ringing in my ears like joyful bells that never stop.
Forgiveness that God gives once keeps on being given.
There were times when I had doubts and worries, and I was not sure I was forgiven. But it was still true. Whoever believes in Jesus is not condemned, even if he writes bitter things about himself.
Dear friend, grab hold of that and do not let go.
God’s forgiveness keeps on going.
And God’s forgiveness was completely free.
We did nothing to earn it, and we brought nothing to pay for it.
He forgave us for Christ’s sake, not because of anything we had done.

It is true that we repented and believed. But God gave us that repentance and faith. So he did not forgive us because of them. He forgave us only because of his own dear love. He delights in showing mercy. He is never more like himself than when he lets go of wrongdoing, guilt, and sin.
Remember also that he forgave us completely.
He did not wipe out one sin here and another one there. He destroyed the whole horrible list of our wrongs all at once.
Our Lord took our place, and that settled the matter perfectly:—

blocks.x:
“Because the Savior without sin has died,
My sinful soul is counted free;
For God, who is just, is satisfied
To look at him and pardon me.”

s: All our sins are swept away at once, as if carried off by a flood. They are so completely taken away that not a trace of guilt is left.
They are all gone!

You who believe, think about this. That word “all” is no small thing. It includes sins against a holy God and sins against his loving Son. Sins against the gospel as well as the law. Sins against people as well as against God. Sins of the body and sins of the mind. Sins as many as the grains of sand on the seashore, and as big as the sea itself. All of them, every one, have been taken away from us as far as the east is from the west.
All this evil was rolled into one huge heap and laid on Jesus. He carried it all, and he has put an end to it forever.
When the Lord forgave us, he forgave the whole debt.
He did not take the bill and say, “I will cross out this item and that one.” No, the pen went through the whole thing—PAID.

It was a receipt that paid every charge in full. Jesus took the written record that was against us and nailed it to his cross. He did this to show the whole universe that it could never condemn us again.
In him we have complete forgiveness.
Remember too that the forgiveness God has given us for Christ’s sake lasts forever.
He will never dig up our past wrongs and charge us with them a second time.
He will not catch us on some bad day and say, “I have been very patient with you, but now I will treat you as your sins deserve.”
Not at all! Whoever believes in Jesus has eternal life and will never be condemned.
Heaven’s pardon can never be undone.
“God never regrets his gifts or his call.”
He never regrets what he has given or what he has forgiven. It is done, done forever. Jehovah declares us free, and that verdict stands firm forever.
“So now, no one who is in Christ Jesus will be condemned.”
“Who can bring any charge against the people God has chosen?
God is the one who declares them right.
Who is there to condemn them?”
Praise God for a pardon that lasts forever!
I could not find any other word to finish with, so I will use this one: he has forgiven us the way only God can.

God’s forgiveness has a truth, a reality, and a power that you will never find in human forgiveness. Suppose you treated someone very badly. Even if he forgave everything you did against him, you could hardly expect him to forget it completely. But the Lord says, “Their sins and their wrongs I will remember no more, ever.”
If someone has betrayed you, you may forgive him. But you probably will not trust him again.
There is an old saying: “Never ride a horse that has fallen and broken its knees.” It is not a bad saying, either.
But look at how the Lord treats his people.
When Peter was put back on his feet, he was just like a horse that had fallen and broken its knees. And yet look how gloriously the Lord rode that warhorse on the day of Pentecost!
Didn’t he ride out as a conqueror, winning victory after victory?

The Lord lets the past be the past so completely that he trusts forgiven people with his secrets. For “the Lord shares his secrets with those who fear him.” He even trusts some of us with his most precious treasures. Paul said, “He trusted me with the gospel, even though I used to insult God.”
He puts into our care that priceless treasure box that holds the greatest hope people have—the gospel of Jesus.
“We carry this treasure in pots made of clay.”
This shows how perfect our forgiveness is. No—I have to say it better: it shows how divine the forgiveness is that we have received.

Let us celebrate the great promise that comes to us from the prophet Jeremiah long ago: “In those days, at that time, says the Lord, people will search for Israel’s guilt, and there will be none. They will look for Judah’s sins, and they will not be found. For I will forgive those I keep for myself.”
Here is complete destruction—the only “annihilation” I know of. Sin is wiped out completely, gone forever, through the forgiveness the Lord gives his people.
Let us sing it as if it were a favorite hymn: “People will search for Israel’s guilt, and there will be none.”
III. Now, if you have soaked in the spirit of our subject, you will be strong enough to hear what I have to say about putting it into practice.
“FORGIVE ONE ANOTHER, just as God has forgiven you for Christ’s sake.”
Let me say right at the start that I do not know of anyone here who has fallen out with anyone else. So I will not be pointing at anyone.

Even if I did know about quarrels and arguments, I would probably say much the same thing. But I do not happen to know of any. So if what I say hits home, I beg each person it touches to believe that it is meant for him. Please take it as a sharp, personal message from God.
“Forgive one another, just as God has forgiven you for Christ’s sake.”
Now notice how the apostle says it.
Does he say “forgiving someone else”?
No, look closely. That is not what the verse says.
It says “forgiving one another.”
One another! Ah, so that means this: if you have to forgive someone today, you will very likely need to be forgiven yourself tomorrow. That is why it says “forgiving one another.”
We take turns. It is something we do for each other. We all work at it together.
In fact, it is like a company owned by all of us together, and its business is forgiving each other. Church members should buy lots of shares in it.
“Forgiving one another.” You forgive me, and I forgive you. We forgive them, and they forgive us. And so a circle of endless patience and love goes around the world.

There is something wrong with me that my brother needs to forgive. But there is also something wrong with my brother that I need to forgive. That is what the apostle means. All of us should be practicing, with each other, this holy art and secret of forgiving one another.
If we always did this, we would not put up with people who have a special talent for spotting other people’s faults.
Some people always speak badly of their church, whatever church they belong to.
I have heard many people say things like this: “There is no love among Christians at all.”
Let me tell you what kind of man says that. He does not love others, and he is not easy to love either. So he has wandered off the road that love’s pilgrims travel.
Another person complains, “There is no honesty left in the world anymore.”
That man is a hypocrite. You can be quite sure of that.
You can tell a bird by its song, and a person by what he says.
Fault-finders measure other people’s grain, but they use their own measuring baskets.
You can tell a lot about a person by what he says about others.
Here is a test of character that will almost never fool you: judge people by the way they judge others.
What they say shows what is in their heart.
Show me your tongue, sir!
Now I can tell whether you are sick or healthy.
If someone speaks evil about his neighbor, he has an evil heart. You can be sure of that.

Let us start our Christian life knowing for sure that we will have to forgive other people a great deal. But others will have to forgive us even more. So let us expect that we will need to be gentle with others, and that others will need to be gentle with us: “Forgive one another, just as God has forgiven you for Christ’s sake.”

Notice something else. When we forgive, it is a small and humble thing compared with God forgiving us. We are only forgiving one another—that is, servants forgiving fellow servants. But when God forgives us, it is the Judge of the whole earth forgiving. He is not forgiving his equals. He is forgiving his rebellious subjects, who are guilty of treason against their King.
When God forgives, it is something great. When we forgive, some people think it is a big deal. But it should be seen as a very small thing.
Next, think about what needs to be forgiven.
In one of his parables, our Lord tells us about a servant. His fellow servant owed him a few pennies. But he himself owed his master many talents—a huge fortune.
What we owe God has no limit. But what another person owes us is a tiny amount.
What did he do that has upset you so much?
“He said something terrible about me.”
No doubt that was very wrong of him.
“Then he played a really nasty trick on me and treated me very unkindly. In fact, he behaved shamefully. If you hear the story, you will be really angry.”
Well, I am angry.
He is a bad man, no doubt about it. And so are you.
You certainly were when you first came to God. As bad as he has been to you, you have been much worse to the Lord.
I promise you, his darkest wrongs against you look white next to your dark wrongs before God.
“Oh, but you would not believe how low he stooped.”
No, and I suppose I would hardly believe it if I heard how low you have stooped with the Lord. Anyway, it should bring tears to our eyes to think how we have hurt our God and grieved his Spirit.
Some of us have been forgiven so much, and so openly. So many outward sins have been forgiven. For us, forgiving others should be as natural as opening our hands.
The Lord has forgiven some of us so much. After that, we would be wicked servants indeed if we grabbed our brother by the throat and said, “Pay back what you owe me!”
We would deserve to be handed over to the torturers by our angry Master if we did not count it a joy to overlook a brother’s fault.
If any Christian here finds it hard to forgive, I am going to give him three words that will help him wonderfully.
I would like to put them in that good man’s mouth.
I gave them to you a little while ago and begged you to taste how sweet they are. Here they are again!
“For Christ’s sake.”
Can’t you forgive someone who has hurt you for that reason?
Maybe your daughter has behaved very shamefully, and you, her father, have said some harsh things. But I beg you: forgive her for Christ’s sake.
Can’t you do it for that reason?
It is true that your son has done very wrong. Nothing hurts a father’s heart more than a son’s wicked behavior.
In a fit of anger you said something very harsh. You told him he could never come into your house again.
