I beg you: take back your words for Christ’s sake.
Sometimes, when I have pleaded in a case like that, the person I was trying to persuade has kindly said, “I will do it for you, sir.”
And I have said, “I will thank you if you do it at all. But I would rather you had said you would do it for my Master. What a wonderful Master he has been to you!
Do it for his sake.”
I may be speaking very plainly and directly to some of you.
I hope I am.

Maybe some of you have let your heart get into a bad state. Maybe you have said you will never forgive a son who rebelled against you. Do not say that again until you have thought it over, for Christ’s sake.
I am not urging you to show mercy for the boy’s sake. Not for the sake of the neighbor who offended you. Not for any other reason. I urge you to do it for Christ’s sake.

Come, you two brothers who have fallen out: love each other for Christ’s sake. Come, you two sisters. Come, you two friends who have drifted apart. Get together right away, and end all your bad feelings for Christ’s sake.
You must not keep even a drop of spite in your soul—for Christ’s sake.
Oh, what a beautiful word! It melts our hearts. And as it melts them, it seems to leave no trace of anger behind. For Christ’s sake our love is patient for a long time, and it never fails.
I am not sure how to say the next thing.
It sounds like a contradiction.
You must forgive, or you cannot be saved. But you must not do it because you are forced to. You must do it freely.
There is a way to live this out, even though I cannot explain it in words.
You must forgive, not because you have to, but because you truly want to, with all your heart.
Remember this: it is no use putting your money in the offering box on your way out unless you first remember to forgive your brother.
God will not accept the gifts, prayers, or praises of a heart that refuses to forgive.
Even if you leave everything you own to God’s work, he will not accept a single penny of it if you die with an unforgiving attitude.
Where people are not willing to overlook faults, there is no grace.
John says, “If someone does not love his brother, whom he can see, how can he love God, whom he cannot see?”
The very prayer that teaches you to ask for mercy tells you to say, “Forgive us, as we forgive those who owe us.”
If you have not forgiven others, then every time you pray the Lord’s Prayer, you are reading out your own death sentence.
Finally, brothers and sisters, I want to say this to all of you. We are brothers and sisters in Christ Jesus. If we are going to forgive one another, there are some other things we should do too.
The first is this: let us not push each other into doing wrong.
If I know someone does not like something, I will not keep pushing it in front of him.
Don’t say, “Well, if he is short-tempered, I can’t help that. He shouldn’t get offended so easily.
I can’t always be tiptoeing around his silly sensitivity.”
No, of course not. But, brother, your friend does get offended very easily, and you know it. So be considerate of his weak temper, just as you would be if he had something wrong with his body.
If you have painful rheumatism or gout, your friends do not stomp across the room saying, “He shouldn’t mind that. He shouldn’t feel it.”
Kind people walk softly across the floor, so they will not hurt the poor aching limb.
If a person’s mind is unwell and he gets annoyed very easily, treat him gently. Feel sorry for his weakness, and do not annoy him.

A little while ago a friend wrote me a letter. He was seriously complaining about a brother who had gotten very angry with him. In the heat of the moment, that brother had said some very sharp things.
I felt I had to hear the other side of the story. Then I had to say, “Now, you two brothers are both wrong.
You, my brother, lost your temper. But you, my other brother, annoyed him, so I am not surprised he lost his temper.
And when you saw he had lost his temper, why didn’t you walk away? Or why didn’t you do something to calm him down?
No, you stayed and made him even angrier. And then you wrote to expose him.”
I blame the wood for burning. But what should I say about the bellows that blew on the fire?
It was wrong for the wood to blaze. But was it right to fan the flames?
Very often, when a person is angry, he is not the only one to blame.
So, brothers and sisters, if we are going to forgive each other, let us not push each other into doing wrong.
Next, do not invent reasons to be offended.
Many times a person has been offended by someone else for no reason at all.
One man said about another who passed him in the street, “He won’t even nod to me.
He is too proud to say hello to me because I am poor.”
But that dear friend who was blamed could not see much farther than his own hand. He was nearsighted.
Another man was criticized for not listening, when in fact he was deaf. Another was criticized for not shaking hands, when his arm was crippled.
Do not imagine people are insulting you when they do not mean to.
Next, do not take offense even when someone means to offend you.
It is a wonderful thing if you refuse to be offended.
Suppose a man meant something as an insult, but you take it as a compliment and thank him for it. Nothing makes him feel smaller than that.
Can you control yourself that well?
Remember, when you have conquered yourself, you have conquered the world.
You have overcome everyone once you have fully overcome your own spirit. Then you stay content even with things that would normally make you angry.
But if you must be offended, dear brother, do not make the offense bigger than it is.
I was about to say “some good women,” but men do it too. When they come to tell tales and accuse someone, they add all kinds of decorations and extra details.
They take the long way around. They drag endless opinions, suggestions, hints, and rumors into the matter. In the end a gnat’s egg has become as huge as any egg an ostrich ever laid.

I calmly start to strip off the feathers and the paint. I say, “Now, I don’t see what that point has to do with it, or what that remark really means. When I look at the bare facts, all I can see is such-and-such. And that was not much, was it?”
“Oh, but they meant more than that.”
Don’t believe that, dear brother, dear sister.
If something really must be wrong, let it be as small as possible.
If you have a telescope, look through the big end. Make things smaller instead of bigger. Or even better, don’t look at it at all.
A blind eye is often the best eye a person can have. And a deaf ear is far better than one that hears too much.
Solomon says, “Also, do not pay attention to every word people say, or you may hear your servant curse you.”
Something you did may annoy a servant. Then he may say things that are rude and disrespectful.
Don’t listen to what he is muttering.
Stay out of earshot.
He will be sorry tomorrow. And if he thinks you did not hear him, he will keep working for you and be faithful to you.
What would you do if your master jumped on every word you said and pounced on every sentence you spoke?
How could you live at all if he were that strict with you?
No, dear friends. Since you have to forgive one another, do not take offense. When someone does offend you, do not make it bigger than it is. And if you can, do not even notice it.
Next, do not spread offenses around.
Someone has said something very offensive.
So what? Do not repeat it.
Do not go first to one person and then to another and say, “Now, this is just between us, so be sure to keep it secret. So-and-so has said something shameful.”
It would be better to let your heart break than to go here and there carrying a burning torch like that.
If a brother has done wrong, why should you do wrong too?
You will be doing wrong if you make his fault public.

Remember how a curse came on Noah’s son because he exposed his father. When something is wrong, it is much better for all of us to walk backward and cover it. If we can help it, we should not even look at it ourselves.
Cover it up. Cover it up.
Love covers a great many sins.
Love does not cover just one, two, or three sins. She carries a cloak that covers a whole host of faults.
Most of all, my brothers and sisters—and with this I will finish—never take revenge in any way, directly or indirectly.
Whatever wrong anyone ever does to you, the Master tells you: do not resist evil.
In everything, bend, bow, give way, and submit.
Someone says, “If you step on a worm, it will turn.”
But is a worm your example?
Christ will be my example.
It is a shocking thing when a Christian forgets his Lord and looks for an excuse for himself among the poor creatures under his feet.
But if a worm must be the example, what does a worm do when it turns?
When you have stepped on a worm, does it bite?
Does the worm hurt anyone?
Oh, no. It turns, but only in pain. It twists in front of you, and that is all.
You may do that, if you must.
Brother, the most wonderful revenge you could ever have is this: do good to those who do you harm, and speak well of those who speak badly of you.
They will be ashamed to look at you. They will never hurt you again if they see that nothing can provoke you, except to greater love and more kindness.
This should be the mark of Christians. Not “I’ll take you to court,” or “I’ll get my revenge,” but “I will put up with it and hold back, right to the end.”
“Revenge is mine. I will repay it, says the Lord.”
Do not take into your own hands what God says belongs to him. Instead, just as he has forgiven you for Christ’s sake, forgive everyone who wrongs you.
Someone asks, “How long do I have to keep doing that?”
“I wouldn’t mind doing it three or four times.”
Long ago there was someone who was willing to go as far as six or seven times. But Jesus Christ said, “Seventy times seven.”
That is a very large number.
You can count and see whether you have reached that number yet. If you have, you will be glad to start again and keep on forgiving, just as God has forgiven you for Christ’s sake.
May God help us to be patient to the end.
Just now I have not been preaching Christ Jesus as the one sinners should trust. But remember, he must also be the one we imitate.
This is the kind of teaching Christ himself preached. He was always preaching this love for our neighbor and forgiveness for our enemies. So we should both preach it and practice it.
Go and believe in him, and imitate him. Remember that he forgave the people who murdered him, on the very cross where he won our redemption.
May his Spirit rest on you forever. Amen.
“You are my friends if you do everything I command you.”—John 15:14.
Our Lord Jesus Christ is by far the best friend anyone could have. He is a friend when you need him, and a true friend in every way.
Socrates once said, “Friend! There is no such thing as a friend!” But Socrates did not know our Lord Jesus. If he had, he would have added, “except the Savior.”
The heart of our Lord Jesus burns with such friendship for us that every other kind of friendship looks like a weak candle next to the sun.
“No one has greater love than this: to give up his life for his friend.”

When an ordinary man dies for his friend, he has done the most he can possibly do. And yet he would have died someday anyway. So by dying for his friend, he is really just paying a debt a little early. It is a debt he would have had to pay a bit later in any case.
But Christ did not have to die at all. That is why his love and friendship stand completely alone.
He died when he did not need to die. He died in terrible pain when he could have lived in glory. No one has ever given such proof of friendship as this.
Let our Lord’s friendship toward us be the model for our friendship toward him.

It cannot be the same in every way, because we are in very different positions. His love will always be the love of the greater one for the smaller one. It is the love of a helper for someone in need. It is the love of the Redeemer for people he bought at a price. But apart from those differences, the whole tone and spirit of our Lord’s friendship is something we should copy. The closer we copy it, the better.
Friendship like his should be answered by a friendship from us that is warm, wholehearted, and ready to give things up.
I think that in this verse our Lord is not talking about him being our friend. He is talking about us being his friends.
He is “the friend of sinners.” But sinners are not his friends until their hearts are changed.
“You are my friends if you do everything I command you.” We are not his friends until then.
His love for us comes completely from himself. But friendship needs something from us too.
Friendship cannot be only one-sided. If only one side gives, it is better called mercy, grace, or kindness. Real friendship goes both ways.
You can do everything you want for someone and be as kind as can be, and he may still give nothing back. But friendship can only exist where the other person responds.

So the question in front of us is not whether Christ loves us, or whether he has pity on us. In another part of Scripture we read about “his great love with which he loved us even when we were dead in our wrongdoings and sins.”

He was a friend to us when we were his enemies. But that is not our subject right now. The question is whether we are friends to him. We must be made his friends if there is going to be a close friendship on both sides.
As I said before, friendship cannot be only one-sided. It is like a pair of scales. There must be something to balance the other side. The person who is loved must give kindness back.
Here Jesus tells us that if we want to be his friends, we must do whatever he commands us. And we must do it because we love him.
Dear friends, the greatest honor in the world is to be called a friend of Christ.
Surely no title is greater than the one Abraham had. He was called “The friend of God.”
Lord Brooke was so happy to be friends with Sir Philip Sydney that he ordered only these words to be carved on his tomb: “Here lies the friend of Sir Philip Sydney.”
There is something beautiful about that feeling. But it is a small thing compared with being able to say, “Here lives a friend of Christ.”
How amazing that he would come down so low as to call me “friend”!

If I truly believe in him, then he is my friend, and without that I would have no hope, now or ever. But more than that, in his overflowing grace he has chosen to count me as his friend. He has written my name on the honored list of his close friends. These friends are allowed to talk with him freely, like people who keep no secrets from each other. They pour out their hearts to him, and he hides nothing from them. He says, “If it were not so, I would have told you.”
Dear friends, think how this changes the way we see obeying Christ’s commands!
Even this early in the sermon, I cannot help pointing out how the teaching of our verse transforms obedience. It makes obedience the joy and glory of life.
Obedience is so precious. It is a better sign of friendship than having the greatest talents and influence.
Christ does not say, “You are my friends if you rise to an important position among people, or to honor in the church.”
No. However poor you are—and the people he said these words to were very poor—he says, “You are my friends if you do everything I command you.”
Obedience is better than money, and better than high position.
Jesus does not value his friends by what they own or what they wear. He values them by what they do.
We could say that all eleven apostles had remarkable gifts for their life’s work. Yet their Lord does not say, “You are my friends because I have given you the abilities to be apostles.”
Even to these leaders of his holy army, Jesus says plainly, “You are my friends if you do everything I command you.”
That is how your friendship will be tested: “If you obey, you are my friends.”
He says no less and no more to any of us today who long for the great honor of being inside the circle of his personal friends.
My brothers and sisters, you must obey your Master and Lord, and be eager to do it. Otherwise you are not his close friends.
This is the one thing that is absolutely needed, and only grace can give it to us.
Do we fight against this request?
Not at all! Our joy and delight is to carry the easy yoke of the One we love.
I. Let us look at the subject more closely. First, notice that OUR LORD HIMSELF TELLS US WHAT KIND OF OBEDIENCE HE WANTS from those who call themselves his friends.
True friends are eager to know what they can do to please the people they love. So let us gladly listen to what our wonderful Lord now says to the special circle of his chosen ones.
He asks every single one of us to obey.
None of us is excused from doing what he commands.
Whether our position is high or low, we must obey. If we have only one talent, we must obey. And if we have ten, we must still obey.
There can be no friendship with Christ unless each of us is willing to serve him loyally and with all our heart.
So let this message go around to all of you who carry the name of Jesus Christ. If you are counted among the friends of Jesus, you must take care to obey his good will yourself.
Do not forget that even the queen, standing at his right hand in gold from Ophir, is told, “He is your Lord, so worship him.”
Notice this: it must be active obedience.
“You are my friends if you do everything I command you.”
Some people think it is enough just to avoid what he forbids.
Staying away from evil is a big part of doing right. But it is not enough for friendship.

A man may say, “I am not a drunk. I am not dishonest. I am not sexually immoral. I do not break the Sabbath. I am not a liar.” So far, so good. But that kind of goodness is no better than that of the scribes and Pharisees, and they cannot enter the kingdom.
It is good if you do not break God’s law on purpose. But if you are going to be Christ’s friends, there must be much more than this.
It would be a poor kind of friendship that only said, “I am your friend, and to prove it, I don’t insult you, I don’t rob you, and I don’t say bad things about you.”
Surely friendship needs more positive proof than that.
The Lord Jesus Christ puts great weight on the things we should actively do. He says, “if you do everything I command you.”
On the last day he will say, “I was hungry, and you gave me food. I was thirsty, and you gave me something to drink.”
In that well-known twenty-fifth chapter of Matthew, nothing is said about the bad things people avoided. Instead, the good things they actually did are listed and described in detail.
You know the old English saying: “He is my friend who grinds at my mill.”
In other words, friendship shows itself by doing helpful things. Those things prove that it is real.
Nice words are just air. They mean nothing unless they are backed up by real acts of kindness.
Friendship cannot live on empty talk. It needs the solid bread of real action.
God’s inspired word says, “Show me proof of your love. Show it by doing everything I command you.”
The wording of the verse makes it clear that the obedience Christ expects from us is ongoing.
He does not say, “If you do it on Sundays, for example—if you do what I command you at church, that will be enough.” No, we are to remain in him and keep his laws all the way to the end.
I am not saying now that good works are the way to be saved. I am saying they are the evidence that we have fellowship with him. That is something quite different.
In every place, at all times, and in every situation, we must try to do what Jesus tells us. We should do it with a cheerful heart that honors him.
A godly wife gladly and lovingly follows her husband’s lead. In the same tender way, we must gladly follow Christ all our lives if we are his friends.
This obedience must also cover everything.
“You are my friends if you do everything I command you.”
As soon as a true friend of Christ finds out that something is a command, he says, “I will do it.” And he does it.
He does not pick and choose which commands he will keep and which he will ignore. That is doing what you want, not obeying.
I have known some people who claim to be Christians go badly wrong in this.
They have been very strict about one thing. They have blamed everyone who was not as strict as they were. They talked as if that one duty was the whole law.

Many people have made a big business of straining out gnats. They have bought a fine set of strainers with the tiniest holes to get every gnat out of their cup. But on another day, those same people opened their mouths and swallowed a whole camel without a second thought.
That will not do. The test is, “If you do everything I command you.”
I do not mean that little things do not matter. Far from it!
If Christ tells you to strain out a gnat, strain it out very carefully. Do not let even a tiny midge get past you if he tells you to remove it.
The smallest command of Christ may often be the most important. Let me tell you why.

Some things are big, and everyone can see they are big. For many reasons, even a fake Christian will take care of them. But the real test may be in the small things. Hypocrites do not bother to notice those, because no one would praise them for doing them.
This is where your love is proved.
Will you do the small thing for Jesus as well as the big thing?
Too many people say, “I don’t see the point of it. I can be saved without it. People have lots of different opinions about it.” And so on.
All of this comes from evil. It does not fit with the spirit of friendship with Christ, because love wants to please even in small things.
Is it what Christ wants?
Is it clearly a command in his word?
Then it is not your job to ask why or to argue about it.
Whether you are really following your Lord and Master may depend on those small, unimportant-looking things.

Imagine a servant girl in a house. She might put breakfast on the table and think she has done her job. But suppose her mistress told her to put the salt at the corner of the table, and she did not. She would be asked why she had not done it.
Suppose she answered her mistress, “I didn’t think it was needed. I put the breakfast in front of you. A little salt was too small a thing for me to bother about.”
Her mistress might answer, “But I told you to be sure to put out the salt dish.
Make sure you do it tomorrow.”
The next morning there is no salt again. The maid says she did not see the point of putting it on the table.
Her mistress is unhappy. She tells the girl that what she wants must be done.
Wouldn’t she be a very foolish and annoying girl if she refused, just because she did not see the point?
I think the young woman would probably have to find another job before long, because that kind of behavior is very annoying.
It is the same with people who claim to be Christians and say, “I have taken care of the main things. What I skip is only a small matter.”
People like that are not even good servants. They can never be friends.
Dear brothers and sisters, I beg you, work hard at obeying in everything.
“Whatever he tells you to do, do it.”
Only by seriously trying to do everything he wants can you live in happy friendship with him and truly be his friends.
Notice carefully that we are to obey as if we were doing it for Christ himself.
Put the emphasis on the little word “I”: “You are my friends if you do everything I command you.”
We are to do these things because Jesus commands them.
Our Lord is a royal person. Doesn’t that show very clearly how necessary it is to obey?
When we refuse to obey, we are refusing to do what the Lord himself commands.
The Lord Jesus Christ is the Son of God and our Redeemer. When someone refuses to obey him, it is treason.
How can rebels against the King be His Majesty’s friends?
The commands in Scripture are not human rules or the orders of angels. They are the laws of Christ. How dare we look down on them?
We are to do what is right because Jesus commands us, and because we love to do what pleases him. There can be no friendship without this.
Oh, how we need grace to serve the Lord with gladness!
To finish this first point: it seems our Lord wants us to obey him in a friendly spirit.
If we obeyed Christ only because we were forced to, out of fear of pain and punishment, it would be worth nothing as proof of friendship. Anyone can see that.

He is not talking about slaves, but about friends. He does not want us to do our duties because we are afraid of punishment or because we want a reward. What he can accept from his friends must grow out of love.
His will must be our law because we delight in him.

Some who claim to be Christians have to be whipped into doing their duties. They need exciting sermons and thrilling meetings, and they have to live under pressure. But those who are Christ’s friends need nothing to push them except love.
“The love of Christ drives us on.”
True hearts do what Jesus tells them without being whipped and chased, pushed and forced.
Goodness that is forced is ruined while it is being made, just as many clay pots crack while they are being baked.
The wine of our obedience must flow freely from the ripe grapes of the soul’s love. Otherwise it will not be good enough for the King’s cup.
When duty becomes a delight, and God’s commands are as sweet as his promises, then we are Christ’s friends. Not before.
II. So I have explained what kind of obedience Christ asks for. Now, in the second place, notice that our Lord leads us to conclude from this verse that THOSE WHO DO NOT OBEY HIM ARE NOT HIS FRIENDS.

He may still look on them with kindness and become their friend by changing their hearts and forgiving their sins. But for now they are not his friends. A man who does not obey Christ does not give the Savior his rightful place, and that is an unfriendly thing to do.
If I have a friend who is honored somewhere, I make very sure that he gets proper respect from me.
If he is above me in rank, I am careful that he does not think I am pushy. I do not want him to think I would take unfair advantage of his kindness.
I will think more highly of him than anyone else does.
The person who is truly Christ’s friend loves to honor him as a great king. But the person who will not give him his rights as King is a traitor, not a friend.

Our Lord is the head over everything for his church. That means the members of his body gladly obey him. Disobedience refuses to give Christ the honor of being the holy Head, which is his right over every member of his spiritual body. That is not how a true friend acts.
How can you be his friend if you will not accept his rule?
It is useless to boast that you trust in his cross if you do not honor his crown.
Anyone who does not keep his commands cannot be Christ’s friend, because he does not think the same way as Christ. That is obvious.
Can two people walk together unless they agree?

True friendship does not exist between people who disagree about the most basic things. And there can be no agreement between Jesus Christ and the person who will not obey him. That person is really saying, “Lord Jesus, I hate your pure and holy will. Your kind and gracious commands make me tired.”
What kind of friendship could that be?

They do not think alike. Christ is for holiness; this man is for sin. Christ is for a spiritual mind; this man’s mind is on worldly things. Christ is for love; this man is for himself. Christ is for giving glory to the Father; this man is for honoring himself. How can they be friends when they are completely opposite in their plans, their goals, and their spirit?
It is not possible.
The person who does not obey Christ cannot be his friend, even if he claims to be.

He may be a very important and loud churchgoer, and for that very reason he may be even more of an enemy of the cross. When people see him living for his own selfish desires, they cry out, “You were with Jesus of Nazareth too!” They blame all his faults on his religion. And right away they start to speak evil of Christ’s name.
Nothing holds back our Lord’s cause more than the inconsistent behavior of people who claim to be his friends.
Suppose you or I had a very close friend who was found drunk in the street, or caught breaking into a house or stealing. Wouldn’t we feel ashamed of what he did?
When he was taken before the judge, would you like people to say, “This man is the best friend of So-and-so”?
Oh, you would hide your face and beg your neighbors never to mention it.
If a man like that were known as your friend, it would damage your name and your reputation.

We say this with tears: the name of Jesus Christ is damaged, and his honor is stained in people’s eyes, by many who call themselves Christians but do not have the spirit of Christ. People like that cannot be his dear companions.
How sad are the wounds Jesus has received in the house of his friends!
When Caesar fell, it was his friends who stabbed him with their daggers!
Where he had trusted, he found betrayal.
The very people whose lives he had spared did not spare his life.
How terrible it will be for those who dress up as Christians but crucify the Lord all over again and shame him in public.
Nothing stings Christ’s cheek like a Judas kiss, and he has had many of those.
Jesus cannot claim those who disobey him as his friends, because that would truly dishonor him.

There was a time—I don’t know if it is still true—when any man who wanted to be made a count or get a noble title only had to pay a certain amount of money into the Pope’s treasury in Rome. Then he could be made a nobleman right away.
Titles bought like that brought no honor either to the people who gave them or to the people who got them.
Whatever the man who pretends to stand in Christ’s place may do, our Lord himself does not sell honors.
The title “friends of Jesus” belongs only to people of a certain character. There is no other way to get it.
His friends are the people who obey him: “If you love me, keep my commands.”
He gives this noble title to every believer who lovingly follows him. But he writes no one else’s name on his list of friends.
Can’t you see that his honor demands this?
Would you want our Lord to stand up and say, “The drunk is my friend”?
Would you want to hear him say, “That cheating bankrupt is my close companion”?
Would you want Jesus to call wicked and godless people his friends?
People judge a man by the company he keeps. What would people think of Jesus if his close friends were men with loose morals and wrong principles?
Going among such people to help them is one thing. Making them his friends is something else.
Where there is no family bond, no likeness, and nothing in common, the lovely flower of friendship cannot put down roots.
So we may also read the verse the other way around: “You are not my friends if you do not do what I command you.”
III. Here is my third point: THOSE WHO OBEY CHRIST BEST ARE THE CLOSEST TO HIM.
He seems to say, “You are my friends, and you live close to me, when you obey quickly. Then you enjoy real, personal friendship with me and talk with me every day.”
Brothers and sisters, some of you know from your own experience that you cannot walk closely with Christ in holy fellowship unless you keep his commands.
We feel no closeness between our souls and Christ when we know we have done wrong and are not sorry for it.

Suppose we know we have gone wrong, as we often do. Our hearts break because we have hurt the One we love. We go and tell him how sad we are and confess our sin. Then we are still his friends. He kisses away our tears and says, “I know how weak you are. I gladly wipe away your wrongs.
Our friendship is not broken. I will still show myself to you.”
But when we know we are wrong and our hearts do not soften at all, then we cannot pray. We cannot talk with the One we love. We cannot walk with him as his friends.
Closeness with Jesus ends when we get comfortable with sin we know about.
And if we know something is wrong but keep on doing it, there can be no happy friendship between us and our Savior.

Dear brother, suppose your conscience has told you to give up a certain thing, but you keep on doing it. The next time you kneel to pray, you will feel held back. You may sit down with your Bible open, hoping to have the kind of closeness with Christ you used to enjoy. But you will find that he has pulled back and will not let you find him.
Is that any surprise?
If sin is lying at the door, how can the Lord smile on us?
Hidden sin will poison our fellowship with him right at the source.
If you and Christ are quarreling, and you are holding tightly to something he hates, how can you enjoy friendship with him?
He tells you that sin is a poisonous snake that will kill you. But you answer, “It is a necklace of jewels.” So you put it around your neck.
Are you surprised that, because he loves you, he is grieved by such crazy behavior?
Oh, do not hurt yourself like this.
Do not treat his wise commands with such contempt.
Some Christians will never have full fellowship with Christ because they do not bother to study his word and find out what he wants.
Every Christian should take it seriously to find out what his Lord wants on every subject, especially when he is just starting out.
Half the Christians in the world are happy just to ask, “What is our church’s rule?”
That is not the question. The real question is, “What is Christ’s rule?”
Some people say, “My father and mother did it this way before me.”
I partly understand that feeling. Honoring your parents is admirable. But in spiritual things we are to call no one “father.” We must make the Lord Jesus our master and our example.

God has not put your conscience in your mother’s care. He has not given your father the right or the power to answer for you. Everyone must carry his own load and give his own account to God. So each one of you, search the Scriptures for yourselves. Follow no rule except the one God has inspired.
Get your light straight from the sun.

Let the holy Scriptures be the rule you never question for what you believe and how you live. If there is anything you are unsure about, I urge you, by your loyalty to Christ, if you are his friends, try to find out what he wants. And once you are sure about it, pay no attention to any human leaders or important people who go against his law.
Do not question, do not hesitate, and do not delay.
If he commands you, do what he wants, even if the gates of hell thunder against you.
Unless you are determined to please him in everything, you are not his friends. Or at least, you are not the kind of friends who enjoy his friendship.
Sin will disturb the closeness between you and Christ. You cannot rest your head on his chest and say, “Lord, I know what you want, but I am not going to do it.”
Could you look up into that dear face—the face that was once so badly wounded and is now more beautiful than heaven itself—and say, “My Lord, I love you, but I will not do everything you want”?
If you give in to that rebellious spirit, he will discipline you for it, precisely because he loves you so much.
It is a horrible evil. Holy eyes cannot bear it.
He is a jealous lover. He will not put up with sin, because sin is his rival.
“You are my friends if you do everything I command you.”
Oh, dear friends, pay attention to this!
In all the hard times, the losses, and the trials of life, there is no better comfort than knowing that you have tried to do your Lord’s will.
If a man suffers for Christ while he keeps walking the path of holiness, he can be glad about that suffering.
Losses suffered while standing up for what is right and true are really gains.
Jesus is never closer to his friends than when they bravely put up with shame for him.
If we get into trouble through our own foolishness, the pain goes deep into our hearts. But if we are wounded fighting our Lord’s battles, the scars are a mark of honor.
For his sake we can accept insults and wear them like a crown of honor.
Jesus loves to be the Companion of those who are rejected by their family and friends because they stand for the truth and stay faithful to his cross.

People may call the faithful person a fanatic, a crazy enthusiast, and all kinds of ugly names. But there is no need to worry about that. The honor of being Christ’s friend is worth far more than whatever the world thinks.
When we follow the Lamb wherever he goes, the results are his responsibility, not ours.

blocks.x:
“Though my way is dark, since he is my guide,
My part is to obey, his part to provide.”

s: What happens as a result of our doing right is up to God.
Hate the idea that you may do a small wrong for the sake of a great good.
I have heard men say—yes, even Christian men—“If I followed my beliefs strictly, I would have to leave a job where I do a lot of good. So I stay where I am and keep my conscience as quiet as I can.
If I put everything I believe into practice, I would lose chances to do good that I have now. So I stay in a position that I could not defend for any other reason.”
Is that what Jesus thinks?
Is that how you show kindness to your friend?
How many people bow down in the temple of the idol Rimmon and hope the Lord will forgive them for it!
We will see whether he does.
We must not do evil so that good may come from it.

If I knew that doing right would shake this whole island, I would still have to do it. With God’s help, I would do it. And if I heard that doing one wrong thing seemed likely to bless a whole nation, I would still have no right to do wrong for that reason.
No bribe of doing more good should be allowed to buy our conscience.
Right is right, and it will always end in blessing. Wrong is wrong, and it will always end in a curse, even if for a while it looks like something wonderfully good.
Didn’t the devil lead our first parents astray by suggesting that great good would come from their disobedience?
“Your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods,” said the great deceiver.
Wouldn’t it be a wonderful thing for human beings to become gods?
“Of course,” says Eve. “I would not want to miss this chance.
The people who will be born after me would blame me if I did.
I would not want people to stay lower creatures because I did nothing.”
For the sake of the good she was promised, she dared to do evil.
Thousands of people sin because it seems so useful, so wise, so necessary, and so sure to turn out well.
Listen to what Christ says: “You are my friends if you do everything I command you.”
If you do evil so that good may come, you cannot walk with him. But if your heart is set on his laws, you will find that he loves you and comes to live with you.
IV. Fourth, our verse teaches us that THE FRIENDLIEST THING A PERSON CAN DO FOR JESUS IS TO OBEY HIM: “You are my friends if you do everything I command you.”
Rich men have thought that the friendliest thing they could do for Christ was to give a huge amount of money to build a church, or to start homes for the poor, or schools.

If they are believers and have done this to obey Christ’s law about managing what he has given them, they have done well. The more gifts like that, the better. But when big, impressive gifts are given to show off, or because people think they will earn credit with God by giving a lot of money, then the whole thing is unacceptable.
If a man gave all the wealth of his house for love, it would be completely scorned.
Jesus does not ask us to spend lots of money. He asks for us.
He has made this the sign of true love: “If you do everything I command you.”
“Obeying is better than sacrifice, and listening is better than the fat of rams.”
However much we are able to give, we ought to give it, and give it cheerfully. But if we think any amount of giving can take the place of obeying him ourselves, we are badly mistaken.
Bringing our money without giving our hearts is like giving someone the jewelry box and stealing the jewel.
How dare we bring our offering with a hand that is diseased with leprosy?
We must first be washed clean ourselves in the blood that pays for sin before we can be accepted. And our hearts must be changed before our offering can be pure in God’s sight.
Other people have thought they could show their friendship to Christ by some remarkable way of punishing themselves.
Roman Catholics, especially long ago, believed that suffering and earning credit with God went together. So men tortured themselves to try to please God.
They went for many days without washing themselves or their clothes. They imagined this gave them the “smell of holiness.”
I do not believe that Jesus thinks a man is more his friend because he is dirty.
Some have worn a shirt made of scratchy hair, or a belt of chain that rubbed their skin raw.
I do not think the kind Lord Jesus considers these things to be acts of friendship.

Ask any kind-hearted person if he would be pleased to know that a friend was wearing a scratchy hair shirt for his sake. He would answer, “Please let the poor person wear whatever is most comfortable. That will please me most.”
The loving Jesus takes no pleasure in pain and discomfort. Starving and wearing down the body is not something he taught.
John the Baptist may have lived a very harsh, simple life, but Jesus certainly did not. He came eating and drinking, a man among other people.
He did not come to demand the hard life of a hermit or a monk. If he had, he would never have been seen at feasts.
When we hear about the nuns of St. Ann sleeping sitting straight up in their coffins, it gives us no special pleasure. A kind heart would beg them to go to bed.

Some time ago I toured a monastery. Over each bed hung a small whip with many tails, called a cat-o’-nine-tails. I truly hope each owner used his to his own satisfaction. But I did not copy the idea and buy a couple for my sons. And I have not sent one to each of my special friends either, because I would never ask them to whip themselves to prove their friendship.
Our Lord cannot be pleased by pain that people invent and inflict on themselves.
These things are worship that people make up for themselves, and that is not worship at all.
You can go without food for forty days if you want, but you will not earn any credit with God by doing it.
Jesus Christ has not asked for this as the measure of friendship, and he will not count us as his friends because of it.

He says, “You are my friends if you do everything I command you.” But he does not command you to starve yourself, or wear rough sackcloth, or lock yourself away in a little room. Pride invents these things, but grace teaches us to obey.
Some people have thought that the highest form of holy service would be to join religious brotherhoods and sisterhoods.
They imagined they would truly be Christ’s friends if they joined “the Society of Jesus.”

I have sometimes asked myself whether it might be a good idea to form a group of Christian men joined together to live only for Jesus and to give themselves completely to his work. But the New Testament certainly never pictures special societies, sisterhoods, or brotherhoods apart from the great family of the church of God. You will not find any hint of Franciscans or Dominicans there.
All godly women were sisters of mercy, and all Christlike men belonged to the Society of Jesus. But we read nothing about the vows of monks and nuns.
Anything that Scripture does not command is superstition.

We are to worship God the way he wants, not the way we want. Suppose I gave myself completely to what Roman Catholics called “the religious life.” Suppose I got away from ordinary people and tried to spend all my time alone in deep thought. There would still be nothing to it, because the Lord Jesus never asked me to do it.
What he does ask is that we do whatever he commands us.
Why do people try to do things he never commanded?
Any schoolteacher will let me ask him about this.

Suppose he said to a boy in class, “Now it is time for you to get your slate and do your arithmetic.” But instead, the boy got out his handwriting book. Wouldn’t the teacher ask him whether he had understood?
And if a few minutes later he finds the boy writing, does he say, “You have written that line very nicely”?
Not at all. It hardly matters whether the writing is good or bad. Writing at all, when he was told to do math, is openly disobeying.
It is the same with you and me.
We may do something else and do it wonderfully well. Other people may say, “What a godly man he is!” But if we do not do what the Lord wants, we will not be his friends.

We may wear a piece of leather for a sandal and rough brown cloth for clothes, and give up boots and coats. But there is nothing holy about clothing. What really counts is doing what Christ has commanded.
Some people think it is a very friendly thing to do for Christ to go to lots of religious services in a building that has been set apart as holy.
They go to the morning prayers and the evening prayers. They keep more feast days and fast days than anyone can count.

Some of us would rather hold our worship each day in our own homes. It will be a terrible thing if family prayer is dropped in favor of church services. But many people think little of praying together as a family. They feel they have to go to the parish church or to some other building made by human hands. But no one should imagine that this is how Jesus becomes our friend.

We must not stop meeting together, as some people do. It is good to meet with God’s people as often as we can. But you can still keep adding more sacraments and more ceremonies. You can go to this service and then that service, until your heart is worn out from grinding away at the mill of outward religion.
“You are Christ’s friends if you do whatever he commands you.” That is a better test than going to early communion or daily mass.

So it comes down to this, dear friends. We must do God’s will from the heart in everyday life. We must do it steadily, carefully, without giving up, and cheerfully, from the moment we wake up until we close our eyes at night.
About everything, ask yourself, “What would Jesus want me to do about this?
What does Christ teach about this?”
“Whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do it all in the name of the Lord Jesus, and give thanks to God the Father through him.”

You may be a household servant who can never give a pound to church work. But you are Jesus’ friend if you do whatever he commands you. You may be a housewife who cannot do anything outside your little family, because it needs all your attention. But if you are doing your duty to your children and doing what Christ commands you, you are one of Jesus’ friends.

You may be just an ordinary working man, or a shopkeeper with a small shop. Nobody has heard of you. But if you set an example of honesty, integrity, and godliness, and do everything for Christ because he has saved you, he will call you his friend.
What noble title could ever be as great as this?
Being Christ’s friend is worth more than being made a duke a thousand times over.
Here is what this all means in practice. Whenever you wonder what your duty is, test it with this one question: Will this be a friendly thing to do for Christ?
If I do this, will I be acting like Christ’s friend?
Will what I do bring him honor?
If so, I am glad.
If it will bring him shame, I will have nothing to do with it.
As far as you can, put each separate action on the scales. Let this be the weight you measure it with: Is this a friendly thing to do for my Redeemer?
I wish we all lived as if Jesus were always with us. I wish we lived as if we could see his wounds and look into his lovely face.

Suppose that tomorrow you are tempted, because someone asks you to do something questionable. Decide it this way. If Jesus could walk in at that very moment and show you his hands and his feet, how would you act in front of him?
Behave the way you would if you could truly feel that the One you love most was right there with you.
You would not do anything unkind to him, would you?
Of course you would not do anything to hurt him if you could see him in front of you.
Well then, keep him in front of you all the time.
The psalm writer cried out, “I have set the Lord always before me.”
You will need a great deal of the Holy Spirit’s anointing to do this.
May God give it to you.
Dear friends, live as if Christ might come right now and catch you in the very act.
Only do things you would not be ashamed of if, the very next moment, you saw the Lord sitting on his glorious throne and calling you to stand before him to be judged.
If you live like this, you will delight in peace that overflows.

blocks.x:
“Then your walk with God will be close,
Your heart calm and at rest;
Then clearer light will show the road
That leads you to the Lamb.”

s: Obeying will make you glad, because you will enjoy the wonderful presence of your Lord. And in his presence you will find complete joy.

All wise people will envy you, because you will be loved by the Lord. Your path may not always be smooth, but it will always be safe. Jesus never leaves his friend. He will never leave you, but he will keep you right to the end.
May this be my happy experience and yours. Amen.
“You, Israel, are my servant. You are Jacob, whom I have chosen. You are the family of Abraham, my friend.”—Isaiah 41:8.
“And he was called the Friend of God.”—James 2:23.
Abraham was called the Friend of God because he really was God’s friend.
The title just states a fact.
Abraham, the father of all who believe, was “the Friend of God” more than anyone else. He was also the head of the chosen family of believers whom Jesus calls his friends.
It is the right name for him.

The Bible tells us that “whatever Adam called each living creature, that became its name.” So we can be even more sure of this: whatever name God’s Spirit gives to someone is their true and proper name.
James does not only say that this was Abraham’s name. He says that people actually called him by it.

The name does not appear in the story of his life in the book of Genesis. People have even wondered whether it appears anywhere else in the Bible. That is because many prefer to translate the word in Isaiah, and in 2 Chronicles 20,
verse 7, as “lover” or “loved one” instead of “friend.”
Whatever the answer, one thing is certain: the Jewish people often spoke of Abraham as “the Friend of God.”
Even today, Arabs and other Muslims do not often say the name Abraham. Instead, they call him Khalil Allah, which means “Friend of God.” Or they simply call him El Khalil, “the Friend.”

Some tribes proudly say they come from him, through Ishmael or through the sons of Keturah. They greatly honor this great ancestor. They usually call him by the very name the Holy Spirit gives him here.
It is a noble title. All the grand titles that kings have ever handed out could not match it, not even if one person had them all.
Official titles of nobility are worthless next to this amazing honor.
I think I can hear you saying, “Yes, Abraham reached a very high level. It is so high that we could never get there.
It would be pointless for us even to dream of being counted as God’s friends.”
My brothers and sisters, please do not think like that.
We can be called friends of God too. My goal this morning is to make you want to know this wonderful friendship.
Let me read you what our blessed Lord said in John chapter 15: “If you do whatever I tell you, you are my friends.

From now on I will not call you servants, because a servant does not know what his master is doing. Instead, I have called you friends, because I have shared with you everything I heard from my Father.”
So this friendship is within our reach. Jesus himself invites us to live and act and be his friends.
Surely none of us will ignore any gift of grace that is possible for us to reach.
None of us will be satisfied with just a little grace when we can have life to the full.
I hope you are not foolish enough to say, “If I can just barely make it into heaven, I don’t care what kind of person I am along the way.”
That would be wicked talk. And if you talk like that, I am afraid you will never get to heaven at all.
A person who is being made ready for glory is always hungry for as much grace as possible.
Someone who is born of God wants his Father’s love while he is still a child. He has no plan to wait for it until he grows up and receives his inheritance.
Let me have as much of heaven as I can, even now.
Yes, let me be the friend of God right now.

Not long ago a boat full of people landed on the coast of France. They were soaked with rain and seawater. They had lost all their luggage and had nothing but the clothes they were wearing. They were very glad to have been saved from a shipwreck.
It was good that they landed at all. But when I cross over to France again, I hope I arrive in better shape than that.
I would rather cross the Channel comfortably and land happily.
That is the difference between being “saved, but only as if through fire,” and being given “a rich and full entrance” into the kingdom.
Let us enjoy heaven on our way to heaven.

Why not? We don’t have to be pulled out of the sea like shipwrecked people, washed up on the shores of mercy. Instead, let us buy a ticket on the fine ocean liner called Free Grace. If possible, let us travel first class. Let us enjoy every comfort of the trip and spend time with the great Captain of our Salvation.
Why should we be happy just to be stowaways who sneak on board?
Dear friends, I want to encourage you today to reach for the best gifts.
Grow in grace. Love God more, and come closer to him. Then the Lord may bend down to us right now as our great Friend, and lift us up to be known as his friends.
I have a lot to say to you this morning, so I must be very brief on each point. I am a little worried that I may have to be so brief that I am not very clear.
First, I ask you to notice this amazing title: “Friend of God.”
After we have thought about it and been amazed, I will move to my second point: the title proven right. It was a fitting and proper title for Abraham, and we can see why.
Third, I will talk about the title as something to seek.
May we all win it and wear it!
After all that, I will finish with a few words about how to use this title in everyday life.
May the Holy Spirit kindly help me right now!

blocks.x: I. First, may God teach us as we look at the name “Friend of God” and see it as A TITLE TO MARVEL AT.

s: Admire and worship the God who stoops down so low that he speaks this way about a man like us, and calls him his friend.
Even the heavens are not pure to him. He found fault even with his angels. And yet he takes a man and sets him apart to be his friend.
O Lord, what is man, that you would even remember him? Or the Son of Man, that you would come to visit him?
Who in our sinful human race could ever deserve to be friends with Jehovah?
Only his grace can make it possible for anyone to walk with God as his close companion.
Here this great and glorious Friend shows pure love, because he has nothing to gain.
God certainly does not need friends.
You and I need friendship. We cannot always live alone and keep to ourselves. We are refreshed when a friend who thinks like us keeps us company, understands us, and gives us advice.
It is very foolish to trust ourselves to lots of casual acquaintances. But we are wise if we have found one faithful friend and know how to lean on him.
Friendship is one of the sweetest joys in life. Many people might have given up under bitter troubles if they had not found a friend.
But the all-sufficient God has no such need.
We know how sweet it is to share our life with a very close friend.
Can God have a friend?
Can he really want to open up his heart to someone else?
Can Jehovah share his secrets with a weak creature?
Does the Holy One want to have fellowship with anyone outside himself?
He cannot be lonely. Within himself he is complete. He is one, and he is also three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. That is fellowship enough.
And yet look! The Lord stoops down so low that he comes to get to know his own creature. He seeks the love of a man, the friendship of Abraham.

I don’t dare say everything I am thinking. But it is truly amazing that the Creator of heaven and earth looked to Ur of the Chaldeans to find a man. He set him apart for himself. He taught him and trained him until he made him his friend. Not even the cherubim and seraphim have ever reached that honor.
Friendship cannot be one-sided.
In this case, God wants us to know something. God was Abraham’s friend, but that was not all. Abraham was also God’s friend.
He received God’s friendship and gave it back.

In one way, Abraham was always someone God pitied and showed mercy to. But by his grace the Lord also lifted him to a different place. Abraham became someone the Lord was pleased with and delighted in.
God gave Abraham his heart, and Abraham gave God his heart.
Their hearts were joined together in love.
To use a vivid picture from Scripture, Abraham’s soul was tied up in the bundle of life with the Lord his God.
The Lord spoke to Abraham the way he spoke to Moses, “face to face, like a man talks with his friend.” But more than that, he always treated Abraham as his friend and talked with him as a friend.

blocks.x:
“Amazing grace of the Most High!
Look what the Lord has given to worms:
Called to the council of the sky,
And counted with the friends of God!”

s: Friendship makes the two friends somewhat equal.

I am not saying that friends must be completely equal. A great king can have a loyal friend who is one of his lowest subjects. But friendship tends to bring the two friends closer to the same level. One gladly comes down, and the other rises up because they care about each other.
Friendship leads to fellowship, and that builds a bridge over the gap between them.
There can be no thought of God the Lord and man the servant being equals. In fact, we can only be his friends when we see that we are truly his servants.
Didn’t Jesus say, “If you do whatever I tell you, you are my friends”?
We must remember our place, or we will not be friends.

But look how the Lord comes down to Abraham and has fellowship with him at his table. At the same time he lifts Abraham up to his own level. Abraham sees the things of God. He even sees the day of our Lord Jesus Christ, and he is glad.
When we say two men are friends, we put them in the same group. But how amazing that the Lord would stoop down to be friends with a human being!
I say it again: no noble rank can compare with this.
Parmenio was a great general. But people forget all his fame as a soldier, because he was known as the friend of Alexander.
He loved Alexander as a person, while others only cared about him as a conqueror and a king. Alexander saw this, so he relied heavily on Parmenio.
Abraham loved God for who God is, and followed him completely. So the Lord made him his trusted friend. He enjoyed showing himself to Abraham and trusting him with his holy words.
O Lord, how wonderful is your loving kindness, that you would make a man your friend!
I also want you to notice how unusually good Abraham was.
How could he have been God’s friend if grace had not done amazing work in him?
People are known by their friends. You can’t help judging someone by the company they keep.
Wasn’t it a big risk for God to call any man his friend? After all, we tend to judge God’s character by the character of the man he chooses as his friend.
Yes. Abraham was a man with feelings just like ours. He had weaknesses, and the Holy Spirit did not hesitate to write them down. Even so, Abraham was a remarkably admirable person.
God’s Spirit gave him deep sincerity, firm principles, and a noble way of carrying himself.
He was a simple man who lived in tents. Yet the father of all believers always comes across as truly royal.
A calm dignity surrounds him, and the Hittites and the kings of Egypt feel its power.
His character is well balanced.
He is what people call a well-rounded man.
He walks with God and is blameless among the people of his time. So God is not ashamed to be called his God.

I could almost say about Abraham’s life in general that, like the Lord, he was light, and there was no darkness in him at all. Of course, I only mean this in the way our Savior meant it when he talked about the whole body being full of light, “with no part dark.”
(Luke 11:36.) Father Abraham is a man fit to be the head of the family of believers.
His quiet son Isaac is like a valley. His father rises above him like a mountain in the Alps, because his character is so much stronger.
He also stands above his famous grandson Jacob, even though Jacob had a great personality.

Jacob is full of fuss and worry and worldly scheming, and this somewhat hides his faith, which was certainly great. But you don’t see this in Abraham. He moves along his path like a king, shining like the sun at noon. Before him even clouds become chariots of glory.
I am not saying Abraham deserved to be called the Friend of God because he earned it. But I am saying that God’s grace had made him fit to share fellowship with the God of light.
He was made right with God by his faith. But when the Lord called him righteous, his actions also proved the Lord right.
James asks, “Wasn’t our father Abraham declared right by his deeds, when he laid his son Isaac on the altar?”
Yes, he was. This great act of obedience proved that he was in a right relationship with God.
His being declared right was itself proven right.
God was fair, even in a legal sense, when he declared a man like this to be righteous. After all, he clearly was righteous.
Oh, I pray that the Spirit who makes us holy will prove our faith is real by the holy lives we live!
Come with me as I point out some of the ways this friendship with God showed itself.
The Lord often visited Abraham.
Friends always visit each other.

We read, “The word of the Lord came to Abram in a vision.” We read, “The Lord appeared to Abram.” And again, “The Lord appeared to him in the plains of Mamre, while he was sitting at the door of his tent in the heat of the day.”
Three mysterious visitors came to Abraham. He welcomed them to his tent under the tree, prepared a feast for them, and served them at the table himself.
Wasn’t he honored above everyone else, to have God himself as his guest?
The Lord stayed with Abraham while he lived as a stranger in a foreign land. Day after day he heard the prayers and praises of his servant.

For his part, Abraham was quick to build altars to the Lord. He also had a special place where he met with God in private. We read, “Abraham rose early in the morning and went to the place where he had stood before the Lord.”
The great Lord and his trusting servant often came close to each other.
Because of these friendly visits to Abraham, secrets were shared.
The Lord told Abraham what he planned to do about the Canaanites. In the end they would be destroyed, but their sin had not yet reached its full measure.

He told Abraham that Isaac would be born. He told him that the blessing of the covenant would pass down through this child, who was born because of God’s promise. And when he had decided to destroy Sodom and Gomorrah, the Lord said to himself, “Should I hide from Abraham what I am about to do?”
I suppose it is only someone’s added comment. But Philo quotes this verse from the Septuagint and gives it like this: “Shall I hide this thing from Abraham my Friend?”
The copies of the Septuagint we have today say, “Abraham my servant.” But the other reading is a very natural one.
It was special proof of God’s friendship that the Lord would not carry out his judgment until he had heard what Abraham had to say about it.
Abraham, for his part, kept no secrets. He opened his heart completely for his Divine Friend to look into.
Visits were made, secrets were shared, and so the friendship grew.
More than that, they made agreements.
On some great occasions we read, “The Lord made a covenant with Abram.”
Once, during a solemn sacrifice, a light passed between the pieces of the animals that had been cut in two.
Another time we read that God swore an oath by himself, saying, “I will certainly bless you, and I will certainly multiply you.”
The two friends shook hands and gave each other their word.
Here were a faithful God and a faithful Abraham, tied together in a covenant that could not be moved.
God trusted Abraham, because he said, “I know him. He will command his children and his household after him, and they will keep the way of the Lord.”
And Abraham knew his God and trusted him with no suspicion at all. So there was a strong friendship between them.
This friendship led to countless blessings.
Abraham’s life was full of mercies.
We read, “Abraham was now old, very far along in years, and the Lord had blessed Abraham in everything.”
Friends bless their friends, or at least wish they could.
Abraham’s Almighty Friend did not hold back any good thing from him.
Abraham was rich, and his riches were blessed. We can say of him, “The gold of that land was good.”
He was unusually blessed in everything he did.

Jacob compared himself with his grandfather and said, “The days of your servant have been few and hard.” And his life was certainly lived on a much lower level than the life of Abraham, the first of the three great fathers of God’s chosen people.
The Lord is a friend with no limit to how much he blesses his friends.
Once he has loved his own people, he loves them to the very end.
Through the grace of his Divine Friend, difficulties were blessings for Abraham, and trials were blessings too. Even the hardest test of all was the blessing that made him most noble.
Because Abraham was God’s friend, God listened to his requests and was moved by what he said.
Friends always listen to friends.
When Abraham begged God for Sodom, the Lord patiently listened as he asked again and again.
We can learn so much from the story of Abraham praying for Sodom!
How humbly he speaks! He says, “I have been bold enough to speak to the Lord, though I am nothing but dust and ashes.”
And yet how boldly he pleads! He even dares to say, “Will the Judge of the whole earth not do right?”
The way he prays deserves special attention.
It was not so much a prayer for Sodom as an argument with God—friend with friend.
If we were praying for London, we would naturally ask for God’s mercy. But Abraham takes a bolder approach. He appeals to God’s justice.

In fact, he is pleading not only for Sodom but for God himself: “You would never do such a thing! You would never put good people to death along with the wicked, so that the good end up just like the wicked. That is not like you!”
It is as if he cared even more about keeping God’s name from being dishonored by something that might look unfair than about saving the guilty people.
That was a bold move.
He pleaded more as a friend of God than as a friend of Sodom. And the Lord fully recognized the power of his friendly appeal.

Because of that prayer, Lot was rescued and Zoar was spared. In the same way, Ishmael had been given earthly blessings when Abraham pleaded, “If only Ishmael could live in your sight!” And Abimelech’s household had been healed when Abraham prayed for them.
These friends also loved each other and delighted in each other.
Abraham rejoiced in Jehovah!
God was his shield and his very great reward. And the Lord himself loved to spend time talking with Abraham.
Abraham’s life was peaceful because he was always joyful in God.
I don’t have time to go into this wonderful subject now.
But notice that this friendship stayed strong and steady.
The Lord never abandoned Abraham. Even when Abraham made mistakes, the Lord remembered him and rescued him.
He did not throw him aside when he was old.
God was his God until Abraham was buried in the Cave of Machpelah. Yes, and God is still his God today. Didn’t God announce himself to Moses as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob?
Abraham is alive, and God is still his God.
Faithfulness is also seen on the human side of this famous friendship. Abraham never turned away to worship any false god, and the Lord never turned away from the man he had chosen.
More than that, the Lord kept up his friendship with Abraham by being kind to his descendants.
That is what our first Bible text tells us.
The Lord called Israel, even rebellious Israel, “The family of Abraham my friend.”

You know how David looked for Jonathan’s descendants and was kind to them for Jonathan’s sake. In the same way, the Lord loves believers, who are the children of believing Abraham. And he still looks for the children of his friend Abraham so he can do them good.
In the last days he will save the actual nation of Israel. The natural branches of the olive tree, which have been broken off for a while, will be grafted back in.
God has not forgotten his friendship with their father Abraham. So he will come back in love to Abraham’s descendants and be their God again.
So I have looked briefly at enough facts to show why this title, “The Friend of God,” is something to marvel at.

You have all admired the friendship of Damon and Pythias. But here is an even greater wonder: the friendship between the Lord God and Abraham. In this friendship Abraham gave more than his own life to prove he was loyal. And the great God was even more faithful than he was.
II. Now let us look at THE TITLE PROVEN RIGHT.
Abraham truly was the Friend of God.
The name fit him perfectly and was full of meaning.
First, Abraham trusted God completely.
To show you what I mean, let me tell you about the patriarch Job.
Job was a great believer. In some ways he “reached the level of the first three.” But Job still argued with God. He found it hard to believe that the Lord was treating him fairly.

In spite of all his questions, he could say, “Even if he kills me, I will still trust him.” But his soul was tossed about and turned upside down. And his three friends kept filling his head with doubts.
Their ideas troubled him. And Job was not as firmly settled as he could have been in the truth that God rules over everything.
Abraham had no such argument with God. “He did not stumble.”
David, too, was sometimes troubled by unbelief, so that he almost came to the same conclusions as an unbeliever.
He could not understand why the wicked did so well while he himself was punished every morning.
He went down into the fog of the valley. But Abraham usually walked on the hilltops.
His face was bathed in the sunlight of Jehovah’s love. He lived above all questions and distrust.
What a happy man, who never doubted but believed like a hero!
There is a blessed kind of not-knowing that my soul longs for.
Knowing things is not always a gain.
What a fool I am! Too often I have eaten the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.
I wish I could forget everything I have ever been told that makes me doubt my great Lord and his faithful word.
If I can, I will forget all human ideas, because they are empty. I am determined that among you I will know nothing but Jesus Christ, and him crucified.
Abraham had a higher kind of knowledge. It stomps unbelief under its feet, as something not even worth arguing with.
He was a perfect child toward God, and that is why he was a complete man.

If you do not turn around and become like little children, you will never get into friendship with God. This is what God requires most in his friends: that they never doubt him, but believe him without question.
Abraham “did not stumble at the promise because of unbelief.” He knew that the Lord was able to do what he had promised.
Along with this complete trust, Abraham had a practical confidence that everything God had promised would come true.

For a long time he had no children. He was tempted to think that he had to use human ways to make God’s promise happen, and for a moment he gave in. But even then he did not doubt that the promise would come true.
His big mistake actually showed clearly that he believed the promise would be kept. His fault was that he interfered with the way God planned to keep it.

When God told him to sacrifice his son, he never doubted that God would keep his promise. He counted on God being able to raise Isaac up from the dead. And in a picture, that is just how he received him back.
Faith means accepting things that seem to contradict each other, and believing what seems impossible, when Jehovah’s word comes first.
If you and I can do this, then we can enter into friendship with God, but not otherwise. Distrust kills friendship.
If the Lord brings someone close to himself, then at the very least that person must trust him completely.
“Whoever comes to God has to believe that he is there, and that he gives a reward to people who seek him with all their heart.”
If you think God could lie, you cannot be his friend. When you distrust him, you are setting your interests apart from the Lord’s interests and breaking the friendship.
Between people, it is possible to trust too much. But with God you can trust all the way, without holding back at all.
Believe without any limit, and then you will enjoy fellowship with the Lord.
Next, Abraham obeyed God without asking questions.
Whatever God told him to do, he did it quickly and completely.
The Lord said to him, “Go out from your country, from your own people, and from your father’s household, to a land that I will show you.” And off he went, not knowing where he was headed.

Later, the Lord told him to go to a mountain he did not know and offer up his son as a burnt offering. He got up early in the morning and traveled for three hard, painful days to the place where his faith would be tested.
Both his sense of right and wrong and his love as a father could have held him back. But he kept going, because he felt it was not his place to ask questions once the command was clear.
For him, Jehovah’s will was law.
Even now, not everyone has learned that God is the author of all law. It is his will that makes one path right and the opposite path wrong.
Abraham was God’s servant and also his friend. So he obeyed as someone who could see the invisible God, and he trusted the God he could not understand.
Above everything else, Abraham always wanted God to be honored.
He did not do what other people would have done, because he feared the Lord.
I think Abraham shows his greatness in the story where he chased the kings who had robbed the cities of the plain.
He defeated them and got back everything they had taken.

When Melchizedek, the priest of the Most High God, met him, Abraham right away gave him a tenth of everything. Then the king of Sodom suggested that Abraham keep all the goods he had taken back, and just return the people who had been captured. It was a great thing that Abraham would not touch even a tiny bit of the loot. Instead he said, “I will not take even a thread or a shoelace. I will take nothing that belongs to you, so that you can never say, ‘I made Abram rich.’”

He did not want some small-time prince, or anyone else, to brag that he had made Abraham rich. He trusted in his God alone. He had every right to keep what he had captured in battle. But he would not touch it, in case it brought even the smallest dishonor to the name of his God.
Abraham was always in close fellowship with God.
What a happy man! He lived up on the heights, while other people crawled in the dirt at his feet.
What joy he knew in those early morning talks with God!
What peace he felt all day long, in his tent and out on the plain, because he walked before the Lord and was wholehearted toward him!
Whether he was with the desert tribes or with his own servants, you see the man of God more than the tribal chief, and the friend of God more than the prince.
Oh, I pray that you and I may be made clean and live such a pure, holy, and noble life that we too can rightly be called Friends of God!
III. Third, dear friends, please be patient with me while I encourage you to see this name as THE TITLE TO SEEK.
Oh, may we receive this high honor, this diploma: “Friend of God”!
Do you want to be a friend of God?
Well then, first you must be completely at peace with him.
Of course, you cannot stay his enemy and be his friend. That is obvious.

If you are forgiven through the sacrifice of Jesus, if you are made right with God by his righteousness, and if you are born again by his Spirit, then you are no longer God’s enemy. But that alone does not give you the right to be called the friend of God.
It gives you the right to call God your friend and your helper. But if you want to be his friend, you must go further than that.
Love must be created in your heart. Thankfulness must grow into loyalty, and loyalty must turn into delight.
You must be glad in the Lord and stay in close touch with him.
To be friends, both sides must choose each other. The God who has chosen you must be chosen by you.
You must choose God to be your God and your friend, on purpose, with all your heart, firmly, and without holding anything back.
Dear friends, there can be no friendship between you and God unless you fully agree to it and deeply want it.
What do you say to that?

When sin is forgiven, there is no longer any reason for being enemies. But now grace must come in and rule through righteousness, leading to eternal life. It must bring you to a place of tender love and burning desire for the Lord our God.
But you have not gone far enough yet.
If we are going to be God’s friends, our heart, our will, our goals, and our character must be shaped to match God.
How can two people walk together if they do not agree?
Will God accept someone as his friend who looks down on holiness, who does not bother to obey, who does not care about the plans of God’s love, and who finds no joy in the good news of Christ?
Dear friends, the Holy Spirit must make us like God. Otherwise we cannot be God’s friends.
We must love Jesus the Son, or we cannot love the Father.
We cannot reach the level of being God’s friends if selfishness controls us. God is not selfish, and he is not a friend of selfish people.
Unless we love what God loves and hate what God hates, we cannot be his friends.
For the most part, our lives must run alongside the life of our kind, holy, and loving God. Otherwise we will be walking against him, and he will walk against us.
If we have come that far, the next step will surely follow: we must be in constant contact with him.
A friend of God must not spend a single day without God. He must not start any task without his God.
Oh, to live with God, and in God, and for God, and like God!
You cannot be God’s friend if you only spend time with him now and then, in fits and starts, from a distance, with lots of gaps.
If you only think about him on Sundays or at baptism and Communion, you cannot be his friend.
Friends love being together. The friend of God must stay in God and walk with God. Then he will live in peace and safety.
What do you say to that?
Has God’s grace made your feet like the feet of a deer, so you can stand on such high places?
He can do it.
Let us go after this blessing.
Brothers and sisters, if we are going to be God’s friends, we must be his partners.
He gives us everything he has. And friendship with God means that we must give him everything we have.
Someone once said it well: if God is ours, we cannot be poor, because God owns everything, and when we have God, we have everything.
On the other hand, God’s cause should not be poor if we can make it rich. His work should never run short if we can provide what it needs.
If we really are the Lord’s friends, we see his cause as our cause and his work as our work. We put everything we have into a shared bank account with the great God who is All in all.
